# INTRODUCTION.

## PART I.

### THE TEXT OF TERTULLIAN.

In preparing an Edition of a portion of the works of <term>Tertullian<note>Quintus Septimius Florens Tertullianus (c. 155 – c. 220 AD) was a prolific early Christian author from Carthage and the first to produce a large corpus of Latin Christian literature.</note></term> for the Press, the first point to which my attention was naturally directed was the condition of the text.

Of the various Editions which have appeared of the works of this author and of the <term>MSS.<note>An abbreviation for manuscripts—handwritten copies of texts produced before the invention of the printing press.</note></term> used by the Editors, there is a copious account in the last Paris Edition^1 of Tertullian, published at the Migne Press, in 1844, and in the recent Edition of Oehler^2.

The history of the Text is this.

So early as 1485 a printed Edition of the *Apologeticus* <note>Tertullian's most famous work, the "Apology," a defense of Christianity against paganism.</note> appeared as an appendage to an Edition of Lactantius, and this treatise was frequently re-published, usually together with Lactantius.

I. **RHENANUS** <note>Beatus Rhenanus (1485–1547) was a prominent German humanist and classical scholar who produced the first collected edition of Tertullian's works.</note> was the first Editor of the *Works of Tertullian*. His Edition was printed at BASLE, 1521. He had the use of only two MSS., one of *Päterlingen* and one of *Hirschau*, of uncertain age^3. Rhenanus de-

The value of this Edition is greatly enhanced by the scrupulous fidelity with which <term>Rhenanus<note>Beatus Rhenanus (1485–1547) was a pioneering German humanist and a key figure in the history of classical and patristic editing.</note></term> professes to have transcribed from the **manuscripts**$^4$: particularly as Rhenanus considered the state of the text hopeless, and almost abandoned the task of editing it in despair$^5$. This Edition did not contain several treatises which have since appeared as part of Tertullian's Works. Among these are the books *On Public Shows* <note>original: "De Spectaculis"</note> and *On Idolatry* <note>original: "De Idololatria"</note>. So that the *On the Soldier's Crown* <note>original: "De Corona Militis"</note> is the only one of the three, here published, which is found in the first Basle Edition. Rhenanus added a few notes, and affixed *Definitions of Ecclesiastical Dogmas* <note>original: "Definitiones Ecclesiasticorum Dogmatum"</note>, as an antidote to any heterodox opinion of Tertullian. There were reprints of this edition in 1525, 1528$^6$, 1536.

In the year 1539, Rhenanus, with the assistance of <term>Gelenius<note>Sigismund Gelenius (1497–1554) was a Czech scholar who worked closely with the Froben publishing house in Basle and was known for his skilled, though sometimes bold, textual corrections.</note></term>, published a second Edition of Tertullian at Basle. The same works of Tertullian are in this as in the former Edition; but Rhenanus, who begins to take heart as to his task, seems to have given up the scrupulous fidelity he professes in the former Edition. In 1545, **GANGNÆUS** <note>Jean de Gagny, a French scholar and chancellor of the University of Paris.</note> first published at Paris, together with the works previously known, nine fresh treatises of Tertullian, including *On Public Shows* <note>original: "De Spectaculis"</note> and *On Idolatry* <note>original: "De Idololatria"</note>$^8$. What manuscripts **Gangnæus** used is not known$^9$.

**GELENIUS** in 1550, at Basle, published a complete Edition of the works of Tertullian, ‘revised’ (he tells us) ‘by reference to several manuscripts from various parts of Germany and France,’ but especially to the *British Codex* <note>original: "Codex Britannicus"</note>. This manuscript, which **Gelenius** calls by far the most uncorrupted <note>original: "longe incorruptissimus"</note>, contained only three of the works of Tertullian published by **Rhenanus**, namely: *On the Prescription of Heretics* <note>original: "De Præscriptionibus"</note>, *On the Resurrection of the Flesh* <note>original: "De Resurrectione Carnis"</note>, and *On Monogamy* <note>original: "De Monogamia"</note>; but it also contained all the treatises first published by **Gangnæus**$^{10}$.

There were reprints of this Edition at Basle in 1562, and at Paris in 1566.

In 1580 an Edition was published at Paris by **Barræus**

II. **PAMELIUS** <note>Jacques de Pamele (1536–1587) was a Belgian theologian known for his systematic organization of Tertullian's works.</note> rendered most important services to the text of <term>Tertullian<note>Tertullian (c. 155 – c. 220 AD) was a prolific early Christian author from Carthage, famous for his complex style and for being the "father of Latin theology."</note></term>. His first Edition of his works was published at Antwerp in 1579. He employed especially three manuscripts from the Vatican, two from Belgium, and one from England (all of uncertain date¹¹). He revised the text and introduced many alterations—some from manuscripts, but some, as his notes tell us, from his own conjectures and those of others. He added some poetical works and fragments in Latin and Greek, not previously edited, and divided the treatises into their present chapters. He prefixed a life of Tertullian and the *Paradoxes of Tertullian with the Antidotes of Pamelius* <note>original: "Paradoxa Tertulliani cum Antidotis Pamelii." The "antidotes" were Pamelius’s explanatory notes to justify Tertullian’s more difficult or unorthodox statements.</note>.

The text of this Edition seems to have been preserved in the Editions of Paris, 1583; Antwerp, 1584; and Paris, 1585.

In 1587, **JUNIUS** <note>Francis Junius (1545–1602) was a prominent French Huguenot scholar and theologian.</note> published an edition at Franeker, adding his own notes to those of **Pamelius**, but scrupulously retaining the text of **Pamelius**.

The most valuable contribution which **Junius** made to the text of Tertullian was the collation of the *Fulda Manuscript* <note>original: "MS. Fuldensis." This was a famous manuscript from the monastery of Fulda in Germany.</note> (now lost), containing *The Apology* <note>original: "Apologeticus"</note> and *Against the Jews* <note>original: "Adversus Judæos"</note>. This collation had been made by Franciscus Modius of Bruges and was given to **Junius** by Gasper Schoppius. **Junius** considered that more than one manuscript had been used, but **Oehler** <note>Franz Oehler (1817–1866) was a German classical scholar who produced a definitive edition of Tertullian.</note> says that an observation of the various readings will show that only a single manuscript was collated.

# ON THE TEXT OF TERTULLIAN.

<columns>2</columns>

...was the Fuldensian <note>The Fuldensian manuscript, from the Abbey of Fulda in Germany, is one of the most important sources for Tertullian’s text, though it is now lost and known only through early descriptions.</note>, and that this was a manuscript of a family distinct from all the common manuscripts of these treatises.

The Pamelian Editions <note>Produced by Jacques de Pamele.</note> were repeated at Geneva, at Paris, at Franeker, at Heidelberg, at Cologne, in various forms, up to 1617, the date of the Cologne Edition.

**LA CERDA** <note>Melchor de la Cerda (1550–1643) was a Spanish Jesuit scholar known for his incredibly detailed commentaries.</note> published at Paris, 1624–30, two volumes of an Edition which was never completed. He gives no information as to the principle upon which he formed his text, but he appears, as far as I can judge from examining the treatises here published, to have taken Pamelius’ text, and introduced such emendations from the conjectures of himself and others, as seemed to him necessary for the explanation of the author. In many cases he has professedly altered the text on mere conjecture. His object was especially to illustrate and explain. **LA CERDA** made use of the Editions of **Rhenanus**, **Pamelius**, and **Junius**; and his notes contain most of their information enriched with copious illustrations, both from classical and ecclesiastical writers. The whole of the text is broken up into paragraphs, and to each paragraph is annexed (distinct from the notes) a paraphrase, wherein every difficulty is either explained or attempted to be explained. This Edition has been much used by Oehler and other Editors.

In 1625 the two Books *To the Heathen* <note>original: "Ad Nationes"</note> were first published at Geneva, by **James Gothofred**, from the *Codex Agobardi* <note>The Codex Agobardinus is a 9th-century manuscript given by Archbishop Agobard to the Cathedral of Lyon; it is a primary source for many of Tertullian's works.</note>, a manuscript of the 9th Century. The Editor presented the manuscript to the Royal Library at Paris, where it is still preserved. The manuscript is imperfect, but contains, among other treatises, the treatises *On the Shows* <note>original: "De Spectaculis"</note>, *On Idolatry* <note>original: "De Idololatria"</note>, and *On the Crown* <note>original: "De Corona"</note>.

*On the Shows* or *On Idolatry*. The *Clementine Codex* <note>original: "Cod. # INTRODUCTION.

<columns>2</columns>

III. **RIGALT** <note>Nicolas Rigalt (1575–1654) was a French classical scholar and librarian to King Louis XIII, known for his rigorous approach to textual criticism.</note> is the most distinguished of the Editors of Tertullian. He published his first Edition at Paris, 1634. The text differs widely from those which preceded it. The Editor premises that the text of Tertullian as it stood in all editions and most manuscripts extant, had been miserably corrupted by the alterations of scribes ignorant of the peculiarities of Tertullian, and that to obtain the true text recourse must be had to manuscripts earlier than these corrections. He does not set a high value on the manuscripts used either by Rhenanus or Pamelius, but conceives that his two great aids towards obtaining a genuine text were,

1. The emendations which *John a Wower* <note>Jan van der Wower (1574–1612), a Dutch scholar.</note> transcribed from the handwriting of *Fulvius Ursinus* <note>Fulvio Orsini (1529–1600), a renowned Italian humanist and librarian of the Vatican.</note>, in a manuscript preserved in the Vatican, and published in 1603, under the title of *Emendationes Epideicticæ* <note>The title translates roughly to "Demonstrative Emendations."</note>, stating that Ursinus had taken these corrections from manuscripts.
2. The *Codex Agobardinus*<sup>12</sup>.

Rigalt added notes, chiefly explanatory, mentioning only in a few cases the alterations he had made in the text, and the grounds upon which he made them. The alterations are very numerous. He sums up in an Index under the name of each Treatise the extent of his alterations. Thus, ‘*On the Spectacles* <note>original: *De Spectaculis*</note>. Corrected one hundred and eight times <note>original: *Emendatus octies et centies*</note> from the Codices of Agobard and Ursinus.’ ‘*On Idolatry* <note>original: *De Idololatria*</note>. Corrected one hundred and thirty times from the Agobard and Ursinus Codices.’ ‘*On the Crown* <note>original: *De Corona*</note>. Corrected seventy-eight times from the Agobard and Ursinus Codices.’

->### ON THE TEXT OF TERTULLIAN.<-

The text has also in many cases (as we learn from the notes) been altered from mere conjecture.

4 Besides, he used the *Puteanus Manuscript* and the *Fuldensis Manuscript* as compared <note>The text uses "collated," meaning to compare different copies of a text to identify variations.</note> by Junius; and a manuscript called the *Dijon Codex* <note>original: *Codex Divionensis*</note>, which in Rigalt’s opinion was of no great worth.

The text thus formed by Rigalt has been most widely accepted. Leprieur in 1661, says of it, "With unwearied labor, and with such diligence, he compared all the books with the ancient manuscripts, that nothing can be added, nor do we think that any gleaning remains to be done after so great a harvest." <note>original: "Labore indefesso, atque ea sedulitate cum antiquis codd. libros omnes contulit, ut nihil addi possit neque post tantam messem spicilegium ullum faciendum existimemus."</note>

It may, however, be remarked (1) that Rigalt’s conviction of the corrupt state of all manuscripts but one, inclined him to a very free use of corrections based on conjecture. (2) That of the numerous alterations he has made, he has seldom mentioned where he has the authority of manuscripts. (3) That he has in many cases adopted in the text readings that were admittedly conjectural; and (4) that his alterations rest mainly upon two sources, one the *Agobard Codex* <note>original: *Codex Agobardi*</note>, the other supposed manuscripts used by Ursinus, which he describes as "far better than those of Rhenanus" <note>original: *Rhenanianis longe meliores*</note>. A recent examination, however, of the manuscript in the Vatican, made for the Editor of the Oxford translation, 1842, has proved that the notes of Ursinus were merely conjectural emendations <note>Improvements or corrections made to a text by a scholar’s logical inference rather than from a physical source.</note>. See Preface to Oxford Translation, 13.

# INTRODUCTION.

Omitting one or two less important Editions, we come to that of *Priorius* (Le Prieur), published at *Paris*, 1664. This is the first of an intended series of Latin fathers, undertaken by a Society; but is the only volume which appeared. It was for some time considered as the *Best Edition* <note>original: *Editio Optima*</note>, containing all Rigalt’s notes, with selections of those of Rhenanus, Pamelius, La Cerda, and others, with some notes by the Editor.

Le Prieur adheres to the text of Rigalt.

The Editions of Rigalt and of Priorius were republished at various times and places.

These have been the sources from which subsequent Editions have in general been derived.

Of modern Editions we may notice that commenced by Semler at Halle, in 1769, and completed by Schutz. Semler in general restored the text of the first edition of Rhenanus, but also altered much from conjecture. Schutz followed the same plan, adopting the readings of Rhenanus and Pamelius, except where they were altogether intolerable <gloss>14</gloss>.

More important is the Edition published at the Migne Press at Paris, in 1844. The Editors profess to adopt as their basis the text of Le Prieur, that is of Rigalt, but at least as frequently they adopt the more ancient reading. They note the varieties of reading of various Editions in many instances; but this is very imperfectly done, and there are some errors. A selection

Finding that the record of various readings was very imperfect in the editions of Tertullian, I had, prior to the appearance of Oehler’s edition, compared <term>collated|The scholarly process of comparing different versions of a text to document every variation in wording or spelling</term> the editions of Gelenius, Pamelius, and Rigalt, as the representatives of the three sources of the text for the treatises *On the Spectacles* <note>original: "De Spectaculis"</note> and *On Idolatry* <note>original: "De Idololatria"</note>. I had not been able to procure the edition of Gangnæus, nor had I the opportunity of consulting any original manuscript <note>original: "MS."</note>. The appearance of the edition of Oehler, in which so much more was done in respect to the text than I could even attempt, rendered it quite unnecessary for me to complete my comparatively insignificant comparison. I have therefore made use of Oehler’s **Critical Apparatus** <note>original: "Apparatus Criticus"; the technical notes at the bottom of a scholarly text that list all the different versions of words found in various manuscripts</note> in order to determine the text which I should adopt, only noting such varieties of reading as seem materially to affect the interpretation of any passage. Those who wish for more particular information in this respect will find it in Oehler’s edition.

The text which I have adopted does not precisely agree with that of any edition that has hitherto appeared. The imperfections of the **Agobard Codex** <note>original: "Cod. Agobardi"; a famous 9th-century manuscript from Lyon, considered one of the most important sources for Tertullian’s writings</note>, which Oehler himself allows and notices, have led me to consider that somewhat too high a value has been set upon it. Where the other ancient sources agree, I have in general adopted the reading derived from them, although it is true that in the first two treatises here published, the sources are so few, that it may be fairly thought by many that one actual manuscript—and that ancient and good—should outweigh the authority of two or three whose readings are only known through early printed editions. But agreement even of only two or three manuscripts, if these are independent, as in this case there seems reason to suppose, has had with me the preponderance.

The principal purpose which this edition of three Treatises of Tertullian is meant to serve, is that of rendering this portion of a very difficult author intelligible to readers not familiar with his style. Niebuhr <note>Barthold Georg Niebuhr, a 19th-century historian of Rome</note> denies that there are any provincialisms to be found in **African Latinity** <note>A term used by scholars to describe the distinct style of Latin written by authors from the Roman province of Africa, such as Tunisia and Algeria</note>, and asserts that its peculiarity consists merely in the introduction of ancient phrases from the earlier Latin writers^17. And, as in early writers, like Lucretius, and in those who recurred to archaic phraseology, like Tacitus, we find constructions upon a Greek model, there is often a doubt whether particular expressions in Tertullian are to be set down to his imitation of early writers, or to his familiarity with the Greek language. It is remarkable that in the case of the other writer, who especially represents the African style (Apuleius), Greek was the language of his youth, and Latin was acquired afterwards by study^18, and Tertullian certainly wrote in Greek as well as Latin^19.

Independently however of any peculiarity of this kind, Tertullian’s writings are frequently obscure, not so much on account of his language as of his **mode of thought**^20. And in order to facilitate the study of his works it is quite as necessary to explain his arguments as to illustrate his **Latinity** <term>Latinity|The quality, style, or characteristic use of the Latin language by a specific writer</term>. ## PART II.

# THE PURPOSE OF THE THREE TREATISES: ON THE SHOWS, ON IDOLATRY, AND ON THE CROWN.

## CHAPTER I.

### *On the Date of the Composition of the Three Treatises.*

The date of the composition of these three treatises can be settled only by internal evidence <note>clues found within the text itself, such as mentions of specific events, rather than external historical records</note>. It has been generally assumed by those who have discussed this question, that the *On the Shows* <note>original: "De Spectaculis"</note> was written upon the occasion of some general exhibition of public shows, which brought the question of their lawfulness prominently into notice. Although this is far from improbable, the language of the treatise does not make it necessary. The supposed allusion¹ is far too vague to justify any decided inference from it. The subject of the shows and of idolatry must have been constantly before the mind of the Christian, so that it would require no special occasion to account for the appearance of such treatises. At the same time, if upon other grounds we conclude that these books were written within a period in which any such general exhibition took place, it will not be unreasonable to suppose that this circumstance may have been the immediate cause of their appearance.

The striking similarity of expression and mode of thought observable in these three treatises, incline us to assign to them dates not widely distant from each other, while the distinct mention of *On the Shows* <note>original: "De Spectaculis"</note> in *On Idolatry* <note>original: "De Idololatria"</note> (chapter 13), and the (at least) implied reference to it in *On the Crown* <note>original: "De Corona"</note> (chapter 6), determines the priority of order to *On the Shows*. *On Idol-*

# THE DATE OF THE THREE TREATISES.

<margin>² *On Idolatry*, chapter 19. ³ *On the Crown*, chapter 11.</margin>
The treatise *On Idolatry* <note>The source text reads "tria," likely a fragment of the Latin title *De Idololatria*</note> seems so closely connected with the *On the Shows* <note>original: *De Spectaculis*</note>, that we are naturally disposed to place it immediately after the *On the Shows*. In this we are confirmed by the more decided tone of Montanism <note>A movement in the early Church that emphasized new prophecy and strict moral discipline; Tertullian eventually joined this group</note> in the *On the Crown* <note>original: *De Corona*</note>, which marks a somewhat later period in Tertullian’s life. And the brief notice of military service in the *On Idolatry*² would scarcely have been unaccompanied by a reference to the fuller discussion of the same subject in the *On the Crown*³, had that treatise then been in existence.

If then we can ascertain the probable date of the *On the Crown*, we may, by taking a few steps backward, approach nearly to the dates of the other two treatises. We are not without means of ascertaining this. The first Chapter proves,

1 That it was written at a time at which there was more than one Emperor ("most excellent Emperors" <note>original: *præstantissimorum Imperatorum*</note>);

2 That the Christians had been long enjoying immunity from severe persecution;

3 That a donative <note>A monetary gift distributed to soldiers, usually to celebrate a transition in power or a military victory</note> had just been given to the soldiers.

Niger was defeated and slain in 196, Albinus in 197, and Caracalla was associated in the empire with his father Severus in 198. The *On the Crown* then must have been written in or after 198.

Some have supposed that the persecution, although begun, had not reached the East where the incident mentioned in the *On the Crown* <note>original: *De Corona*</note> took place; but it is improbable that Tertullian would not have known of the edict of 202, or that he would have written as he did without referring to it. We may also remark, that although the treatise tells of the punishment of the soldier as being a Christian, it does not imply that there was then any violent persecution raging. At all times under heathen emperors the open profession of Christianity would have met with punishment, especially in the case of a soldier acting against common discipline. And Tertullian’s hesitating admission of the possibility of a Christian remaining in the army without blame⁵ would not have been made in times of a public persecution. This then seems to determine the date of the *On the Crown* as not later than 202.

3 Having thus brought ourselves within four years, we examine the history of the times, and find records within these years of three acts of imperial liberality <note>Acts of "liberality" (liberalitas) were formal distributions of money or gifts from the Emperor to the public or the military</note>: (1) in 198, to the people when Severus set out for the East⁶; (2) to the soldiers, in honour of giving to Caracalla the title of Augustus, and to Geta that of Cæsar⁷; (3) in 202, when Severus and Caracalla were meditating an expedition into Egypt⁸. Of these three the second most accords with the case of Tertullian, the first being rather a <term>largess</term> <note>original: *congiarium*; a gift specifically for the civilian population</note> to the *people*, the third an increase of pay. ### THE DATE OF THE THREE TREATISES.

But it must be remarked that there may have been many minor distributions of donatives <note>donatives: gifts of money given by Roman emperors to their soldiers to ensure loyalty</note> not mentioned by the historian, any one of which may have been accompanied by the incident mentioned by Tertullian; so that the determination of the year is only conjectural.

If we are to consider that the two former treatises were written upon some public occasion, we may find one in the festivities which followed the overthrow of Albinus <note>Clodius Albinus was a Roman usurper defeated by Septimius Severus in 197 AD</note> in 198⁹. At all events the season of rejoicing, which followed upon the complete establishment of Severus' power, would call for such treatises; and we may therefore conclude, with a great degree of probability, that these three treatises were all written in the course of the four years following upon the defeat of Albinus.

It will be observed that I have drawn no argument from the Montanistic <note>Montanism was an early Christian movement characterized by a belief in new prophetic revelations and strict moral discipline</note> views which appear in the several treatises, excepting so far as affects their relative order.

The truth is that we have no certain means of determining the year in which Tertullian joined the ranks of Montanus, and, as Bishop Kaye remarks¹⁰ in answer to an insinuation of Gibbon <note>Edward Gibbon, author of "The History of the Decline and Fall of the Roman Empire"</note>, the determination of an early date to the *On the Crown* <note>original: *De Corona*</note> would only prove the early date of Tertullian's adhesion to Montanism.

There is no evidence as to the place from which any of these treatises were written. We may however infer from an expression in the *On the Spectacles* <note>original: *De Spectaculis*</note> that it was not written at Rome¹¹, and his strictures upon lax ministers in the opening chapter make the same probable of the *On the Crown*. It is most likely all three were written at Carthage <note>A major Roman city in North Africa, located in modern-day Tunisia, where Tertullian lived</note>.

## CHAPTER II.

->*The State of Pagan Society, and the resulting difficulties of a Christian.*<-

To understand the position of a Christian under the early Emperors, we must look briefly at some of the main features of the life and customs of the pagans <note>original: "heathens"</note> at this time. These were most visible in Rome itself, but every provincial town followed the example of the capital city, though at a distance.

1 The public amusements held an important place in the life of the community. When the wealth of conquered cities flowed into Rome, and the arts and luxuries of foreign nations were moved to Latin soil, this wealth and these arts were soon used to invent and increase public entertainments and shows. But this natural result of increased power was greatly encouraged under the Empire for other reasons. The policy of Augustus¹—to keep the citizens loyal by providing them with food and public entertainments <note>This refers to the famous concept of "Bread and Circuses" (panem et circenses)</note>—was followed by his successors. Many of them, such as Caligula, Nero, and Domitian, shared the public's taste and increased it through their own support and example. Some of the worst Emperors were originally corrupted by these entertainments², and supported them through the most shameful behavior; while the more sensible ones thought it wise to indulge the tastes of

the populace; as the wise Theodoric <note>Theodoric the Great (r. 493–526), the Ostrogothic king of Italy who maintained many Roman traditions.</note> deemed it not unworthy amid his graver cares to take thought for the amusements of the people³.

The three sources of public amusement were the chariot-races in the circus; the gladiatorial shows and combats with wild beasts in the amphitheatre; and the exhibitions of the theatre.

The passion for the chariot-race had taken early hold of the Roman people. Ennius <note>An early Roman poet (c. 239–169 BC) often called the "father of Roman poetry."</note> describes vividly the excitement caused by a chariot-race in his day (B.C. 170), and Ovid has more than one description to the same effect⁴. The madness of the circus had soon become proverbial, but the height to which this madness mounted under the emperors is almost inconceivable. Caligula, when the populace were clamouring against his favourite charioteer, wished that they had one neck, that he might destroy them all together⁵, and upon one occasion let loose a body of soldiers to massacre a crowd that shewed a similar opposition to his wishes⁶. The quarrels between two factions espousing different colours <note>The "Blues" and "Greens" were the primary competing teams in the circus, often linked to political and social identity.</note> led to frequent bloodshed. The imprisonment of a favourite charioteer was the occasion of an insurrection at Thessalonica⁷, and the murder of its governor, an act which was subsequently revenged by a massacre of the people at a chariot-race. And the <term>rescripts</term> <note>Official written replies or decrees by an authority to a legal question.</note> of Theodoric inform us that senators of Rome made no scruple of sending in armed retainers to deal out death to the populace when their favourite charioteers were assailed with taunts or ridicule⁸.

# INTRODUCTION.

The taste for gladiatorial shows was no less a national obsession for the Romans. This cruel diversion, which had originated in a primitive age of war and bloodshed, lost none of its attractions in the days of a false civilization and polished barbarism. Julius Caesar, when serving as an ædile <note>A Roman magistrate responsible for public buildings and organizing festivals.</note>, exhibited 310 pairs of gladiators. Titus gave shows lasting 100 days; Trajan hosted shows of 123 days, in which 10,000 gladiators were engaged. Nor were these shows, any more than the chariot races, confined to the capital city. Each provincial town had its own circus and its amphitheater. In every town of even the least importance, the arena was stained with the blood of men slain either in combat with their fellows or in contests with wild beasts. It is computed by Lipsius <note>Justus Lipsius (1547–1606), a famous Flemish scholar who wrote extensively on Roman history.</note> that in the time of Trajan, no less than 20,000 or 30,000 gladiators fell in each month throughout the year. "And these things they called delights and the food of the eyes!" <note>original: "Atque hæc delicias vocabant et cibum oculorum"</note>⁹

The theatre at Rome had at all times differed widely from that of Greece. Tragedy was but a tame copy of a Greek original, lacking most of its worthiest elements; comedy, even in the hands of Terence <note>A famous Roman playwright (c. 190–159 BC) whose comedies were based on Greek models.</note>, had aimed at little more than representing the productions of Athenian masters in a native dress. The Romans of the Empire did indeed delight in the theatres, but not to enjoy either tragedy or comedy. The age of Roscius <note>Quintus Roscius Gallus, the most celebrated comic actor of the Roman Republic.</note> was past. The very name of actor (*histrio*) was synonymous with that of pantomimist (*mimus*). These pantomimes resembled in some respects the modern ballet. A story was told through action accompanied by music, but without spoken words; "silent music," <note>original: "musica muta"</note> as Cassiodorus <note>A Roman statesman and writer of the 6th century AD.</note> calls it¹⁰. The pantomimists possessed great art in repre-

## THE STATE OF HEATHEN SOCIETY.

But the actions^11 were commonly such as involved the grossest indecency, and the wantonness and immodesty of these pantomimists was the constant subject of complaint with the graver sort of the heathens <note>The author uses "heathens" to refer to the non-Christian population of the Roman Empire.</note> themselves^12. Such were the theatrical exhibitions of Imperial Rome, varied by rope-dancing and such posture-work, and disgraced yet more by the grossest of all exhibitions—the public exposure of naked women at the Floral games <note>The Floralia was a festival in honor of the goddess Flora; it became notorious for theatrical performances where mimes and actresses stripped to satisfy the audience.</note>.

Besides these amusements, which had originated under the Republic, the Emperors encouraged games after the Greek fashion^13 <note>Nero, in particular, established the "Neronia," a festival of music, poetry, and athletics modeled on the Greek style.</note>. The introduction of athletes was indeed earlier than this. But Nero took the most decided steps to bring in the Greek form of contests, and was censured by some who regarded these foreign amusements as indicative of degeneracy^14. But the fashion grew, and in the vast <term>Thermæ</term> <note>Large public bathing complexes that served as central hubs for Roman social life.</note> built by successive emperors, the Stadium and <term>Palæstra</term> <note>A wrestling school or gymnasium, often part of a larger bath complex.</note> always had their place. We shall be little inclined to consider these amusements as degenerate in comparison with those of the circus, theatre, and amphitheatre. But their introduction was a mark of the entire abandonment of the populace of Rome to pleasure, and helped to make the life of the citizens a life of idle enjoyment and dissipation.

The vicious excitement, the barbarity and the impurity connected with all these entertainments, might well make them odious to those who had embraced the precepts of the Gospel.

...ness. They were bound up with a religion which had been forsaken and renounced. The games of the circus were introduced with a religious procession and sacrifices to the idols, placed in such numbers within the circus. The bloodshed at the gladiatorial shows was supposed to propitiate the god Dis <note>original: "Dis"; the Roman god of the underworld, also known as Pluto.</note>, whose altar was in the amphitheatre^15. The theatre was expressly dedicated to Venus <note>The Roman goddess of love, beauty, and fertility.</note>, being annexed to a temple of that goddess^16. Not to dwell on minor points, these circumstances were enough to brand all such amusements with the stigma of idolatry, which it was one of the main purposes of Christianity to overthrow.

2  The more serious occupations of heathen <note>A term used by the author to describe the non-Christian, polytheistic population of the Roman Empire.</note> life were of course connected in various ways with the state-religion. The very construction of idols, their shrines, and their temples, found employment for a very numerous body of men, like Demetrius <note>A silversmith in Ephesus who opposed the Apostle Paul because Christianity threatened his trade in making shrines for Artemis (Acts 19).</note> and those of his craft at Ephesus. The use of incense had created a traffic in which many were engaged; and, besides those who were solely devoted to the making and worship of idols, the goldsmith, the carpenter, the painter, the gilder, the plumber <note>In this historical context, a worker in lead (from the Latin *plumbum*), often involved in building or decorating religious structures.</note>, all found employment in their service^17. The professions too were equally allied to this service. Astrology and magic were practised and followed by numbers in the last days of superstition, and, notwithstanding their repeated banishment by different emperors, the astrologers were in high favour^18. The connexion of these arts with false worship is obvious. But other professions, less obviously idolatrous, were also bound up with idolatry. The schoolmaster had to teach heathen literature, to receive fees dedicated to heathen gods, and to keep heathen festivals^19. The duties of a magis-

# THE STATE OF PAGAN SOCIETY.

<note>The text begins mid-sentence, likely continuing from "the office of the magis-" on the preceding page.</note> trate required him to take the lead in pagan <note>original: "heathen"; referring to the non-Christian religious traditions of Rome.</note> processions and exhibitions, and to perform other acts which were by Christians deemed unlawful 20. The slave was often called upon by his master to assist in the household sacrifices 21. The rejoicings for victory or for the birthday of their rulers were celebrated with pagan rites 22. The common language of society, whether in swearing an oath, cursing, or blessing, involved an invocation of the gods of the country 23. All the events of life—marriage, the assumption of the *toga virilis* <note>The "toga of manhood," a white wool garment assumed by Roman boys around age 14 to 17 to signify their transition to adult citizenship.</note>, and the like—were mixed up ordinarily, though not necessarily, with sacrifices and idol-worship 24. The form of contracts prescribed in ordinary business included an appeal to the deities as objects of reverence and guardians of the sacred trust 25, while the insignia of office were the same decorations as those with which they decked out their idols. The military service in which so many were engaged gave rise to such duties as participation in sacrifices at the headquarters, bowing down before the images of Emperors, and putting on ornaments which were apparently idolatrous 26.

3 Much of the dress and decorations in common use was similarly mixed up with idol-worship. The insignia of magisterial office, the purple robes, the *fasces* <term>fasces: a bundle of rods bound together around an axe, carried by Roman officials as a symbol of their power to punish or execute.</term>, and the like, were the accessories of images and their service 27. The triumphal robes were worn by generals, by priests, and by gods. The most common ornament, the crown, used continually on every festive occasion, in the city and in the camp, was not only idolatrous in its origin 28, but the very occasions of its use were of the same idolatrous character. # INTRODUCTION.

...to a false god, recognized distinctly by the spoken formula used<sup>29</sup>. During triumphs <note>The "triumph" was a grand civil ceremony and religious rite in ancient Rome, held to publicly celebrate and sanctify the success of a military commander.</note>? The procession led to the temple of Jupiter <note>original: "Jove"</note><sup>30</sup>. At the public games? They too were considered idolatrous. Every public ceremony included offerings of thanks to the recognized gods of the country. Even the decorating of doors, windows, and similar things was commonly viewed as an honor to the guardian spirits <term>tutelary deities: minor gods or spirits believed to protect and watch over specific places or things</term>, such as Forculus <note>The Roman god of the door-leaves.</note> and Limentinus <note>The Roman god of the threshold.</note><sup>31</sup>.

In this way, the living—whether in military camps, the capital city, or the provinces—were constantly brought into contact with idols and their rituals; even the dead were adorned with decorations similar to those worn by the false gods<sup>32</sup>.

It must be remembered that for the Christians, the charge of idolatry encompassed all the sins of mankind<sup>33</sup>. It was seen as the one great offense of the human race, from which all other sins were merely branches and subdivisions. Murder, adultery, and fraud were all considered parts of this sin. Greed, lack of restraint, vanity, and injustice were its companions; and since every offense against God was viewed as an act of homage to the devil, every crime carried with it the guilt of demon-worship—that is, of idolatry. For the idols of the pagan world <note>original: "heathendom"</note> were not viewed as mere wood and stone, but were believed to be occupied and possessed by evil spirits, the servants of Satan. This belief was encouraged and confirmed by the pagan theory of consecration<sup>34</sup>, according to which a certain divine breath <term>afflatus: a literal "breathing upon" or supernatural inspiration</term> of Divinity came upon the images after their formal ceremony of dedication. This would naturally lead a Christian to believe that at such a time the evil spirits entered into the idols, and that worshipping them was therefore the worship of devils<sup>35</sup>.

Thus surrounded by idolatry, unable to enter the streets or marketplaces without seeing things which—

## CHAPTER III.

### *The different views of different parties in the Christian Church.*

The same treatises which draw attention to the position of Christians in a heathen state, discover a difference of sentiment in reference to this subject developing itself in the Church.

In the first stage of Christianity, the chief opposition to the cause was from the Jews. The heathen cared little for religious dogmas, while singularity of life and manners in a small body of men attracted only sufficient notice to excite the contempt of the community at large. But when Christianity began to make its way among the Gentiles, having ceased to be insignificant, it became odious to those against whom it lifted up the voice of condemnation. For it was soon understood that it involved a principle entirely subversive not only of the old worship, but of the most deeply-seated prejudices, and the most inveterate habits. In proportion as the new religion increased, the splendour of the temple-services declined, and the public entertainments became less thronged, and therefore less brilliant. These effects augmented the dislike that singularity commonly cre—

No sooner was he suspected, than he was accused, put to the proof, and if he failed to clear himself, condemned, and martyred. 

But when the still growing numbers of Christians made it highly inconvenient to hunt them out, and impossible to exterminate them, their opponents shewed a willingness to offer terms of compromise. When no violent persecution, such as from time to time broke out, was raging, they would suffer the Christians to abstain from such things as were absolutely opposed to their faith, content to wink at this abstinence, provided the Christians would on their part join in the common usages of life, and not obtrude their peculiarities upon those who disagreed with them. You need not, it was urged, participate because you are present at a sacrifice. You need not profess belief in the national gods, because your trades are connected with the service of these gods. Much less will you deny your faith by partaking in the national amusements, even although these amusements may accidentally be connected with the religion you have abandoned. Only let things go on as they are. Do not provoke enquiry by openly protesting against the customs of society, and you may be assured of liberty of worship, and indulgence in all graver particulars, provided

The offer of this compromise at once brought before the Christians the question, how far it was lawful to conform; and this question was variously answered by various parties within the Church. The one extreme was the view of those who glossed over all differences, took part in the amusements and employments of heathen <note>The term "heathen" refers to the practitioners of the traditional Roman polytheistic religion.</note> society, and even thought idol-makers fit to be received into the Church, and admitted freely to bear rule in it. The truth is, that between the two extremes was wide room for differences of opinion, and the determination of the golden mean <term>Golden mean: the ideal moderate path between two extremes.</term> was not arrived at immediately or with certainty. The true philosopher will recognize the vital power of Christianity, and trace its gradual conquest over the world, in obliterating the worst features of heathen society, sensible all the while that the conquest neither was consummated when the empire became nominally Christian, nor will indeed be completed until temptation, sin, and error shall be no more. # INTRODUCTION.

...tracts <note>Likely the end of a word like 'contracts' or 'extracts' from the previous page, or a reference to legal treatises</note> were, as a matter of course, materially altered when the empire became Christian, but we find many usages retained, which the Christians of an earlier age thought essentially idolatrous. Such, for instance, was the use of **chaplets** <term>Chaplet: A circular wreath or garland of flowers or leaves worn on the head, often used in ancient times for religious rituals or as a sign of honor</term>. The *Apologies* of Minucius Felix and Tertullian⁷ would convey the impression that the Christians universally abstained from the use of chaplets, and Tertullian speaks of the abstinence as the Christian rule⁸. But his treatise on the subject shews that there were Christians who demurred to this rule. And when the more obvious objection (viz. their use in heathen worship⁹) was removed, or at least became less prominent with the decline of Paganism, this scruple was generally given up, and the poet <note>Likely referring to Claudian, the court poet, though the citation is to a work on crowns</note> does not hesitate to call upon Stilicho <note>A high-ranking general of the Western Roman Empire (c. 359–408 AD)</note> to assume the chaplet at the nuptials of his son-in-law, the Christian Honorius¹⁰. And although the use of chaplets was actually forbidden by a **rescript** <term>Rescript: A formal decree or edict issued by a Roman emperor in response to a legal question or petition</term> of Arcadius and Honorius, Prudentius <note>A Roman Christian poet (c. 348–413 AD)</note> allows the use of flowers to deck the biers of the dead¹¹. We are more surprised to observe the change of sentiment that appeared in the Christian community. Even in the days of Arnobius <note>An Early Christian apologist of the 3rd century</note> the use of temples, altars, incense, flowers, and lights, was thought absolutely unchristian¹². But one by one each of these was appropriated to the service of God¹³, until at last the images of saints took the place of those of false deities. It is foreign to my purpose to point out the various stages in this progress, or to shew how idolatrous ceremonies were grafted upon Christianity. ### CHAPTER IV.
->*The views of Tertullian.*<-

<meta>This page continues the character study of Tertullian, focusing on his uncompromising nature and his rejection of any middle ground between Christian life and secular Roman culture.</meta>

the world and Christ <note>original: "De Spectaculis" (On the Spectacles), chapter 26; "De Corona" (On the Crown), chapters 10 and 12</note>. Any attempts to reconcile the two seemed to him unworthy and unlawful, and were the more suspected when they took the line which might have been suggested by the love of pleasure or the fear of man. To his ardent temperament the dangers and self-denial required for a certain course were its recommendation; and if on any point Scripture seemed less explicit than he would have desired, he would sigh for a yet stricter rule, and discover it by implication if not by letter <note>original: "De Spectaculis", chapter 3</note>, persuaded the while of the certainty of his deductions and of the present aid of the Spirit of Illumination <note>A term for the Holy Spirit providing direct guidance to the believer</note>. These feelings impressed themselves upon the method and the language of Tertullian, besides suggesting the particular topics that he selected. The vehemence of his temper and the strength of his convictions made him intolerant of opposition, and accordingly we find a strong vein of irony running throughout his works, whereby the views of his adversaries are represented as manifestly absurd. This is one striking characteristic of his style. Another is the love of paradox <note>A statement that seems self-contradictory but expresses a possible truth</note>, which is traced up by some to his education as a jurist <note>A legal expert or lawyer; Tertullian likely practiced law in Rome before his conversion</note>, but is probably at least as much owing to the eager hardihood, which led him to maintain the more resolutely every point assailed or assailable, and to believe with the more earnestness what was called incredible <note>original: "De Carne Christi" (On the Flesh of Christ), chapter 5: "it is not shameful, because it is a cause for shame—it is altogether credible, because it is inept—it is certain, because it is impossible."</note>. We must not then be surprised to find in Tertullian's writings many extreme views, and far-fetched arguments; but our judgment of him would be indeed superficial, should we insist upon the harshness of particular features, or be led by any ruggedness of manner and expression to disparage the inward spirit of the man. He had higher merit than that which Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea (c. 260–339 AD), often called the "Father of Church History"</note> accords to him as a

deep philosopher, an expert logician, a practised rhetorician, and a learned antiquarian⁵. Zealous, self-devoted, and thoroughly sincere, he was one who was seduced into error by his very desire to do and suffer for the truth,—no unapt representation of the stern old Roman character, which counted no toil severe enough, no obstacle great enough, to interrupt the straight course to national power and individual renown, only that Tertullian substituted for the love of country a love of Christ, and for the empty vision of undying fame, the more fair and more certain prospect of eternal happiness in heaven.

We shall find no difficulty in discovering the points in Tertullian's character that unhappily inclined him towards the errors of Montanus <note>A 2nd-century movement, also known as the "New Prophecy," which emphasized rigorous fasting, a desire for martyrdom, and the belief in ongoing direct revelation from the Holy Spirit.</note>. Not to enter into details upon the subject of Montanism, it will be sufficient to remark, that the feature of that system which proved attractive to so many, was its profession of a more perfect rule than that of the Gospel, more elevated in knowledge, and more austere in practice; this rule being established by direct communication of the <term>Paraclete<note>From the Greek 'parakletos,' meaning 'advocate' or 'helper'; a title used in the New Testament for the Holy Spirit.</note></term> to man, especially to Montanus and his associates. This principle was in fact the exaggeration of the truth that Christianity must be interpreted not by the letter but by the spirit, and that the assistance of the Holy Ghost was given to the people of God. The exaggeration resulted in fanaticism and imposture ; but Tertullian was not the man to weigh evidence very scrupulously, or to start back from apparent improbabilities ; and the highflown pretensions of the Montanists suited his vehemence, always striving to soar above the world and all that was in the world. In the Roman Church, there was from the first a leaning towards moderation in regard to discipline⁶ <note>discipline here refers to the strictness of church rules and the punishment for sins.</note>, which to Tertullian must have seemed culpable laxity, and this may not improbably have brought him into collision with the presbyters <note>priests or elders</note> of Rome, to whose arrogant treatment of him Jerome <note>Saint Jerome (c. 347–420 AD), a prominent early Christian scholar and translator of the Bible.</note> ascribed his secession⁷, much as in modern days Whitfield and Wesley <note>George Whitefield and John Wesley, 18th-century preachers whose intense zeal led to the founding of Methodism outside the established Church of England.</note> were said to have been driven from the Church by the persecution of its rulers, because these rulers felt the necessity of interfering to check and moderate the excesses of their enthusiasm. We may therefore expect to meet with many points of resemblance in the opinions maintained by Tertullian in his Montanistic and his non-Montanistic Treatises. In some we shall find positive assertion of the tenets of the new sect, and positive attacks upon the members of the Church⁸. But where these are wanting, we discover the same method of argument, references to the same Scriptural passages in the same sense, and a prominency given to those topics which were the favourite topics of Montanism. The mere mention of the New Jerusalem, Revelations, the Universal Priesthood, and the like, are not enough to determine that Tertullian was a Montanist when he made them⁹. That the indulgence of eye and ear (at the games or theater) did not interfere with religious devotion^1 was clearly contrary to both logic and lived experience. Nor would the difficulty of earning a living justify using immoral or forbidden means of subsistence^2. The question of whether one should avoid persecution, try to win social favor, and similar matters must obviously depend on whether the actions themselves were morally neutral. It is notable that Tertullian meets such excuses by pointing back to the baptismal vow^3. He demonstrates the nature of the service into which the baptized person had entered and what they had promised to abandon. Having proven to his own satisfaction that the things he objects to were included in the renunciation at baptism, he triumphantly appeals to the Christian’s duty to forsake the world and to suffer or even die for Christ’s sake.

### § 2. *Upon the excellence of God’s Works.*

One argument, however, deserved special attention, and the way he answered it reveals much about Tertullian's general worldview. The world, it was argued, was created by God^4. Everything in it was intended to serve man’s benefit and joy. Why then, people asked, should we not enjoy these things which are all part of God’s own creation? Tertullian’s reply was both philosophical and just. True, that the works of creation were good. True, that man was created in the image of God, but his nature was corrupted at the fall, and so he substituted for the natural the unnatural use of the things which God had made. True, that there are many created things, common to all mankind, sanctioned by Christ as man, and yet misapplied to the service of devils. But the mere fact of its being a creature of God does not solve the doubt. We must distinguish, on grounds of Scripture, reason and authority, what are and what are not necessary, and in the true sense natural usages.

### § 3. *Upon Scripture.*

To settle the preliminary question—Where is the true canon, and the true principle of interpretation?—we must consider the source from which it is derived. If we find, on the one hand, a number of Churches which can trace the <term>succession<note>The continuous line of bishops or leaders reaching back to the original founders.</note></term> of their ministers to the Apostles themselves, agreeing and holding what they do hold as a legacy bequeathed to them by their predecessors, and on the other, a body of men bringing forward some new principle, the result of their own private thoughts, we may determine, according to Tertullian, that the truth lies with the former¹⁶. The nearer the apostolic times were, the more powerful this argument was, as there was a greater probability that the judgment of the Apostle was preserved. And hence the great value of the succession¹⁷ (the <term>apostolic tradition<note>original Latin: "traditio apostolica"</note></term> upon which Irenaeus¹⁸ insists so frequently), because it might fairly be supposed that in a Church where the rule had passed in an unbroken line, the truth would be preserved.

Further than this, the agreement of all such Churches in one belief was, in Tertullian’s mind, a strong presumption in favor of their conclusions; nor shall we, I think, be inclined to hesitate in adopting his rule, which was an anticipation of the famous one of Vincent of Lerins: <term>what has been believed always, everywhere, and by everyone<note>original Latin: "quod semper, quod ubique, quod ab omnibus"</note></term>¹⁹. Here too, we shall scarcely dissent from the position that the Holy Spirit has preserved in the Church of Christ a body of fundamental truths. But in the application of the rules the difficulty lies. What are *universal*, what are fundamental truths? Nor can we disguise from ourselves that Tertullian's answers to these questions were often wrong; and it is here that controversialists of all days have made their departure, often into very different lines of argument.

But while we admit the general principles laid down by Tertullian, we must allow that he to a considerable extent lost sight of the circumstance that the guidance of the Spirit does not exclude the admixture of error with truth, whether in the individual or in the Church visible; that one consequence of human infirmity is this, that even in the transmission of truth error will grow up, and that it requires learning, thought, and patience, to discover it. The exaggeration, I had almost said the caricature, of the principle that truth is in the Church, which would make mere <term>lineal succession<note>The idea that authority and truth are passed down in an unbroken chain from one bishop to the next.</note></term> an adequate guarantee for its presence, is the foundation upon which the errors of the Church of Rome rest. These deductions belonged to a later age than that of Tertullian's, for his constant appeals to Scripture as the supreme authority, shew that if he took the doctrine at first hand from authority, he subjected it to the trial of Scripture and of reason, and thence argued back to:

> <note>original: "Apostolus de testimonio reddendo quibusdam, nullam respexerit Spiritus Sanctus..." from Tertullian's *De Praescriptione Haereticorum*, chapter 28.</note> "Is it possible that the Apostle, in giving testimony to some, was overlooked by the Holy Spirit, who was meant to lead the Church into truth? A farm manager or overseer; here used to describe the Spirit's management of the Church.</note></term> and Christ’s <term>vicar<note>original Latin: *vicarius*. When many different events occur, they do not result in one single outcome; if the doctrine of the churches had been an error, it surely would have varied in its forms."

cal testimony of such tradition. Both tradition and law were enunciations of that which was imperative, not on account of the law, nor on account of the tradition, but on account of the principle which was involved therein <gloss>25</gloss>.

To discover this <term>principle<note>Latin: "ratio." In legal and theological terms, this refers to the underlying logic or justification for a rule.</note></term>, or the reason of the *thing*, was highly edifying, as confirmatory of faith, but was not necessary. The law or the tradition must be first accepted without question, and then might be established against gainsayers by an examination of the principle. No doubt this view sets a very high value upon tradition; but when reason is once set to judge, as Tertullian proposes, it will not always be content with returning an answer in support of authority; and Tertullian himself found this to be the case. Where he is arguing on the side of universal custom, he insists upon that as paramount, but in laying down his general axioms on the authority of custom, he seems himself conscious of the need of some qualification. When he comes forward afterwards to dispute against a custom of the African Church <gloss>26</gloss>, he is not content with a mere appeal to reason in the case of a disagreement in custom, but states some general propositions that are scarcely consistent with what he had advanced upon the former occasion. Truth must never be sacrificed to custom. Lapse of time, respect of persons, and the prerogative of localities, often give birth to customs that militate against truth. Heresy is not convicted by its novelty, but by its falsehood. The Spirit promised to the disciples is to stand in the place of custom <gloss>27</gloss>. We

# CHAPTER VI.

## *The value of the Works of Tertullian.*

THE adhesion of Tertullian to <term>Montanism<note>A movement in the early Church that emphasized new prophecy and strict asceticism, eventually deemed heretical.</note></term> necessarily threw discredit upon his writings. In the year 492 Pope Gelasius, who made a very diligent enquiry into <term>canonical and apocryphal books<note>The official list of books accepted as scripture versus those excluded.</note></term>, classed the works of Tertullian (*the short works of Tertullian*) with those of various heretics, not merely disowned but utterly cast forth by the whole Roman Catholic and Apostolic Church<sup>1</sup>. Gelasius' uncompromising condemnation had its effect. All the early Roman Catholic editors thought it necessary to apologize for undertaking the works of such an author. <term>Rhenanus<note>Beatus Rhenanus (1485–1547), a humanist scholar and early editor of Tertullian's works.</note></term>, in his preface, refers to the respect in which Tertullian was held by S. Cyprian and other early writers, and would qualify the censure of Gelasius<sup>2</sup>.

This was a common title for works summarizing official Church teachings.</note>. Pamelius <note>Jacobus Pamelius (1536–1587) was a Flemish theologian known for his scholarly editions of early Christian writers.</note> prefixes a list of Paradoxes of Tertullian, with the Antidotes of Pamelius. And Rigalt <note>Nicolas Rigalt (1577–1654) was a French scholar who edited several classical and patristic texts.</note>, in his preface, endeavours to shew that the <term>Montanism<note>A movement in the early Church characterized by a belief in new, ongoing prophecy and very strict moral discipline. Tertullian's later association with this group made him a controversial figure for later orthodox writers.</note></term> of Tertullian was of a very moderate tone, and expresses his unwillingness to sanction any <term>heterodox<note>Opinions or doctrines that differ from the officially established standards of the Church.</note></term> opinions in terms which have been thought rather politic than sincere^3.

I have not attempted to define very accurately Tertullian’s opinions, or to distinguish what are and what are not Montanistic. The value of his writings consists not so much in his special opinions, as in the light which his works throw upon the history of the early Church. His acknowledged unsoundness in some particulars will of itself warn us to use a caution which is scarcely less necessary in the study of writers more strictly <term>orthodox<note>Beliefs that conform to the "right" or traditionally accepted teachings of the Church.</note></term>. For we should in all cases consider the position of the <term>Fathers<note>The "Church Fathers" were the foundational theologians and leaders of the first few centuries of Christianity.</note></term> as witnesses and as men. Both their testimony and their opinions are affected by the age in which they lived. The value of the former is manifestly enhanced by proximity to apostolic times. Their opinions derive some weight from the same cause. But in judging of them we must make the proper allowances for the character of the individual and of his age. Disregard to this consideration has led some to estimate the Fathers by modern notions and modern habits of thought, and to ridicule the outward peculiarities of those whose intrinsic excellence they do not understand. It has led others to attach to their writings an authority which they themselves never dreamt of claiming, and to view their works as a series of separate maxims and propositions to be collected into a code, all but infallible, and applicable, without modification, throughout all genera-

<header>VALUE OF TERTULLIAN'S WORKS.</header>

...the institutions of mankind. Church history is concerned with determining the facts and the doctrines of primitive Christianity <note>The term "primitive" here refers to the earliest era of the Church, closest to the time of the Apostles.</note>; but this is not all. If we wish to understand how the kingdom of heaven grew from a small seed into a mighty tree, and gradually gained authority over the hearts of men, we must study the state of the world during its growth, and how thought developed in various directions within the Church itself. The careful study of an ancient author informs us not only of the truths held in the past, but of the way in which they were understood. In both these respects, Tertullian is highly valuable. His strong individuality allows us to see what an early Christian was like, and how he was affected by Christian truths. His wide-ranging learning in both sacred and secular <note>Original text uses "profane," which in this context means "not sacred" or "worldly" academic subjects rather than "disrespectful."</note> subjects makes his works a rich storehouse of everything concerning the manners and customs of his era. 

Most interesting information is provided by him regarding ancient rites and ancient liturgical forms <note>The structured patterns and rituals used in public worship.</note>; while his very errors <note>A reference to his later leanings toward Montanism, which the mainstream Church eventually rejected.</note> make his testimony to those doctrinal truths that were not in dispute all the more trustworthy. Above all, his close knowledge of and constant reference to the Holy Scriptures give his words a special value. In him, we have an author who lived no more than 100 years after the death of the Apostle St. John, providing both direct and indirect testimony to almost every book in the <term>Scriptural Canon<note>The definitive list of books recognized by the Church as the divinely inspired and authoritative Bible.</note></term>, proving that these Scriptures, and no others, were regarded in that early age as the voice of the Holy Spirit⁴, as the rule of life—whose authority was beyond doubt⁵ and whose decision was final—through the study of which men were to understand and believe⁶.

# THE BOOK OF TERTULLIAN¹ <note>original Latin: "TERTULLIANI LIBER"</note>

## *ON THE SHOWS.* <note>original Latin: "DE SPECTACULIS." This famous work by the North African theologian Tertullian, written around 197–202 AD, argues that public games—theaters, gladiator fights, and chariot races—are incompatible with the Christian faith due to their pagan origins and emotional excess.</note>

<margin>CHAPTER I.</margin>
<margin>Learn your obligations to abstain from shows, and be not deceived by the false reasonings of the Gentiles. It is not only your wisdom, but also your duty to abstain.</margin>
Servants of God, learn what the condition of faith is, what the logic of truth, and what the rule of discipline <note>original Latin: "status fidei, quæ ratio veritatis, quod præ-scriptum disciplinæ"</note>, which, among the other errors of the world, also takes away the pleasures of the shows. You who are at this very moment drawing near to God, recognize this; and you who have already testified and confessed that you have approached Him², acknowledge it once more, lest any should sin either through ignorance or through pretense. For so great is the power of pleasure that it stretches out ignorance to provide an opportunity for sin, and corrupts the conscience into a state of pretense³. To both of these, perhaps, the opinions of the heathens <note>original Latin: "ethnicorum"</note> might still appeal, who in this cause against us argue in this way—

---

# THE BOOK OF TERTULLIAN

<margin>CHAPTER I.</margin> they have thought fit to argue⁴: That nothing in these great outward comforts for the eyes or ears stands in the way of religion in your mind and conscience; nor indeed is God offended by a man's enjoyment, which, so long as fear and honor toward God remain intact, it is no sin to enjoy in its proper time and place. But this is exactly what we are now preparing to show—how these things are not compatible with true religion and true obedience toward the true God. There are those who think that Christians—a race ready for death—are trained for this "obstinacy"⁵ <note>original Latin: "obstinationem." This was a common Roman criticism of Christian steadfastness, which they viewed as stubbornness or madness rather than faith.</note> by the renunciation of pleasures, so that they might more easily despise life after its attachments have been cut away, as it were; and that they do not long for what they have already made superfluous to themselves. Thus, they think this is decided by human planning and foresight rather than by divine command. I suppose it would be a burden, forsooth, for those who persist in such great pleasures to die for God’s sake!⁶ <note>Tertullian is being sarcastic here, suggesting that people don't need to be bored with life to be willing to die for their faith.</note> Although, even if it were so, the resolution belonging to so grave a discipline⁷ ought to obey so fitting a plan.

⁴ *to argue.* Two Gentile <note>Non-Christian or "heathen"</note> objections: 1. that the pleasures of the eye or ear need not interfere with the religion of the heart; 2. that the abstinence is only prudential, lest life become too pleasant to abandon.

...tends toward this: that everything established by God and granted to man—as we preach, and surely all things are good as they come from a good Author—among these are counted all those things from which the shows are organized: the Circus <note>original: "Circum"</note>, for example, and the lion, and the strength of the body, and the sweetness of the voice. Therefore, they argue, it cannot seem foreign to God nor an enemy to Him which consists of His own creation; nor should the worshippers of God think that what is not an enemy to God is to be blamed <note>original: "putandum," literally "thought of" or "considered"</note>, because it is not foreign to Him. Clearly, even the very construction of the places—the stones, the mortar, the marbles, the columns—are God’s things, for He gave them for the use of the earth; even the acts themselves are carried out under God’s heaven. How clever a debater human ignorance thinks itself! Especially when it fears losing something of the joys and fruits of the world. Finally, you would find more people whom the danger to their pleasure, rather than to their life, calls away from this sect <note>The "sect" refers to the early Christian community.</note>. <margin>CHAPTER II.</margin> ...and to the wise man, pleasure is the very grace of life. <note>original: "et sapienti vitæ gratia, nisi voluptas"</note> No one denies—for no one is ignorant of what nature itself suggests—that God is the Founder of the universe, and that this universe is as good as it is delivered into the hand of man. But because they do not know God thoroughly—knowing Him only by natural law <note>original: "naturali jure"</note> and not by intimate acquaintance <note>original: "non etiam familiari," referring to the relationship of a household or family member</note>, from a distance and not from nearby—it is inevitable that they are ignorant of how He commands or forbids the administration of the things He established. At the same time, they do not know who the rival <note>original: "æmulus," referring here to the Devil as the "Ape of God"</note> is who, from the opposite side, works to corrupt the uses of the divine creation. For you cannot know the will or the adversary of one whom you do not fully know. Therefore, we must not only consider by whom all things were established, but by whom they have been diverted. For it will thus appear for what purpose they were established, if it appears for what purpose they were *not* established. <note>original: "cujus non sint"</note> There is a great difference between corruption and integrity, just as there is a great difference between the Creator and the corrupter <term>interpolator|Literally one who polishes or alters; here, someone who falsifies or degrades a pure original.</term>. Moreover, all kinds of evils, which even the pagans <term>ethnici|From the Greek 'ethne' (nations), referring here to non-Christians.</term> both prohibit and defend as certainties—

---

^4 *Death is too inevitable...* Death is too inevitable for even the fool to fear excessively, pleasure too powerful for even the wise to disregard; for it is pleasure that makes life sweet whether to the wise man or the fool. <note>The scholar Oehler, based on a logical guess, reads "given" [datam] for "so great" [tantam].</note>

^5 *They know God...* The knowledge of God among the pagans is contrasted with that among Christians. See below: "we therefore, who have known the Lord." The pagans know God only by natural right, as men, not by special right, as members of God’s household <note>original: "naturali jure non etiam familiari"</note>; they know Him from afar, not closely.

^6 *Who is the rival...* <note>Different manuscripts offer variations: "what rival force" or "what rival power."</note> Compare Tertullian's work *On the Soldier's Crown* <note>original: "De Coron."</note>, chapter 6: "wherein the rival of God corrupted the entire creation <note>original: "conditio"</note>, which had been delivered to man for certain uses, along with man himself." He uses "creation" <note>original: "conditio"</note> and "to create" <note>original: "condere"</note> for "creature" and "to create." Also see *On the Apparel of Women* <note>original: "De Cult. Fœm."</note> 1.8: "Incense and wine are God’s creation."

<column-break/>

^7 *We must not only... for what purpose they were not.* The text follows the editors Gangneius and Pamelius, except that they read "by which all things" instead of "by whom all things." The Agobardine manuscript is illegible here. Rigaltius (followed by Oehler) suggests by logical guess: "to what use they were established, if it appears to what use they were not." Dodgson translates this: "we must not only consider by whom all things were made, but from what they are turned away—for so will it be seen to what use they were, if it be seen to what use they were not."

<summary>Tertullian argues that knowing God through nature is insufficient; one must also recognize the "corrupter" (the devil) who diverts God's good creations toward evil ends. He distinguishes between the original integrity of creation and its subsequent corruption by this rival force.</summary>

On the contrary, He does away with every form of murder with one primary commandment: **You shall not kill.** <margin>Exodus 20:13</margin> Likewise, who placed gold, bronze, silver, ivory, wood, and all the materials seized for making idols into the world, if not God, the author of the world? ...of evil speech <note>The previous page ended with "receptacle," and the sense concludes here as "receptacle of evil speech."</note>, and the throat for the crime of gluttony <margin>CHAPTER II.</margin>, and the belly to be a partner to gluttony, and the genitals for the excesses of immodesty, and the hands for violence, and the feet for a wandering life? Or was the spirit implanted in the body so that it might become a factory for snares, frauds, and injustices? I think not. For if God, who demands innocence, hates all malice and all such devised wickedness <note>original: "malitiam excogitatam"</note>, then beyond doubt, He did not create the things He has made for the purpose of leading to the very works He condemns, even if those same works are carried out through the things He created. For this is the entire reason for condemnation: the perverted use of the creation by the created. Therefore, since we have come to know the Lord and have also looked upon His rival <note>The devil</note>, and since we have discovered the Founder and simultaneously detected the Corruptor <note>original: "interpolatorem," meaning one who alters or falsifies a garment or text</note>, we ought neither to wonder nor to doubt...

---

$^{11}$ *The crime of gluttony.* Gluttony [gula] is used here for gluttonousness. From *On Fasting*, chapter 17: "Indeed, the appendages of gluttony are lust and luxury."

$^{12}$ *So much malice.* Oehler <note>A 19th-century editor of Tertullian</note> considers "malignity" and "malice" as the qualities which those people ascribe to God who believe He created man with such an evil design. La Cerda <note>A 17th-century Jesuit commentator</note> adopts the scholarly guess of Ursinus, explaining it thus: "It might be objected, seeing such great perversity in how things are used, that God, by the very creation of the world, made things solely so that they would have a bad end. He refutes this. Do not think this. For as God, as He truly is, hates malignity in use and malice, it likewise remains certain that He did not create things for the outcome of evil works, *which He Himself condemns.*" Dodgson <note>An English translator</note> reads *tantum* [only] and translates: "If God that requireth innocency, hateth all wickedness and malice, when only

<column-break/>

conceived in the thoughts." But the position of the word "only," and the force of "devised" <note>original: "excogitatam," meaning thought out</note>, scarcely allow for this; "malignity" and "devised malice" refer back to the "snares, frauds, and iniquities" mentioned above. God hates all these offspring of the thought, and cannot therefore have created man's faculties in order to find an outlet in thoughts and deeds which He condemns.

$^{13}$ *Changed.* <note>original: "demutatam"</note> Ursinus, by scholarly guess, reads "but that he changed the whole substance..." Oehler follows the *Codex Agobardinus* <note>An important 9th-century manuscript of Tertullian</note>, Gangneius, and Rigaltius in reading "he changed," but places only a comma after "ought." The *Codex Agobardinus*, Rigaltius, and Oehler insert the phrase "equally with himself, appointed for integrity" after "his substance." This text follows Gelenius and Pamelius: "We ought not to wonder or doubt, seeing that man himself, the image and work of God, the lord of the whole universe, has been [changed]..."

</columns>
