# ON THE SPECTACLES

<margin>
CHAPTER II.
Psalm 8:6.
</margin>
...since that power of the corrupting and envious angel <note>The devil, described here as an "interpolator" or one who alters God's original work</note> cast down man himself—the handiwork and image of God, the master of the entire universe—from his original integrity at the very beginning. This angel changed man’s entire nature, along with man himself, into a perverted state against his Creator. He did this so that, in that very image <note>The "image of God" in man</note> which he grieved had been granted to man and not himself, he might both make man a criminal in God's eyes and establish his own dominion.

<margin>
CHAPTER III.
For those Christians, who ask for Scriptural authority, there is an implicit prohibition in the first Psalm.
</margin>
Guided by this inner certainty <term>conscientia: here meaning a deep, inward conviction based on spiritual knowledge rather than just "conscience"</term> against the opinions of the pagans, let us turn instead to the hesitations <note>original: "detractatus"; a rare word here suggesting the arguments or "shirking" of some believers</note> of our own people. For the faith of some is either too simple or too scrupulous, and they demand explicit authority from the Scriptures for this renunciation of the spectacles. They put themselves in a state of uncertainty because a command for God’s servants to abstain is not explicitly or by name proclaimed...

<columns>
2

...from the beginning cast down from his purity by the power of the opposing and envious angel, that man's whole substance was equally with himself perverted to opposition against his Maker.'

$^{14}$ *which he grieved* <note>original: "quam doluerat"</note>, namely, the *image of God*. St. Cyprian, in *On Envy and Jealousy*, page 256 (Benedictine Edition): *That one [the devil], relying on his angelic majesty, he who was once accepted by God and true, after he saw man made in the image of God, broke out into a zeal of malevolent envy. He did not cast down another by the impulse of jealousy before he himself was first cast down by jealousy; he was a captive before he took a captive, and ruined before he ruined another. While, driven by envy, he snatched from man the grace of granted immortality, he himself also lost that which he had been before.*

Ch. III. $^1$ *By this inner certainty* <note>original: "Hac conscientia"</note>, 'furnished with this intimate knowledge,' referring to the phrase *We, therefore, who have come to know the Lord*. Certainty [conscientia] is contrasted here with pagan opinions. Compare the *Apology*, chapter 1:

<column-break/>

*For then a thing deserves punishment when it is known whether it is deserved. But when knowledge of the merit is lacking, on what basis is the justice of the hatred defended? That justice must be proven not from the outcome, but from the certainty of the case* <note>original: "conscientia"</note>. Certainty here means 'a full and certain knowledge,' 'a conviction arising not from outward proof, but from inward assurance.'

$^2$ *hesitations* <note>original: "detractatus"</note>, a word not found elsewhere. The scholar Rigaltius, following Ursinus, reads this as *retractatus* (reconsiderations), as seen below in chapter 11. In *To His Wife*, Book II, chapter 2, the phrase *a decision was refused and put forth* <note>original: "detractata et exerta sententia est"</note> is used, though the Agobardine Codex reads *districta* (strict) there. Most think *detractatus* here is used for *tractatus* (treatments or discussions). Oehler explains it as 'shirkings' or 'evasions,' referring to Christians who try to avoid the strict rule.

$^3$ *authority from the Scriptures*. St. Cyprian, in *On the Spectacles*, page 339: *Where are these things written? Where are they forbidden?* See also below in chapter 23, and *On the Soldier's Crown*, chapter 2.

# TERTULLIAN’S TREATISE

<columns>
2

### CHAPTER III.
Methods. Plainly we find nowhere, in the same way as it is <margin>Exodus 20:14, etc.</margin> clearly stated: *Thou shalt not kill, Thou shalt not worship an idol, Thou shalt not commit adultery, thou shalt not admit fraud*, that it is so explicitly defined: *Thou shalt not go to the Circus, thou shalt not go to the theater; thou shalt not watch the contest or the gladiatorial show.* But we <margin>Psalm 1:1.</margin> find that to this category also belongs that first word of David: *Blessed is the man*, he says, *who has not gone into the council of the ungodly, and has not stood in the way of sinners, and has not sat in the seat of pests* <note>original: "pestium"; historically translated as "the scornful" or "the pestilent"</note>. For <margin>Luke 23:50.</margin> even if he seems to have praised that just man <note>The "just man" refers to Joseph of Arimathea</note> because he did not take part in the council and assembly of the Jews who were consulting about denying <note>original: "negando"; some manuscripts suggest "denegando" or completely rejecting</note> the Lord, yet divine Scripture is always widely applied wherever, according to the sense of the present matter, the Christian rule <term>disciplina: the code of conduct and moral training of the early Church</term> is also fortified, so that here too the voice is not foreign to a spectacle...

---

⁴ *in the seat of pests*. Clement of Alexandria, *The Instructor*, Book 3, quoted by Leprieur: <note>original Greek: "οὐ δὲ ἀπεικότως τὰ στάδια καὶ τὰ θέατρα καθέδραν λοιμιῶν προσείποι τις ἄν"</note> "one might not inappropriately call the stadiums and the theaters a seat of plagues."
⁵ *that just man*. Joseph of Arimathea. Rigalt quotes from the *Commentary on the Psalms*: Tertullian, in his book *On the Spectacles*, asserts that this Psalm can be understood both regarding Joseph, who buried the body of the Lord, and regarding those who do not gather at the spectacles of the Pagans.
⁶ *denying*. Rigalt conjectures *negando* (denying). The manuscripts have *negando* and *denegando*. The murder of our Lord was the final denial of Him.
⁷ *always widely applied*... "Scripture has however always an extended application, wherever in accordance with the meaning belonging to a particular occasion the Christian rule is at the same time supported." *secundum*, "following along with;" in the *Apology*, chapter 46, "next after,"...

<column-break/>

people. At the back of each stage the wall rose in a high step forming a kind of belt (*præcinctio* or *balteus*) round the amphitheatre. Above the *balteus* was a platform of a few feet, from which the seats of the next higher stage rose (*præcinctionis itinera*). Lipsius <note>Justus Lipsius was a 16th-century humanist scholar who wrote extensively on Roman history.</note>, in *On the Amphitheater*, page 52, quotes Vitruvius, Book III, chapter 2: *The belt-walls [præcinctiones] seem to be made in proportion to the height of the theaters; and not higher than the width of the belt-wall's passage.* Pliny, *Natural History* XVIII. 76 (Lipsius edition 1787) tells us that if a line be drawn from North to South across a field, *the path that runs thus through a field is called a hinge [cardo].* Hence probably *cardo* was used for a principal line of division. ### **CHAPTER IV. Lest anyone think we are merely making clever arguments, I shall turn to the primary authority of our own "seal" <note>original: *signaculi*; a common early Christian term for the sacrament of baptism</note> itself. When we enter the water and profess the Christian faith according to the words of His law, we bear witness with our own mouths that we have renounced the devil, his pomp <note>The "pomp" (*pompa*) specifically referred to the ceremonial processions that opened public games and festivals</note>, and his angels. What is the chief and most important thing in which the devil, his pomp, and his angels are reckoned, if not idolatry? It is from this that every unclean and wicked spirit comes, so to speak—for I shall not dwell on this point any longer. Therefore, if it is established that the entire apparatus of the spectacles consists of idolatry, it will be beyond doubt that our testimony of renunciation in the washing of baptism <note>original: *lavacro*</note> also applies to the spectacles, since they are handed over to the devil, his pomp, and his angels, namely through idolatry. CHAPTER V.
The origin of public Games is idolatrous.

### **CHAPTER V.**
Regarding their origins, as these are somewhat obscure and unknown to most of our people, we must investigate deeply, and from no other source than the records of pagan <note>original: *ethnicalium*; literally "heathen" or "gentile" literature</note> literature. There are many authors who have published commentaries on this matter. From them, the origin of the games is recorded as follows: Timaeus <note>A Greek historian (c. 345–250 BC) who wrote extensively on the history of Italy and Sicily</note> relates that the Lydians, migrants from Asia, settled in Etruria <note>An ancient civilization in central Italy, preceding and influencing the Romans</note> under the leadership of Tyrrhenus, who had yielded the kingdom to his brother after a dispute. Therefore, in Etruria, alongside other rites of their superstitions, they established spectacles in the name of religion. From there, the Romans sent for performers and borrowed the practice, the timing, and the name—so that the "games" (*ludi*) were named after the Lydians (*Lydis*). But even if Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BC), a famous Roman scholar whom Tertullian often cites for Roman history</note> interprets *ludi* as coming from *ludo* (that is, from "play" or "sport"), just as they used to call the Luperci <note>Priests of the Lupercalia festival who ran through the streets of Rome</note> "games" because they run about in play, he nevertheless classifies this sport of young men as belonging to festival days, temples, and religious matters. It matters nothing now...

### **CHAPTER V.**
### **Concerning the reason for the name, as long as the reason for the thing itself is idolatry.**

For even when the games were called "Liberalia" <note>A festival held on March 17th in honor of Liber Pater, an ancient Italian god of fertility and wine</note> indiscriminately, they clearly echoed the honor of Father Liber. For they were first held for Liber by country folk because of the benefit they attribute to him: the discovery of wine. From there, the games called "Consualia" <note>An ancient Roman festival held in August and December</note> were named, which in the beginning honored Neptune; for they call him "Consus" as well. After that, Romulus dedicated the "Equiria" <note>Horse races held in the Campus Martius</note> to Mars, although some also claim the Consualia for Romulus, arguing that he dedicated them to Consus as the god—so they claim—of "Counsel" <note>original: *consilii*; Tertullian is playing on the phonetic similarity between the god Consus and the Latin word for a plan or counsel, *consilium*</note>. Specifically, that "counsel" by which he then devised the abduction of the Sabine virgins <note>A legendary episode in which the first generation of Roman men acquired wives by kidnapping women from the neighboring Sabine tribe during a festival</note> to provide wives for his soldiers.

Clearly a "noble" counsel! <note>Tertullian is being deeply sarcastic here, mocking the Roman foundation myth</note> Even now among the Romans themselves, this act would be considered "just and lawful"—to say nothing of how it stands before God. This also contributes to the stain of their origin: you should not consider anything good which took its beginning from evil—from the impudence of violence, from a pagan god, from a founder who murdered his brother <note>A reference to Romulus killing his twin, Remus</note>, and from a son of Mars. Even now, an altar to that Consus is buried in the Circus <note>The Circus Maximus</note> at the first turning-posts beneath the earth, with an inscription of this sort:

<margin>The titles of Games, whether national or funereal, are idolatrous.</margin>
To the testimony of antiquity, later history adds its own weight, preserving the character of its origin in the titles used even in this present time. <margin>CHAPTER VII.</margin>
The equipment of the Circus games is somewhat more ostentatious, to which the name "procession" <gloss>1</gloss> properly belongs, as it precedes the games. This procession proves in itself what it is by the series of statues, the parade of images, the chariots, the *tensae* <term>tensae: sacred wagons used to carry the statues of gods</term>, the *armamaxae* <term>armamaxae: heavy four-wheeled carriages used for carrying royal or divine trophies</term>, the thrones, the crowns, and the spoils <note>original: "exuviis," referring to the robes and ornaments of the gods</note> <gloss>4</gloss>. Beyond these, what great rites and sacrifices precede and follow; how many colleges, priesthoods, and official bodies are set in motion, is well known to the inhabitants of that city in which the assembly of demons <gloss>5</gloss> has taken its seat. If these things are managed with less care in the provinces due to smaller resources, nevertheless all Circus games must be judged by their source; they are tainted by the place from which they are derived. For even a tiny stream from its own spring, or a small shoot from its own branch, contains the quality of its origin. Whether it be through ambition or frugality <gloss>6</gloss>, that which offends God remains the same; whatever the nature of the Circus procession, even if—

---

<gloss>1</gloss> at first peculiar to the **Great Games** <note>original: "Ludi Magni"</note>, instituted by **A. Postumius** after the battle of Regillus. Afterwards it was adopted generally at all Games.

<gloss>2</gloss> *proving*. **Rigaltius** from a conjecture uses "proves." This is unnecessary. The substantive verb "is" is understood: "the equipment (is) somewhat more ostentatious."

<gloss>3</gloss> *concerning chariots, sacred wagons, and trophy-carriages*. *Chariots* <note>original: "currus"</note> were the vehicles that contended in the race; *sacred wagons* <note>original: "tensae," from "tendo," meaning to stretch</note> were chariots containing images of gods drawn by ropes; *trophy-carriages* <note>original: "armamaxae"</note> were large wagons on which arms were piled up as trophies. **Suetonius**, *Life of Julius Caesar*, 76: <note>original: "Ampliora etiam humano fastigio decerni sibi passus et sedem auream in curia, et pro tribunali tensam, et ferculum Circensi pompa, templa, aras, simulacra juxta Deos."</note> "He allowed even greater honors to be decreed for himself than were suited to human stature: a golden seat in the senate-house, a sacred wagon before the tribunal, a litter in the Circus procession, temples, altars, and statues next to the Gods."

<gloss>4</gloss> *concerning thrones, crowns, and spoils*. "Thrones" or "seats" were the chairs on which

<column-break/>

the images were placed; "spoils" <note>original: "exuviae"</note> were the dresses and other trappings of the gods. **On the Crown**, chapter 7: "concerning the spoils of both stepsons." **Oehler** quotes **Apuleius, Metamorphoses**, book XI, chapter 10: "But the high priests of the sacred rites... carried forward the spoils of the most powerful gods."

<gloss>5</gloss> *assembly of demons*. Compare below, chapter 12: "The Capitol is the temple of all demons"; **Apology**, chapter 6: "those barred from the Capitol, that is, driven from the council of the gods."

<gloss>6</gloss> "that which" <note>original: "quod"</note>: "no matter whether there be display or economy in that which offends God." On "Let it be seen" <note>original: "viderit"</note> see **On the Crown**, chapter 2, note 2. **Agrippa's Manuscript**, **Gelenius**, and **Pamelius** read "by which" <note>original: "quo"</note>. **Barraeus** reads "that which" <note>original: "quod"</note>. **Rigaltius** reads: "Let its ambition or frugality see to it. God..." **Oehler** from conjecture reads "if" <note>original: "si"</note>. **Oehler** does not mention the readings "by which" and "that which," but says "which" <note>original: "quos"</note> is the common reading.

<summary>Tertullian details the idolatrous nature of the Circus procession (pompa), arguing that its various ornaments—statues, sacred wagons, and trophies—are dedicated to demons and therefore off limits to Christians, regardless of whether the display is lavish or modest.</summary>

**CHAPTER VII.** ...it carries around only a few statues, idolatry is present in even one; even if it draws but a single sacred wagon <term>tensam: a ceremonial carriage used to transport the images of gods</term>, it is still the carriage of Jupiter. Any form of idolatry, however moderately wealthy or splendid, is rich in the assessment of its own crime <gloss>7</gloss>.

<margin>CHAPTER VIII. The place of Games, the Circus, is idolatrous. We may indeed enter it as passers by, but not as spectators.</margin>

**CHAPTER VIII.** To proceed with the discussion of locations according to my plan: the Circus <gloss>1</gloss> is principally consecrated to the Sun <gloss>2</gloss>. His temple stands in the middle of the space, and his image shines from the roof of the temple, because they did not think it right to consecrate beneath a roof a god whom they have in the open sky. They assert that they received this spectacle first from Circe, who, as they say <gloss>3</gloss>, produced it for her father, the Sun. From her name, they argue, the Circus is called...

---

<gloss>7</gloss> *in the assessment of its own crime.* Dodgson: "in the amount of its sinfulness." Oehler explains "assessment" (*censu*) as "origin" (*origine*); but see Chapter 4, note 4 of Tertullian's *On Idolatry*.

**Chapter VIII.** <gloss>1</gloss> On the Circus Maximus <note>the largest stadium in ancient Rome, used primarily for chariot racing</note>, see Smith’s *Dictionary of Greek and Roman Antiquities*.

<gloss>2</gloss> *To the Sun.* <note>original: "Soli"</note> Tacitus, *Annals* 15.74: "Then decreed gifts and thanks are offered to the gods, and a particular honor to the Sun (who has an ancient temple near the Circus, where the crime was being prepared), who had uncovered many of the conspiracies by his divine power."

<gloss>3</gloss> *that.* <note>original: "quod"</note> The Agobardus Codex reads "who" (*qui*), adopted by Rigaltius and Oehler. The latter by conjecture alters "they have" (*habent*) to "and" (*atque*). The reading of the text, which is that of the other editions, is perfectly intelligible without alteration. The verbs "they have" (*habent*) and "they affirm" (*affirmant*) are used by Tertullian with a general subject, such as "some people," understood. So throughout this chapter, "they vow" (*vovent*), "they support" (*sustinent*), and so forth.

<gloss>4</gloss> *eggs.* <note>original: "ova"</note> Livy, in a very corrupt passage (Book 41, chapter 32), says that Quintus Fulvius Flaccus and Aulus Postumius Albinus the censors (in the year 74 BC <note>original: "A.U.C. 680"</note>) caused to be placed "eggs as markers for counting the laps of the race." This passage has been variously amended. At any rate it

<column-break/>

points to the adoption of *eggs* to number the courses. But this is directly opposed to Dio Cassius (Book 49, page 417), who says of Agrippa, when Aedile (in the year 33 BC <note>original: "A.U.C. 721"</note>): "And in the hippodrome, because people were getting confused about the number of laps, he set up both the dolphins and the egg-shaped structures." Cassiodorus, *Letters* 3.51: "Nor let it be thought useless that the circuit of the turning-posts is marked by the erection of eggs, since the act itself, heavy with many superstitions, professes by the example of the egg that it will give birth to something." See notes in Drakenborch’s edition of Livy at the same location. Panvinius draws a distinction between the "eggs of the Castors" [the twins Castor and Pollux] surmounting the *turning-posts* <term>metæ: the conical pillars at the ends of the central barrier</term>, and "eggs of the laps" on the *central barrier* <term>spina: the long central dividing wall of the circus</term>. Ancient coins show eggs both on the turning-posts and on the barrier. Is it not possible that eggs were first erected on the turning-posts in 174 BC, and afterwards on the barrier in 33 BC?

<gloss>5</gloss> *dolphins.* <note>original: "delphinos"</note> Juvenal, *Satire* 6.589: "She stands before the towers and the columns of the dolphins."

<gloss>6</gloss> *they vow.* <note>original: "vovent"</note> The Agobardus Codex and Rigaltius read: "The columns vomit dolphins to Neptune." Sessias and Gangneius read: "The dolphins... vomit... the columns." Oehler reads "the dolphins..."

</columns>

<summary>Tertullian explains that the Circus is inherently idolatrous because it is dedicated to the Sun and Circe, with its very architecture reflecting pagan worship. He and the annotators detail the religious symbolism of the arena's components, such as the lap-counting eggs and dolphins.</summary>

### CHAPTER VIII

<columns>

...are celebrated. Plainly, that sorceress <note>Circe, mentioned on the previous page</note> certainly carried out this business on behalf of those whose priestess she was: namely, the demons and their angels. How many forms of idolatry, then, do you recognize in the very appearance of the place? Every single ornament of the Circus is a temple in its own right. They attribute the **Eggs** <gloss>4</gloss> to the honor of the Castors <note>Castor and Pollux</note>, as those who believe they were born from an egg produced by Jupiter in the form of a swan do not blush at such a story. They dedicate the **Dolphins** <gloss>5</gloss> to Neptune <gloss>6</gloss>. They support pillars named **Sessia** from "sowing" (*sementationibus*), **Messia** from "harvesting" (*messibus*), and **Tutulina** <gloss>7</gloss> from the "protection" (*tutelis*) of the fruits. Before these, three altars are devoted to a trio of gods: the **Great**, the **Mighty**, and the **Strong** <gloss>8</gloss>. They believe these are the same as the Samothracian gods.

---

<gloss>4-6</gloss> The text discusses how race-markers were shaped like eggs and dolphins. The reading "men dedicate" (*vovent*) and "men tolerate" (*sustinent*) is preferred here over other scholarly variations. *Sustinent* may be a play on words regarding the physical pillars "supporting" the weight and the people "tolerating" the religious inscriptions.

<gloss>7</gloss> **Sessia, Messia, Tutulina.** Pliny the Elder (Natural History 18.2) notes: "They called Seia from sowing, and Segesta from the crops, whose statues we see in the Circus." Macrobius (Saturnalia 1.16) adds that the ancients observed festivals for Salus, Senonia, Seia, Segetia, and Tutilina. Compare also Tertullian's *Apology* (c. 52), *On Idolatry* (c. 15), and *On the Crown* (c. 13). Arnobius (Against the Heathen 3, p. 115) mocks this: "Unxia presides over anointings, Cinxia over the loosening of the girdle, Victa and Potua, most holy, manage food and drink. O what an excellent and singular interpretation of divine powers! Unless the doorposts of men were smeared with fatty ointment by brides, unless the marriage-girdles were loosened by husbands, and unless humans ate and drank, **the gods would have no names!**"

<column-break/>

St. Augustine (*City of God* 4.8) expands on such minor deities as Segetia, Tutilina, Runcina, etc. Martin Luther (Works, Vol. I, p. 8 [Wittenberg, 1582]) compares popular saints with these pagan deities: "Even now we Christians are not ashamed to divide the business of temporal things among the saints, as if they had now become the servants and slaves of craftsmen; so that this Lerna <note>the multi-headed Hydra</note> of superstitions has almost returned, and we have built again that Roman chaos of gods and a kind of Pantheon." Polytheism always appears in much the same shape. "The Chinese," says the Bishop of Victoria, in an account of a late tour, "have peopled heaven, earth, and sea, and even the elements, with myriads of *Shin* <note>spirits or gods</note>, inferior divinities, the angels, ministers, and subordinate agents of the Supreme Being, *Shang-ta*." He mentions *Tow-shin*, the god of the smallpox. It is found that the Chinese are too ready, when converted by Roman Catholic missionaries, to adopt saint-worship in the place of Shin-worship.

<gloss>8</gloss> **Great, Mighty, Strong.** <note>original: "Magnis, Potentibus, Valentibus"</note> Macrobius (Saturnalia 3.4). Cassius Hemina says these are the Samothracian gods...

### CHAPTER VIII.

<columns>
2

The massive scale of the **obelisk** <gloss>9</gloss>, as Hermateles <note>Likely a reference to a lost author on Egyptian history or an error for Hermapion, an Egyptian priest who translated obelisk inscriptions</note> asserts, is prostituted to the **Sun**; its inscription, from which its prestige <note>original: "census" — here referring to its value or historical record</note> derives, is an Egyptian superstition. The council of demons would have been "chilly" <note>A rhetorical way of saying the assembly was incomplete or lacked its central figure</note> without their **Great Mother** <note>Cybele, the Phrygian mother-goddess whose cult was central to Rome</note>; she, therefore, presides there over the *euripus* <term>euripus: a decorative water-channel or ditch running through the center of the stadium</term> <gloss>10</gloss>. **Consus**, as we have already mentioned, lurks underground at the *metae* <term>metae: the turning posts at each end of the racing track</term> <note>Tertullian previously argued that Consus, a god of grain storage, had a hidden altar at the Circus</note>. **Murtia** has also turned the place into a shrine of idols. For they claim Murtia is a goddess of love, and they have dedicated a temple to her in that section. Take note, O Christian, how many unclean names have taken possession of the Circus. This religion is foreign to you, occupied as it is by so many spirits of the devil. Concerning the locations themselves, there is a point to be reconsidered here to anticipate the questions of some. "For what," you might ask, "if I enter the Circus at some other time? Will I be in danger of being defiled?" There is no absolute prohibition regarding the places themselves. For a servant of God may visit not only these gathering places of the shows, but even the pagan temples themselves, without endangering his religious discipline, provided there is a simple and urgent reason that does not relate to the specific business or duties of that place. Otherwise, even the streets, the forum, the baths, the stables, and our very homes [could not be entered] without...

---

...and similarly that they are called the Penates <note>The Roman gods of the household and state</note> of the Romans, namely: "the **great gods**, the **good gods**, and the **mighty gods**." <note>original Greek: θεοὺς μεγάλους, θεοὺς χρηστούς, θεοὺς δυνατούς</note> — Oehler <note>Franz Oehler, a 19th-century editor of Tertullian</note>.

⁹ **massive scale of the obelisk**. An Egyptian obelisk, 125¾ feet high excluding the base, carved from a single stone, was placed by Augustus in the Circus Maximus and dedicated to the sun. (Pliny, *Natural History* xxxvi. 14, 5). The Hippodrome of Constantinople also had a very large obelisk brought from Egypt.

¹⁰ **Euripus**. The *euripi* were ditches around the Circus, originally constructed by Julius Caesar to protect the spectators from the wild beasts in the arena. (Pliny, *Natural History* viii. 7). Dodg-

<column-break/>

son considers the *euripus* to be an artificial lake for sea-fights, but it does not appear that such a lake ever existed in the Circus. Suetonius (*Life of Julius*, ch. 39) mentions such a lake in the *minor Codeta*, which was in the Campus Martius; and Dio Cassius, quoted by Lipsius (*Amphitheatres*, p. 40), says that Nero exhibited naval battles in the amphitheater. Lipsius quotes in the margin Seneca (*Letter 91*): "those who fill the *euripi* with a sudden rush of water or drain them," which perhaps led to the confusion between these channels and artificial lakes.

He also offers a nuanced view on whether Christians may enter these spaces for neutral, everyday reasons provided they do not participate in the religious rites.</summary>

# ON THE SPECTACLES

<columns>
2

<margin>CHAPTER VIII.</margin>
<margin>1 Corinthians 5:10</margin>
...are not entirely of idols <note>Tertullian is finishing a thought here: that things like the sun or the earth are not themselves idols just because they are worshipped by others</note>. Satan and his angels have filled the entire world. However, the fact that we are in the world does not mean we have fallen away from God; we only fall if we touch any of the world's crimes. Therefore, if I enter the Capitol or the Serapeum <note>The Temple of Serapis, a major Greco-Egyptian deity</note> as a sacrificer or a worshipper, I shall fall from God, just as I would as a spectator in the Circus. Places do not contaminate us by themselves, but rather the things that are done in those places—by which the places themselves are contaminated, as we have argued. We are contaminated by the contaminated. For this reason, we recall to whom such places are dedicated, so we may show that the things done in these places belong to those to whom the places themselves are dedicated.

<margin>CHAPTER IX.</margin>
<margin>The art of chariot-racing is idolatrous, having gods for its patrons.</margin>
Now let us speak of the art by which the Circus games are presented. In the past, horsemanship was a simple matter of riding on horseback, and certainly its common use was not a crime. But when it was pressed into the service of the games, it passed from being a gift of God to the service of demons. Thus, this form of sport is assigned to **Castor** and **Pollux** <note>The Dioscuri, twin deities associated with horses</note>, to whom Stesichorus <note>An early Greek lyric poet</note> teaches that horses were distributed by **Mercury**. But **Neptune** is also "Equine" <gloss>of horses</gloss>, whom the Greeks call *Hippios*¹ <note>original: Ἱππιον</note>. Regarding the yoke, however...

---

¹¹ ...is hidden. See above, chapter 5. Plutarch, *Life of Romulus*, page 25, D. (Frankfurt edition, 1620): "For the altar of **Consus** is hidden in the larger of the racetracks <note>The Circus Maximus</note> for the rest of the time, but is uncovered during the horse-racing games."

¹² **Murtian**, specifically the *metae* <term>metae: the turning posts at the ends of the racing track</term>, "It was an idol that originated the Murtian goal too." A particular part of the Circus near the goal was called *at the Murtia*, from *Venus Murtia*, or *Myrtea*, to whom it was sacred. Pliny, *Natural History* book 15, chapter 36: "There was even an ancient altar to Myrtlean Venus, which they now call Murtia"; where Harduin <note>A 17th-century Jesuit scholar</note> quotes Varro: "The innermost part of the Circus is called 'at the Murtia'... Others say it is derived from the myrtle-grove, because it [was there]..."

<column-break/>

"...was once there, of which a trace remains, because there is even now a small shrine to **Murtian Venus**." Compare Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* <note>also known as The Golden Ass</note> book 6, chapter 8: "behind the Murtian goals." The Agobardine Codex reads *Murcias*, while the rest read *Murtias*. Where Gelenius and Pamelius <note>Renaissance editors of Tertullian</note> read "of love" <note>original: "amoris"</note>, the Agobardine Codex and Gangnerus have "of marble" <note>original: "marmoris"</note>. This led Rigaltius to adopt the name *Murcias* and conjecture it meant "of decay" <note>original: "marcoris"</note>, quoting Saint Augustine, *The City of God* book 4, chapter 16, who speaks of Murcia as the "goddess of decay." Rigaltius also reads "the Murcian goddess lurks." "These also"; and he is followed in this by Oehler. But it is merely conjectural; the Agobardine Codex here agreeing with the rest.

<margin>CHAPTER IX.</margin> ...they dedicated four-horse chariots to the Sun, and two-horse chariots to the Moon. But also:

<margin>Virgil, *Georgics* III. 113.</margin>
> Erichthonius was the first who dared to yoke 
> four horses to a car, and to stand as victor 
> over the rapid wheels.
<note>original: "Primus Erichthonius cursus et quatuor ausus Jungere equos, rapidusque rotis insistere victor."</note>

Erichthonius, the son of Minerva and Vulcan—and produced, in fact, from lust spilled upon the ground—is a demonic monstrosity; indeed, he is the devil himself, not just a serpent <note>Erichthonius was a legendary king of Athens often depicted as half-man, half-serpent, or guarded by snakes</note>. If indeed Trochilus of Argos <gloss>The name appears as Prophylus or Acrophilus in other manuscripts</gloss> is the creator of the chariot, he dedicated that work of his to the goddess Juno. If Romulus was the first to display the four-horse chariot <term>quadriga</term> at Rome, I believe he himself has been enrolled among the idols, if indeed he and the god Quirinus <note>The deified form of Romulus</note> are the same. With such founders, the four-horse chariots have naturally clothed their drivers in the colors of idolatry. For in the beginning there were only two colors: white and red. White was dedicated to winter because of the bright snow, and red to summer because of the sun's heat. But later, as both pleasure and superstition advanced, some dedicated red to **Mars**, others white to the **Zephyrs** <note>The West Winds</note>, green to **Mother Earth** (or the spring), and blue to the **Sky and Sea** (or the autumn).

---

<gloss>2. *Trochilus*. The Agobardus Codex reads *Prophylus*. Gangneius and Gelenius read *Acrophilus*. Pamelius, Rigaltius, and Oehler read *Trochilus*. Oehler notes that Jerome attributed the invention of the chariot to both Erichthonius and Trochilus.</gloss>

<gloss>3. *For in the beginning*. Variations in the manuscripts suggest "For at the beginning of the horses" or "And from the beginning only two." The reading used here is a reconstruction. The "horses" are omitted to focus on the two colors. These colors were adopted by rival factions with intense passion—the **Green Faction** <term>factio prasina</term> and the **Red Faction** <term>factio russea</term>—and there were specific "Lords of the Faction" in the Circus. See Suetonius, *Life of Nero*, ch. 5. The poet Martial (Epigrams x. 48, 23) refers to the danger of</gloss>

<column-break/>

openly favoring a racing faction that the emperor opposed: *“Let my guest speak of the Green and the Blue; let our cups not make anyone a defendant.”* <note>In Rome, backing the "wrong" team could be seen as a political statement against the Emperor's preferred colors</note>. Compare Pliny the Younger (Letters ix. 6): *“If, however, they were drawn by the speed of the horses or the skill of the men, there would be some reason for it; but now they favor a scrap of cloth, they love a scrap of cloth, and if in the middle of the course and the heat of the contest this color were swapped for that, their zeal and favor would follow the color, and they would suddenly abandon those drivers whom they recognize from a distance and whose names they shout.”*

<margin>CHAPTER IX.</margin>
Since every form of idolatry is condemned by God, it follows that any form which is profaned by being dedicated to the elements of the world <note>Tertullian refers to the worship of physical things like the sun, moon, and earth, which he calls "worldly elements"</note> is also condemned.

<margin>CHAPTER X.</margin>
<margin>Of stage-plays both the place and art are idolatrous.</margin>
Let us now move on to the matters of the stage. We have already shown that their origin is shared with other games and their titles are similar, as they were named and managed alongside the equestrian events from the beginning. Their elaborate preparations are shared as well; the procession to the stage moves from temples and altars with all that wretched business of incense and blood <note>original: "infelicitate thuris et sanguinis"</note> amid the sound of flutes and trumpets. It is presided over by two of the most polluted masters of funerals and sacrifices: the funeral director <term>designatore</term> <note>A master of ceremonies who arranged funeral processions and assigned seating in the theater</note> and the soothsayer <term>haruspex</term> <note>A priest who interpreted the will of the gods by inspecting the entrails of sacrificed animals</note>. Just as we moved from the origins of the games to those of the Circus, we now direct our course to the theatrical shows, starting from the inherent vice of the place. The theater is, properly speaking, a shrine to **Venus**. Indeed, this is how this type of building managed to survive in the world. For the censors <note>High-ranking Roman officials responsible for public morality</note> often destroyed the theaters as soon as they began to rise again, looking out for the people's morals, which they saw were in great danger from... <meta>catchword: from</meta>

---

sion; but funeral processions being most common, he became to be considered as especially belonging to funerals. So the *soothsayer* was concerned with the offices of the dead. *Apology, chapter 13: "For even the soothsayer appears for the dead."* <note>original: "Nam et haruspex mortuis apparet."</note>

<sup>3</sup> *we have passed.* This is a conjecture of Junius adopted by Oehler, and previously by La Cerda. The ancient reading is *we pass*. Above *chapter 9, line 4*. Gangnaeus and Gelenius read *it passes*, where Pamelius, from the Clementine Codex, has *it has passed*. "Since from the origins of Games we made a transition to the Circensian, we now direct our course to theatrical shows, starting from the corruptness of the locality." Tertullian had discussed the origins and titles of Games both

<column-break/>

of the Circus and Theater, (*chapters 5, 6*). When he came to equipment, he was led especially to the Circus, and confined himself entirely to the Circus in the question of place and art. He now therefore, after again briefly touching on the equipment, considers the place and art of theatrical shows.

<margin>CHAPTER X.</margin>
...they viewed these things as wantonness. Thus, from this point, the heathens’ own judgment serves as a testimony for us; their own human regulations provide a precedent that reinforces our own strictness <note>original: "ut jam hinc... humanæ prærogativa". Tertullian is saying that if even the "immoral" Romans had laws against theater, Christians should be even more careful.</note>. Therefore, **Pompey the Great**—a man smaller only than his own massive theater—once he had built that citadel of every kind of filth, feared that the censors <note>High-ranking Roman officials who guarded public morality</note> might one day punish his memory. Therefore, he placed a temple of **Venus** at the top of the structure. When he issued an edict calling the people to the dedication, he did not call it a theater, but "the temple of Venus," adding, "under which," he said, "we have placed the tiers of the spectacles." Thus, he used the title of a temple to cloak a work that was already condemned (and destined for further condemnation), using superstition to bypass moral discipline.

But this arrangement suits both **Venus** and **Liber** <note>Also known as Bacchus, the god of wine and theater</note>. These two demons are joined in a conspiracy: the demons of drunkenness and lust. Thus, a theater dedicated to Venus is also the home of Liber. Indeed, other stage-plays were specifically named the <term>Liberalia</term> <note>A Roman festival in honor of Liber</note>, and besides being dedicated to Liber (just as the <term>Dionysia</term> <note>Festivals of Dionysus/Bacchus</note> are among the Greeks), they were also established by Liber...

...protected. And it is quite clear that within the theatrical arts, too, **Liber** <note>Also known as Bacchus, the god of wine, ecstasy, and the theater</note> and **Venus** <note>The goddess of love and sexual desire</note> hold patronage. <margin>CHAPTER X.</margin>
The things that are private and unique to the stage—the gestures and the fluid movement of the body—they offer up as a sacrifice⁹ of effeminacy¹⁰ to **Venus** and **Liber**¹¹; the former [Venus] through her sex, the latter [Liber] through his fluid wantonness¹². But those things which are performed through voice, melodies, instruments, and lyres have **Apollo**, the **Muses**, **Minerva**, and **Mercury** as their patrons¹³. You should hate these things, O Christian, since you cannot help but hate their authors. Now we wish to suggest something about the arts and those whose authors we detest by their names¹⁴. We know that the names of the dead are nothing, just as their idols themselves are nothing; but we are not ignorant of who works under those names and established idols, and who rejoices in them and feigns divinity—namely, wicked spirits, demons. We see, therefore, that even the arts are dedicated to the honors of those who inhabit the names of their authors; nor are these arts free from idolatry, since their founders are even regarded as gods for that reason.

**CHAPTER X.** Indeed, as far as the arts are concerned, we ought to have established our rule from a deeper source <note>original: "altius præscripsisse debemus"</note>¹⁵—namely, that the demons, looking ahead for themselves from the beginning, intended the filth of the spectacles to be among the other pollutions of idolatry. Their goal was to use these to call man away from the Lord and bind him to their own honor; thus, they inspired the inventions of such arts. For these things would not have been provided by any others than those to whom they were ultimately destined to belong. Nor would they have brought these arts into the world through any other men than those very individuals in whose names, images, and histories they had established the trickery of a consecration <note>The process of declaring someone or something divine</note> that would serve their business¹⁷.

<margin>The same is the case as to the origin, titles, equipment, place, and art of the Stadium:</margin> **CHAPTER XI.** To ensure the proper order is followed, let us also enter into the matter of the athletic contests¹

**CHAPTER XI.** ¹ *contests.* <note>original: "agonum"</note> Tertullian briefly considers these contests <term>agones: Greek-style athletic competitions, as opposed to the Roman "ludi" or games</term> under the categories of *origin*, *titles*, *equipment*, *place*, and *arts*. In Greece, *agones* were what the *ludi* were in Rome, and they shared a common origin. Although Tarquinius Priscus is said to have introduced boxers <note>original: "pugiles"</note> into the Circus, the only games that became truly national at Rome were the chariot races. C. Fulvius first introduced athletes after the Aetolian war in 186 B.C.; and in later days, Greek Games became fashionable under the name of *Agones*. *The Antidote for the Scorpion’s Sting* chapter 6: "With how much favor the world celebrates these contests—contentious ceremonies and superstitious competitions of both Greek religions and pleasures—is clear even in Africa." <note>original: "Agonas istos contentiosa solemnia... etiam Africæ liquuit."</note> There was a "Circus of Contests" <note>original: "Circus Agonalis"</note> at Rome, and Panvinius <note>Onuphrius Panvinius, a 16th-century historian of Roman antiquities</note> illustrates a coin representing the Emperor Aurelian sacrificing at the turning-posts <note>original: "metæ"</note>, inscribed "The Augustan Agonalia of Aurelian the Augustus."

<margin>CHAPTER XI.</margin>
...reviewed. These contests share a common origin with the games already mentioned. Because of this, they are established as either sacred or funeral rites, performed either for the gods of the nations or for the deceased. Thus, their titles reflect this: the **Olympian Games** <note>original: "Olympia"</note> are for Jupiter (which are called the **Capitoline** games in Rome); the **Nemean** are for Hercules; the **Isthmian** for Neptune; and the rest are contests held for the dead. This involves profane crowns, priestly presiding officials, attendants from the various religious guilds², and finally, the very blood of slaughtered bulls. and of the Amphitheatre.

There remains for us to review that most distinguished and most popular spectacle. It is called a **Gift** <term>munus: plural "munera"; originally a "gift" or service paid to the dead, which evolved into the gladiatorial games</term> from the word for "duty" <note>original: "officio"</note>, since "duty" is also a name for a gift. The ancients believed they were performing a duty to the dead with this spectacle, though they later tempered it with a more "civilized" cruelty <note>original: "humaniore atrocitate"</note>. In olden times, because it was believed that the souls of the deceased were appeased by human blood, people would purchase captives or slaves of poor character and sacrifice them at funeral rites. Later, it pleased them to [disguise] this impiety⁴—

---

*...by running and boxing, wrestling and horse-racing until a certain victory is reached, established in the circus; in the seating area through singing, the voice, and the lyre and flutes, provided these things are moderate, as prescribed by law.* The erection and use of stadia was more common under the emperors. The stadium was especially for athletic and musical contests, both of exotic <note>non-Roman, primarily Greek</note> growth. In the vast Baths built during the empire there was always a stadium for athletes. So Martial writes in his *Epigrams* (iii. 68): *A gymnasium, the Baths, and a stadium are in this area; go back, we are stripping, spare yourself the sight of naked men.*

**CHAPTER XII.** ...in these idols, however, demons dwell. Let us also consider the titles of the offices. Even though this type of public show <note>original: "editionis"</note> has shifted from honoring the dead to honoring the living—I am speaking of **quaestorships** <term>quæsturas: an entry-level Roman magistracy responsible for the treasury and games</term>, and other magistracies, and **flamenships** <term>flaminia: the office of a flamen, a priest assigned to a specific state deity</term> and priesthoods—the dignity of the name is still held by the crime of idolatry. It is necessary that whatever is administered in the name of that dignity also shares the stains of its origin. We should interpret the equipment used by the officials on their platforms in the same way: the purple robes, the **bundles of rods** <term>fasces: a bundle of wooden rods, sometimes with an axe, symbolizing a magistrate's power</term>, the sacred headbands, the crowns, and finally the speeches and edicts⁹, and the **previous day's porridge** <note>original: "pultes pridianæ"</note>¹⁰; none of these exist without the devil’s parade and the invitation of demons. Why should I finish my speech by describing that horrid place—the amphitheatre—which not even those who commit perjury can endure¹¹? For the amphitheatre is consecrated with more and harsher names than the Capitol, which is the temple of all demons¹². As many unclean spirits sit there as the place holds men. To conclude regarding the arts involved: we know that Mars and Diana are the presiding deities of both types of games <note>Mars for the gladiators, Diana for the animal hunts</note>.

<margin>
**CHAPTER XIII.**
These idola-
</margin>
I believe I have sufficiently fulfilled the order of explaining how many and what—

---

⁹ *quaestorships, etc.*—referring to the custom of magistrates hosting **gifts** <note>original: "munera"</note> to celebrate their appointment. See Lipsius, *Saturnalia* i. ch. 9.

¹⁰ *dignity of the name*. The honor attached to the titles of *flamen* and *priest* was clearly idolatrous. Tertullian regards all pagan magistracies in the same light. In *On Idolatry*, ch. 18, he says: "For the demons are the magistrates of this world" <note>original: "Nam dæmonia magistratus sunt sæculi"</note>.

¹¹ *speeches and edicts*. The gladiatorial games began with public addresses and proclamations. Pamelius quotes Livy, book ii, ch. 24: "He then gave credibility to the assembly by an edict, in which he decreed that no one should hold a Roman citizen in chains or confinement."

<column-break/>

¹² *previous day's porridge*. Dodgson considers this an allusion to the feasts given to gladiators the night before a combat. See note 2 in this chapter and below, ch. 18, n. 3. More likely, it refers to the custom of placing offerings of food and cakes before the gods. Arnobius, book vii, p. 235.

¹³ *which not even those who commit perjury can endure*. A place too terrible even for the pagans to swear falsely in. It was customary to take oaths in the Capitol; Tertullian uses this as an argument for the local terrors of the amphitheatre, suggesting that men were more afraid of the demons there than they were when swearing falsely in the Capitol.

<summary>Tertullian argues that Roman political offices and the amphitheatre are inherently demonic because of their roots in idolatry and sacrifice. He asserts that even the symbols of authority, like purple robes and the fasces, are part of a "devil's parade."</summary>

<keywords>idolatry, Roman magistrates, quaestorship, flamen, fasces, amphitheatre, demons, Mars, Diana, gladiatorial games, Capitolium</keywords>

<margin>CH. XIII.</margin>
<margin>These monstrous exhibitions are utterly unfit for those who have at their baptism renounced idols. 1 Cor. viii. 4.</margin>
...in [various] ways, the spectacles commit idolatry: through their origins, their titles, their equipment, their locations, and their crafts <note>original: "artificiis"</note>¹, which makes us certain that they in no way belong to us—we who have twice renounced idols². It is not because "an idol is anything," as the Apostle says, but because "what they do, they do for demons," who reside in the consecrations of these idols, whether they are of the dead or, as the pagans believe, of gods. Therefore, because both types of idols are of the same nature—since the dead and the "gods" are essentially one—we abstain from both forms of idolatry³. We despise temples⁴ no less than we despise tombs; we recognize the altar of neither, we adore the image of neither, we do not offer sacrifice, and we do not perform funeral rites <note>original: "parentamus"</note>. Furthermore, we do not eat of what has been sacrificed⁵ or offered at a funeral, because we cannot eat "the supper of the Lord and the supper of demons."

<margin>1 Cor. x. 21.</margin>
If, therefore, we keep our gullet and our belly free from such defilements, how much more should we keep our more noble senses—our eyes and ears—away from pleasures offered to idols <term>idolothytis: food or entertainment dedicated to a pagan deity</term> and pleasures offered to the dead <term>necrothytis: rituals or gifts dedicated to the deceased</term>.

15 *Mars and Diana. Mars* presiding over the **gladiators**, *Diana* over the **hunters**. *Martial, On the Spectacles 12: Amidst the cruel dangers of Caesar’s Diana. Cassiodorus, Variae v. 42: in honor of the Scythian Diana.*

² *who [have] twice [renounced] idols. Gangnaeus reads "to whom." The Ag., Gel.* and *Pamelius manuscripts read "who."* The reading in the text is a conjecture by Ursinus. Compare *On the Crown ch. 3*.

<margin>CH. XIV.</margin>
<margin>Shows are forbidden not only as being idolatrous, but also as included among worldly lusts;</margin>
Now, having set the charge <note>original: "nomine"</note> of idolatry before us—which alone should be sufficient for the renunciation of the shows—let us further discuss the matter for good measure <term>ex abundanti: doing more than is strictly necessary to prove a point</term>, especially for the sake of those who flatter themselves with the idea that this abstinence is not specifically commanded by name, as if too little were pronounced against spectacles when "worldly lusts" are condemned. <margin>Tit. 2:12.</margin> For just as there is a lust for money, or for status, or for gluttony, or for libido, or for glory, so too there is a lust for pleasure. Furthermore, spectacles are a species of pleasure. I believe that lusts, when named in a general sense, include pleasures within them; likewise, when pleasures are understood generally, they are specifically branched out into the spectacles.

-># ON THE SHOWS<-
<columns>2</columns>

<margin>CH. XV.</margin>
<margin>Eph. 4:30, 31.</margin>
Therefore, as we have said, since the primary indictment is idolatry, let us now consider all the other qualities of these entertainments which are contrary to God <note>Footnote 2 discusses textual variations here; some scholars suggest the phrase means "let us set the activities of the shows against the discipline of God."</note>. God commands us to treat the Holy Spirit—who is, by the goodness of His own nature, tender and delicate—with tranquility, gentleness, quiet, and peace. We are not to disturb Him with fury, bitterness <note>original: "bile," literally bile or gall, associated in ancient medicine with anger</note>, wrath, or grief. How can the Holy Spirit be compatible with the shows? For there is no spectacle that does not involve a violent agitation of the spirit. For where there is pleasure, there is also a passionate interest <term>studium: a devoted partisanship or "fandom" for a particular performer or team</term>, which is what gives pleasure its flavor. Where there is this passionate interest, there is also rivalry <term>aemulatio: a jealous or competitive spirit</term>, which gives that interest its zest. Furthermore, where there is rivalry, there you also find fury, bitterness, wrath, grief, and all the other things that spring from them—none of which are compatible with our Christian discipline. Even if a person enjoys the shows in a moderate and upright manner—as befits their rank, age, or natural temperament—their mind is still not truly motionless; they cannot avoid a quiet, hidden passion of the spirit. No one approaches pleasure without some emotion; no one experiences emotion without its own particular "accidents" or outbursts <note>original: "casibus suis"</note>. These very accidents are themselves the incitements...

<column-break/>

...the roar of the entire crowd struck him [Alypius] with great force, and overcome by curiosity... he opened his eyes, and was struck with a deeper wound in his soul than the man whom he desired to see was struck in the body; he fell more miserably than the gladiator whose fall had caused the roar. <note>This refers to a famous passage in St. Augustine's *Confessions* (Book 6, Chapter 8) about his friend Alypius, who was addicted to the gladiatorial games against his better judgment.</note> Oehler follows the interpretation of La Cerda. But it is better understood this way: "No one comes to an entertainment without passion; no one feels passion without its incidentals. The incidentals are themselves stimulants of passion." Here, "emotion" <note>original: "affectus"</note> is a quiet passion of the spirit—the gratification of which constitutes enjoyment—while "its incidentals" <note>original: "casus sui"</note> are the emotions triggered by that passion, such as bitterness...

<summary>Tertullian argues that the shows are spiritually harmful because they provoke passions—like rivalry and anger—that are fundamentally incompatible with the gentle and peaceful nature of the Holy Spirit.</summary>
<keywords>Holy Spirit, emotional disturbance, Alypius, St. Augustine, psychological impact of entertainment, rivalry, Christian discipline</keywords>

CH. XV. **emotion**. <note>original: "affectus," referring to the state of being moved by passion or external stimuli</note> Furthermore, if emotion ceases, there is no pleasure; and the person is then guilty of vanity <term>vanitas: in this context, a useless or spiritually empty pursuit</term> by attending where nothing is gained. I believe, however, that even vanity is foreign to us. What of the fact that a person judges himself by placing himself among those whom he surely confesses to detest, despite himself? It is not enough for us if we ourselves do nothing of the sort, unless we also avoid being associated with those who do such things. <margin>Psalm 50:18</margin> *If you saw a thief,* the scripture says, *you ran with him.* Would that we did not even dwell in the world <term>saeculum: the physical world or the current "age" of man</term> along with them! But nonetheless, we are separated in "worldly things" <margin>1 John 2:16</margin> <note>original: "saecularibus," specifically the sinful habits and pomps of the age</note>, because the world belongs to God, but worldly things belong to the devil.

## CH. XVI.
<margin>CH. XVI. The prohibition of rage prohibits the mad rage of the Circus.</margin>
Therefore, since fury <note>original: "furor," a state of madness or uncontrolled rage</note> is forbidden to us, we are removed from every spectacle, even from the Circus, where fury properly presides. Look at the people already arriving at the spectacle with fury, already tumultuous, already blind, already excited over their wagers <note>original: "sponsionibus," the bets placed on chariot teams</note>. The [charioteer is] slow...

---

<note>Footnote 1: **furor.** The "madness of the Circus" was a common saying. Apuleius (Metamorphoses 10.29) writes: "Led into the enclosure of the theater with pompous fury." Lactantius (Divine Institutes Epitome, c. 9) says: "The Circus is actually considered more innocent, but the fury here is greater; indeed the minds of the spectators are carried away by such insanity that they often rise not only to insults, but to brawls and even into battles and disputes." Lucian (Nigrinus, c. 29) says in Greek: "Turning away from these things, he remembered other men, and recounted the disturbances in the city, the shoving, the theaters, the racecourse, the statues of the charioteers, the names of the horses, and the conversations in the alleys about these things; for truly the horse-madness [hippomania] is great and has seized many who are thought to be serious people."</note>

<column-break/>

<note>Footnote 1 continued: A memorable instance is that of the Emperor Caligula’s fury when the people favored a different team color from his own. Suetonius (Life of Caligula, c. 30) writes: "Hostile to the crowd raging against his own preference, he cried out: 'I wish the Roman people had only one neck!'" On a similar occasion, the Emperor Caracalla sent soldiers into the crowd with instructions to kill everyone who spoke against his faction.</note>

<note>Footnote 2: **sponsionibus**, "wagers laid upon the races." Oehler quotes Juvenal (Satire 11.199): "Let the young men watch, whom the noise and bold betting [Sponsio] suits, and whom it becomes to sit by a well-dressed girl." Martial (Epigrams 11.1) writes: "But when the betting and the tired talk about Scorpus [a famous charioteer] or Incitatus [a famous horse] are over..." Petronius (c. 70) writes: "He began [to bet with] his master..."</note>

<summary>Tertullian argues that Christians must avoid the Circus because its inherent atmosphere of "fury" and "vanity" is spiritually incompatible with the Holy Spirit. He uses the obsessive betting and fanatical violence of the Roman races as evidence of this madness.</summary>

<margin>CH. XVI.</margin>
The praetor³ <term>praetor: the Roman magistrate who presided over and funded the public games</term> is there for them: their eyes are always rolling in his urn along with the lots <note>original: "sortibus," refers to the drawing of lots for starting positions</note>: then they hang anxious for his signal; the voice of a single madness is as one. Witness their madness from its very vanity. "He has sent it!" they cry, and they announce to one another what was seen by everyone at the same moment. I hold here the evidence of their blindness: they do not even see what was "sent." They think it is a napkin <note>original: "mappa," the white cloth dropped to start the race</note>, but it is actually an image⁵ <note>original: "figura"</note> of the devil cast down from on high. From that moment, they fall into furies, passions, and discords⁶, and everything that is not permitted to the priests of peace⁷ <term>priests of peace: a reference to the Christian belief that all believers serve as a "royal priesthood"</term>. From this come curses and insults without the justice of a real grievance, and even applause without the merit of true love. For what of their own will those who act there achieve, since they do not even belong to themselves? Except perhaps this one thing, by which they cease to be their own masters: they are saddened by another’s misfortune and delighted by another’s happiness. Whatever they desire, whatever they loathe, is foreign to them: thus, their love is idle and their hatred is unjust. And perhaps⁸ without

⁶ *let them blush*. The light in which even the pagans regarded these spectacles may be seen from the following law, *On Divorces* <note>original: "De repudiis"</note>, quoted by Lipsius in *On Amphitheaters*, chapter 3:

> *A man shall in no way expel his wife unless she is an adulteress, or if she delights in the Circus, theater, or arena spectacles against his prohibition.*

See also a letter of Pliny, *Letters* VII. 24. The Emperor Julian <note>Julian the Apostate, the last pagan emperor</note> in a decree for the reformation of the pagan religion, prescribes to all priests abstinence from the circus, theater, and amphitheater. Julian, *Works*, p. 555 (Paris, 1630). *Once a year* <note>original: "Semel anno"</note>, at the annual celebration of the Floralia.

<summary>Tertullian continues his condemnation of the theater, focusing on the sexual exploitation of performers and the public display of prostitutes during festivals like the Floralia. He argues that the Senate and all citizens should be ashamed of these spectacles, which openly celebrate behavior that would be scandalous in private.</summary>

<margin>CH. XIX.</margin> ...the guilty are punished. Who but a guilty person would deny this? And yet, an innocent person cannot rejoice in the punishment of another, since it is more fitting for the innocent to grieve that a fellow human being has become so guilty that he is so cruelly executed. Who, moreover, can guarantee to me that it is always the guilty who are condemned to the wild beasts or to whatever punishment, such that no injury is ever inflicted upon innocence—either by the judge's desire for revenge, or the weakness of the defense, or the pressure of interrogation? 

How much better it is, then, to be ignorant of when the wicked are punished, lest I also know when the good perish—if indeed they have any taste for the good <note>original: "si tamen bonum sapiunt," which the commentator notes is a qualification added to limit the term "good" when applied to any pagan. See Tertullian's *On Idolatry*, ch. 1: "they have a taste against the Lord."</note>. Certainly, at least, innocent gladiators <note>original: "innocentes," referring to volunteers in such contests (see Suetonius’ *Life of Julius Caesar*, ch. 39, and Juvenal’s *Satires* 11. 143, etc.), or captives in war, or hired combatants.</note> come into the arena to become victims for the public’s pleasure <note>original: "publicae voluptatis." Arnobius (Book II, p. 72) writes: "in the other [amphitheater] they might see men eaten and torn apart by the mangling of wild beasts; others killing each other for no deserving cause, but to gratify the pleasure and delight of the spectators." Apuleius (*Metamorphoses*, IV. 13) mentions a man who "was preparing public pleasures with the splendor of his fortune." Same work, IV. 14: "the splendid apparatus of public pleasure."</note>. 

Even for those who are condemned <note>original: "damnantur." Apuleius (*Metamorphoses*, IV. 13) calls wild beasts procured for the amphitheater "those noble funerals for condemned heads."</note> to the arena, what kind of thing is it that they "progress" through correction from a lighter crime to becoming murderers? But I have said these things in response to the heathens. For the rest, far be it that a Christian should learn any longer about the turning away from this spectacle. Although no one can express all these things more fully than one who still watches them, I prefer to leave the account incomplete than to remember them <note>Tertullian implies that as a Christian, he no longer attends these shows and finds the memory of his past attendance distressing.</note>.

It is vain then to ask for special prohibitions in Scripture.</margin> How vain, then—or rather, how desperate—is the argument of those who, beyond doubt, [resort to] a way to avoid admitting...

<summary>Tertullian argues that even if the spectators are "innocent" of the crimes being punished, rejoicing in the cruel execution of others—guilty or not—is incompatible with Christian grief and compassion. ...they use pleasure as a pretext <note>original: "voluptatis." The commentator notes that some manuscripts suggest this refers to a "shuffling" or "evasion" to avoid giving up pleasure.</note>, claiming that no mention of this abstinence is specifically or locally determined in the Scriptures that directly forbids a servant of God from attending such gatherings. I recently heard a new defense from a certain "pleasure-lover" <note>original: "suaviludii," a term for one who enjoys games or spectacles; see Tertullian's *On the Soldier's Crown*, ch. 6.</note>. "The sun," he says, "nay, even God himself looks down from heaven and is not contaminated." To be sure, the sun sends its rays even into the sewer and is not polluted. You are comparing, O man, the criminal and the judge: the criminal, who is guilty because he is seen, and the judge, who is judge because he sees. Do we then pursue madness outside the boundaries of the Circus? Or do we devote ourselves to immodesty outside the doors of the theater? ...rather leave my subject incomplete than bring them to my recollection." Tertullian had, it seems, before he was a Christian, been a passionate lover of these shows.

<summary>Tertullian debunks the argument that Christians can attend spectacles because God sees everything without being defiled, arguing that while God sees all, He does so as a Judge, and believers should avoid being seen by Him in places of sin.</summary>

**CHAPTER XX.** ...[God's eyes reach even beyond the galleries, and] never is that excused which God condemns. Nowhere and never is that permitted which is always and everywhere forbidden. This is the integrity of truth, and the fullness of discipline owed to it, as well as the consistency of our fear of God and the faithfulness of our obedience: to not change our opinion nor vary our judgment. What is truly good or truly evil cannot be anything else. For all things are fixed according to the truth of God.

<margin>CH. XXI. The heathen gaze with delight in the Circus, Theater, and Amphitheater, on things at which they elsewhere shudder.</margin>
The heathens—who possess no fullness of truth because God is not the teacher of truth—interpret good and evil according to their own whim and lust. They call something good in one place which they call evil in another, and evil in one place which is good elsewhere. Thus it happens that the same man who would hardly lift his tunic in public, even for the necessity of the bladder, will rejoice in the Circus in no other way than by exposing his whole sense of shame before the faces of all. He who protects the ears of his virgin daughter from every filthy word leads her himself to the theater to hear those very voices and see those gestures. And he who in the streets either restrains or detests a man settling a quarrel with his fists...

---

**Chapter XXI.** $^1$ *whips and rods* <note>original: "flagellis et virgis"</note>. Lipsius (in his work *Saturnalia*, Book II, ch. 5) quotes from Seneca’s *Letter 7*, capturing the language of the infuriated populace: "Kill him, burn him, whip him! Why does he run so timidly into the sword? Why does he kill with so little boldness? Why does he die so reluctantly? They are driven into their wounds by lashes, and they receive mutual blows with bare and exposed chests."

$^2$ *to every more notorious murderer* <note>original: "insigniori cuique homicidæ"</note>. Apuleius (*Metamorphoses* x. 28) gives an account of a woman who had committed murder and other crimes: "And he pronounced that she—though it was less than she deserved, but because no other torture could be devised—should be openly thrown to the beasts." Lactantius, *Divine Institutes*

<column-break/>

Book VI, ch. 20: "For he who considers the slaughter of a man to be a pleasure in his sight—even if that man is condemned for his crimes—pollutes his conscience; surely he is as guilty as if he were a witness and accomplice to a murder committed in secret."

$^3$ *the wooden sword and the cap* <note>original: "rudem et pileum." The <term>rudis</term> was a wooden sword given to gladiators as a sign of their discharge from service; the <term>pileum</term> was a felt cap worn by freed slaves, symbolizing the gladiator's liberation.</note>. Martial, *On the Spectacles* 29: "Caesar sent the wooden swords to both, and the palms of victory to both."

$^4$ *as for that man...* <note>original: "illum vero..."</note> "Moreover it comes to pass, that he calls again for the gladiator who has received his death-blow, in order that he may gaze upon his face." The savage delight of the people in scenes of blood is shown by the mimic representation of the cruel death of Laureolus <note>Laureolus was a famous stage character, a bandit whose execution was often enacted realistically in the arena using a condemned criminal</note>. Juvenal, *Satires* VIII, 187; Martial, *On the Spectacles* 7.

<margin>CH. XXII.</margin>
<margin>Romans 1:32.</margin>
...they even prostitute their own bodies <note>original: "corpora sua substernunt"</note> for those very people on whose account they commit the things they condemn. On the same side from which they glorify them, they degrade and diminish them—indeed, they openly condemn them with disgrace <note>original: "ignominia"</note> and the loss of civil rights <term>capitis minutio|In Roman law, this was a reduction in a person's legal status, stripping them of certain rights of citizenship</term>. They bar them from the council house, the public platform <note>original: "rostris," the speaker's platform in the Roman Forum</note>, the senate, the equestrian order, and all other honors as well as certain official distinctions. What perversity! They love those whom they punish; they disparage those whom they approve; they glorify the art, but brand the artist with shame. What kind of judgment is this—that a person should be tarnished by the very things for which he earns favor? Rather, what a confession of an evil thing it is, when its authors—though they are most popular—cannot escape being marked with disgrace.

It is clear then that these are the ‘pomps of the devil’ which we have renounced.

**CH. XXIV.** In how many ways shall we yet argue that none of these things which are assigned to the spectacles are pleasing to God, or suitable for the servants of God—since what is not pleasing to the Lord is not fit for His servants? If we have shown that all these things were instituted for the sake of the devil and constructed from the devil’s resources (for nothing belongs to anyone but the devil if it is not of God or if it displeases God), then this is the "pomp of the devil" <note>original: "pompa diaboli"; the idolatrous ceremonial procession that opened the games</note> which we renounce in the "seal of faith"¹ <note>original: "signaculo fidei"; a common early Christian term for the sacrament of baptism and its accompanying vows</note>. Furthermore, that which we renounce, we must not participate in by deed, word, sight, or even by looking toward it. Otherwise, do we not break our oath and void the seal by voiding our testimony of it? Is there anything left, then, but to demand an answer from the pagans <note>original: "ethnicis"</note> themselves? Let them tell us whether it is lawful for Christians to attend the spectacles. Indeed, it is by this very thing that they most clearly understand a person has become a Christian: by their rejection of the spectacles. Therefore, he who [attends] clearly denies [his faith]...

⁹ <note>translator: This note clarifies a difficult passage regarding arena violence.</note> *I say nothing of that man...* Rigaltius by conjecture reads "who" for "than he who," explaining that sometimes when the beasts were let in, one gladiator to save himself thrust another forward; if that man survived the lion, he might then be killed by the first gladiator, who would thus be twice a murderer. This interpretation is approved by Oehler, but seems forced. The reading of the manuscripts, "than he who," is adopted by La Cerda, who believes "the one who cuts the throat" refers to the lion. But there is little probability in this. The contrast lies between

<column-break/>

the gladiator who, as far as he can, causes the death of another by thrusting him toward the lion, and the person who actually puts him to death. If after a gladiator had fought, the people demanded his death, another person killed him <note>original: "jugulabat"</note>. "I say nothing of the case of him who thrust forward a combatant to the lion to protect himself, lest he be thought less of a murderer than the person who later cuts the same combatant’s throat." Ch. XXV.
Presence at these shows is incompatible with prayer and meditation.
</margin>
Will that person think of God at that time, positioned there where there is nothing of God? He will have "peace" in his soul, I suppose, while screaming for a chariot-driver <note>original: "auriga"</note>, and he will learn "modesty" while staring stunned at the mimes <note>original: "mimos"</note>! On the contrary, in every spectacle, no scandal is more common than the overly careful dress of the women and men. Their very togetherness—that specific collaboration or disagreement in their favoritism¹ <note>original: "favoribus"; refers to the passionate support for different racing factions like the "Blues" or "Greens"</note>—fans the sparks of lust from their shared contact. Finally, no one enters a spectacle with any thought other than to be seen and to see. While the tragic actor is shouting out his cries, will that man reflect on the words of some prophet? And amidst the melodies of an effeminate actor, will he hum a psalm to himself? And when the athletes are competing, will he be ready to say that "one must not strike back"? <margin>Matthew 5:39.</margin> Can he be moved by mercy while staring fixedly at the bites of bears and the "sponges"² <note>original: "spongias"; used to wipe up blood from the arena floor</note> of the net-fighters <note>original: "retiariorum"</note>? # TERTULLIAN’S BOOK

<margin>2 Corinthians 6:14</margin> [Chapter XXVI] ...serve masters. What has light to do with darkness? What has life to do with death?

### CHAPTER XXVII. We ought to avoid these hotbeds of corruption, even though the devil seasons his poison with some show of excellence.

We must hate these gatherings and assemblies of the pagans, both because the name of God is blasphemed there, and because the daily cry for the "lions" <note>This refers to the "Christianos ad leones" (Christians to the lions) chant often heard in the Roman arena during persecutions</note> to be set upon us is raised there. From such places, decrees for persecution are decided and temptations are sent out. What will you do when you are caught in that swirling tide of impious cheers? I do not mean that you would suffer anything there at the hands of men (for no one recognizes you as a Christian), but consider what becomes of you in heaven. Do you doubt that at that very moment when the devil is in his assembly <note>original Latin: "in ecclesia," often translated as "church," but here meaning the devil's gathering</note>, all the angels look down from heaven and take note of every individual? They mark who has spoken blasphemy and who has listened to it; who has lent their tongue and who their ears to the devil against God. <margin>Psalm 1:1</margin> Will you not then flee the seats of the enemies of Christ—that "seat of pestilence"—and the very air that hangs over it, which is defiled by wicked voices? Let the shows be sweet, if you like, and pleasing and simple, or even honorable in some respects. No one mixes poison with gall and hellebore <note>A poisonous plant used in ancient medicine</note>, but rather throws that evil into seasoned side-dishes, well-flavored and mostly sweet. So too, the devil takes the lethal thing he prepares and disguises it with the most pleasing and

### ON THE SPECTACLES.
### TERTULLIAN 3

<margin>CHAPTER XXVII.</margin>
...into the most delicious and highly favored things. Consider everything there—whether it be brave or honorable, loud or musical, or subtle—as if they were drops of honey from a poisoned pastry <note>original Latin: *lucunculo*, a small pancake or honey-cake</note>. Do not value the appetite for such pleasure as much as you fear the danger hidden in its sweetness.

<margin>
CHAPTER XXVIII.
These are the pleasures of the heathen; our pleasures are yet to come.
</margin>
Guests of this sort are fattened up on such sweets. The places, the temples, and the one who invites them [the devil] all belong to him. Our feasts, our wedding celebrations are not yet here. We cannot sit at the table with them, because they cannot sit with us. Things are arranged by turns. Now they rejoice, and we are afflicted. <margin>John 16:20.</margin> "The world," He says, "will rejoice, but you will be sorrowful." Let us mourn, then, <note>original Latin: *Lugeamus ergo*</note> while the heathens rejoice, so that when they begin to mourn, we may rejoice; otherwise, if we rejoice with them now, we will also mourn with them then. You are too delicate, Christian, if you desire pleasure in this world; in fact, you are incredibly foolish if you think these things are pleasure. Certain philosophers <note>Tertullian refers here to the Epicureans</note> indeed gave this name "pleasure" to peace and tranquility; in this they find joy, in this they find diversion, and in this they even glory. But you long for the race-course markers, the stage, the dust of the track, and the sand of the arena. I would like to ask you: Can we not live without pleasure, we who ought to die with pleasure? For what else is our prayer...

¹ See above, chapter 15, note 4, *in his own misfortunes.* In *On Idolatry*, chapter 13, *we have already completed his volume.* Drakenborch on *Silius Italicus 12.33*, quotes *Cicero, Letters to Friends 11.11: He has not even yet cast off hope concerning Plancus, as can be noticed from his own notebooks.* *Seneca, Controversies, Book 1 in the preface: Nothing is more serious than that man, nothing more pleasant, nothing more worthy of his eloquence.*
