³ *The philosophers indeed.* The Epicureans. This was the favorite philosophy among the Romans in

<column-break/>

the time of Tertullian. *Lactantius, Divine Institutes 3.17: The school of Epicurus was always much more famous than the others, not because it brings any truth, but because the popular name of "pleasure" invites many.* *Cicero, On the Ends of Good and Evil, 1.11: Epicurus thinks that the highest pleasure is defined by the removal of all pain.* *Apology, chapter 38: The Epicureans were permitted to decide upon some truth regarding pleasure. In what way do we offend you, if we assume other pleasures?* Compare *To the Nations 2.2.*

<summary>Tertullian warns that the "pleasures" of the Roman games are actually poisoned traps for the soul and argues that Christians must sacrifice worldly enjoyment for future heavenly joy.</summary>

<margin>CHAPTER XXIX.</margin>
If these things delight you, we have enough literature, enough verses, enough maxims, enough songs, and enough voices. <note>original: *TERTULLIANI LIBER*</note>

## ON IDOLATRY.
<note>original: *DE IDOLOLATRIA*</note>

---

<margin>CHAPTER I.</margin>
<margin>
Idolatry is the chief crime of mankind. It includes in it murder, theft, adultery, and the like; and every crime is demon-service, and therefore idolatry.
</margin>
**T**HE principal crime of the human race, the supreme guilt of the world <note>original: *summus sæculi reatus*</note>, and the entire reason for judgment is idolatry. For although every offense maintains its own specific form, and although each is assigned for judgment under its own name, yet it is settled <note>original: *expungitur*</note>¹ within the crime of idolatry. Set aside the titles² <note>the specific names of crimes</note>, look at the actions: the idolater is likewise a murderer. You ask whom he has killed? If it helps to complete the scope of the charge <note>original: *ad elogii ambitionem facit*</note>³, I answer: he has killed not a stranger, nor an enemy, but himself. By what snare? That of his own error. With what weapon? The offense against God. With how many blows? As many as there are acts of idolatry. He who denies that the idolater has perished <note>meaning spiritually destroyed</note> will also deny that the idolater has committed murder. Furthermore, you may recognize adultery and sexual immorality in the same person; for

---

Ch. I. ¹ *is settled* <note>original: *expungitur*</note>, ‘is disposed of under the charge of idolatry.’ On the term *to strike out/settle* <note>original: *expungere*</note>, see *On the Crown* <note>original: *De Cor.*</note>, chapter 1, note 4.
² *titles* <note>original: *titulos*</note>, ‘the special names of the several crimes;’ for example, *murder* <note>original: *homicidium*</note>, *sexual immorality* <note>original: *stuprum*</note>, etc. The scholar La Cerda quotes Suetonius' *Life of Caligula*, chapter 32: *“He immediately handed over a slave to the executioner for stripping a silver plate from the couches, so that, with his hands cut off and hanging from his neck in front of his chest, preceded by a title* <note>original: *titulo*</note> *indicating the cause of the punishment, he might be led through the crowds.”* Below, in chapter 11, we see the *title of idolatry*.
³ *If it helps to complete the charge...* <note>original: *Si quid ad elogii...*</note> ‘if it helps to complete the accusation [I answer].’ The term *record/indictment* <note>original: *elogium*</note> means ‘the summary of an accusation,’ as in *On the Crown*, chapter 5: *the record of sacri-*

<column-break/>

*lege against God* <note>original: *elogium sacrilegii in Deum*</note>. Also in *On Fasting* <note>original: *De Jejun.*</note>, chapter 17: *“It pertains to the record of your gluttony* <note>original: *elogium gulæ tuæ*</note>, *that etc.”* La Cerda quotes Suetonius' *Life of Caligula*, chapter 27: *“Reviewing the line of prisoners, without looking at any man's record* <note>original: *nullius inspecto elogio*</note>, *standing only within the middle portico, he ordered them to be led away from one bald man to another.”* The term *scope/circuit* <note>original: *Ambitio*</note> refers to ‘the compass;’ as in *On Fasting*, chapter 17, *the circuit of the body* <note>original: *ambitio corporis*</note>; and *On the Soul* <note>original: *De Anim.*</note>, chapter 25, *the whole extent of the belly* <note>original: *tota ventris ambitio*</note>. Thus, the *scope of the charge* <note>original: *Ambitio elogii*</note> is ‘the accusation set out to its full extent,’ including all the specific details: whom? by what snares? with what weapon? with how many blows? Compare *Against the Nations* <note>original: *Ad Natt.*</note> I. 2: *“Moreover, regarding us, whom you charge with more atrocious and numerous crimes, you draw up shorter and lighter records* <note>original: *elogia*</note>.”

He uses Roman legal terminology to illustrate how an idolater's spiritual self-destruction constitutes a form of homicide.</summary>

<note>original: *TERTULLIANI LIBER*</note>

---

<margin>CHAPTER I.</margin> He who serves false gods is, without a doubt, an adulterer of the truth, because every falsehood is a form of adultery. In this same way, he is also submerged in sexual violation <note>original: *stupro*</note>. For who can be at work for unclean spirits without walking away defiled and debauched? And indeed, the Holy Scriptures use the word "fornication"⁴ <note>original: *stupro*</note> in their condemnation of idolatry. The nature of fraud, I believe, is this: if someone seizes what belongs to another or denies what is owed to another; and certainly, fraud committed against a fellow human is recognized as a most serious crime. But indeed, idolatry commits fraud against God, denying Him His own honors and conferring them on others, so that it joins insult to injury. If, then, fraud as well as sexual violation and adultery bring death, then in these matters too, idolatry is not cleared of the guilt of homicide. After such crimes, so destructive and so devouring of salvation, all other sins as well—though distinct and arranged separately—manifest their own condition⁵ within idolatry. In it are also the lusts of the world. For what festival of idolatry is without the ambition of dress and ornament? In it are wantonness and drunkenness, since for the most part, the concerns of food, the belly, and—

---

⁴ *the word 'fornication'* <note>original: *stupri vocabulo*</note>. Compare Ezekiel chapter 23; Hosea chapters 2 and 4; and elsewhere. <note>In the Bible, spiritual unfaithfulness to God is frequently described using the language of physical adultery or prostitution.</note>
⁵ *condition* <note>original: *conditionem*</note>. *Against Marcion* <note>original: *Adv. Marc.*</note> Book II, chapter 22: *by having far different causes from the condition of idolatry*. *To represent* <note>original: *Repræsentare*</note>, a judicial term, ‘to bring into court;’ hence, ‘to bring before us, whether to our senses or minds.’ *Against Marcion* Book IV, chapter 22: *And so now representing him: This is my son*. *On Repentance* <note>original: *De Pœn.*</note> chapter 3: *to such an extent that what it is forbidden to perform, the mind represents to itself quite dangerously*. *On the Crown* <note>original: *De Cor.*</note> chapter 15: *If such images exist in a vision,

<column-break/>

as truths in representation?* *On the Shows* <note>original: *De Spect.*</note> chapter 17: *the filth which the Atellan performer* <note>a type of comic actor</note> *represents*. Same work, chapter 30: *these things we already possess in a way through faith, represented by the imagining spirit*. *Against Marcion* Book I, chapter 14: *nor the bread, by which he represents his very body*. On the last passage see Bishop Kaye’s *Tertullian* page 427. Even Bellarmine <note>Robert Bellarmine, a prominent 16th-century theologian</note> allows that it is not conclusive for the corporal presence.
⁶ *a lie* <note>original: *mendacium*</note>. Compare Isaiah 44:20.
⁷ *the agents of idols* <note>original: *idolorum mancipes*</note>, ‘those demons who take possession of idols.’ *Apology* <note>original: *Apolog.*</note> chapter 11: *the agent of divinity*.

<summary>Tertullian argues that idolatry is a composite sin that includes adultery, fraud, and murder, specifically because it transfers the honor due to God to false spirits. He connects the spiritual betrayal of idolatry to physical vices like lust and drunkenness.</summary>

<page-num>59</page-num>
# ON IDOLATRY
<note>original: *DE IDOLOLATRIA*</note>

...frequented for the sake of lust. <margin>CHAPTER I.</margin> In that [idolatry] there is also injustice. For what is more unjust than that which does not know the Father of justice? In it also is vanity, since its whole reasoning is vain. In it is a lie⁶, since its whole substance is deceitful. Thus it happens that all things are found in idolatry, and idolatry is found in all things. But also in other respects, since all sins savor of opposition to God, and nothing that savors of opposition to God is not assigned to demons and unclean spirits to whom idols are enslaved <note>original: *mancipantur*</note>, without doubt whoever commits a sin admits idolatry. For he does that which belongs to the agents <note>original: *mancipes*; refers to those who take legal possession or control</note>⁷ of idols.

<margin>CHAPTER II.</margin>
<margin>Idolatry consists not only in the acts of sacrificing, burning incense, and the like, but has a more extended application.</margin>
But let the names of all crimes depart into their own specific categories of deeds; let idolatry remain in what it is itself. A name so hostile to God is sufficient for itself, a substance of crime so rich, which puts forth so many branches and pours out so many veins², that for this reason especially has my subject been taken up: in how many ways we must guard against the breadth of idolatry, since it subverts the servants of God in many ways, not only when it is ignored, but even when it is disguised. Most people think idolatry should be interpreted simply in these ways alone...

---

*On the Spectacles, ch. 10: The statues of Apollo have their agents <note>original: *mancipes*</note>. To the Nations, II. 2: the authority of philosophers, like a possession <note>original: *mancipium*</note> of wisdom. Compare below, ch. 13: consecrated to the gods of human superstition; and On the Spectacles, ch. 12: In the idols of the dead, demons reside. See below, ch. 15, note 8.*

Ch. II. ¹ *But let the general...* "But let the names of sins go their separate ways, and let them be arranged each under the special heading indicated by its action; let idolatry be limited to that which is specifically idolatry; there is enough in a name so hostile to God, in so vast a ground

<column-break/>

for accusation, that puts out so many branches, flows into so many channels, that from this source primarily has my theme been chosen, to show in how many ways we must take precautions against the entire range of idolatry."

² *pours out* <note>original: *defundit*</note>. Rigault suggests this from the word *diffundit* (spreads). La Cerda quotes St. Cyprian, *On Patience, p. 253 (Benedictine Edition): The virtue of Patience is widely spread, and its abundance and generosity proceed from the fountain of a single name, but it is spread through many paths of glory by overflowing veins.*

<margin>
CHAPTER III.
---
Idolatry is service performed to any image, whatever it may represent.
</margin>
...worship <note>original: *latria*; the service or religious devotion due to God</note> was being performed, not under that name, but in that very act. For even today it can be performed outside a temple and without an idol. But when the devil introduced into the world the makers of statues and images and every kind of likeness, that crude business of human calamity also gained both its name and its development from "idols." From then on, every art that produces an idol in any way has become the "head" or source of idolatry. For it makes no difference whether a modeler shapes it, or a carver engraves it, or an embroiderer <note>original: *phrygio*, a textile artist known for intricate Phrygian needlework</note> weaves it; nor does it matter what material it is made from—whether the idol is formed from plaster, or colors, or stone, or bronze, or silver, or thread. Since idolatry can happen even without a physical idol, certainly when an idol *is* present, it does not matter what kind it is, what material it is made of, or what shape it takes, lest anyone think that only a consecrated human figure should be considered an idol. To understand this, an interpretation of the word is necessary. <term>Eidos</term> <note>original: *Εἶδος*</note> in Greek signifies "form"; from this is derived the diminutive <term>eidolon</term> <note>original: *εἴδωλον*, meaning a "little form"</note>, which in our language has likewise produced the word "formula." Therefore, every form or "little form" <note>original: *formula*</note> claims the right to be called an idol. It follows that all "idolatry" is the attendance and service performed around every "idol." Consequently, every maker of an idol is guilty of the same and single crime—unless the people who consecrated for themselves the image of a calf <margin>Exodus 32:8.</margin> and not a man committed only a minor act of idolatry.

<margin>
CHAPTER IV.
---
God condemns both image-worshippers and image-makers.
</margin>
God forbids an idol to be made just as much as He forbids it to be worshipped. Insofar as the making of something that *can* be worshipped must happen first, the prohibition against making it comes first, since its worship is not permitted.

<column-break/>

*do we set up an image or form of any of the gods, etc." Heraldus, in his commentary on Arnobius, book vi. p. 194, adduces numerous passages to the same effect.*
*Chapter IV. ¹ Insofar as it precedes...*

<summary>Tertullian provides an etymological and practical definition of idolatry, arguing that any "form" (Greek: eidos) created by an artist constitutes an idol. ¹ "Just as a thing must first be made before it can be worshipped, so a thing must first be forbidden to be made, if it may not be worshipped." Thus, from every age, even from Adam himself, an image of God could be made to be worshipped. Tertullian is to be praised on this point: for he establishes an equality of time in both. Just as in no age could that be made which could not be worshipped, so in every age could that be made which could be worshipped. Whether indeed this was forbidden to the Jews by written law, two of the most serious doctors of this age disagree: Vasquius <note>Gabriel Vázquez</note> affirms it was prohibited; Soarius <note>Francisco Suárez</note> denies it; finally, I, so small as I am, remain in doubt." The Latin words correspond very nearly to ‘reckoning,’ ‘to be reckoned,’ e.g. *On the Spectacles, chapter 7: it is splendid in the reckoning of its own crime* <note>original: "splendida est censu criminis sui"</note>. *On the Military Crown, chapter 13: in the reckoning of crowns alone* <note>original: "in solo quoque censu coronarum"</note>. *Apology, chapter 7: The reckoning of this discipline is from Tiberius* <note>original: "Census istius disciplinæ a Tiberio est"</note>. ‘We may reckon Christianity from Tiberius.’ So ibid. chapter 12: *from there your gods are reckoned* <note>original: "inde censentur dei vestri"</note>. *On the Military Crown, chapter 10: from the reckoning of its origin* <note>original: "ex originis censu"</note>. *To the Nations, Book I, chapter 12: absolutely every kind refers its reckoning to its origin, and by as much as the kind is reckoned by its order, by so much is the origin met in the kind* <note>original: "omne omnino genus censum ad originem refert, quantoque genus censetur ordine, tanto origo convenitur in genere"</note>. If you look upon the likeness made afterward <note>The bronze serpent mentioned in the previous chapter</note>, you too should imitate Moses: do not make any image against the Law, unless God has commanded it to you as well.

### CHAPTER VI.

<margin>
CHAPTER VI.
Image-makers are image-worshippers.
</margin>
If no law of God had forbidden idols to be made by us, and if no voice of the Holy Spirit threatened the makers of idols no less than their worshippers, we would still deduce from our very oath <note>original: *sacramento*; Tertullian refers here to the baptismal vow, which was viewed as a soldier's oath of loyalty to Christ</note> that arts of this kind are hostile to the faith. For how have we renounced the devil and his angels, if we make them? What kind of rejection have we declared against those—I will not say with whom—but *off of whom* we live? What discord have we taken up against those to whom we are bound for the sake of our maintenance <note>original: *exhibitionis*; referring to the income or "exhibition" gained from the trade of idol-making</note>? Can you deny with your tongue what you confess with your hand? Can you destroy with words what you build up by deeds? Can you preach one God, you who make so many? Can you preach the true God, you who make false ones? "I make them," says someone, "but I do not worship them." As if there were any reason he dare not worship them other than the very reason he ought not make them!

<margin>CHAPTER VI.</margin> ...clearly because of the offense to God in both cases. In fact, you worship them, for you are the one who makes it possible for them to be worshipped. You worship them<sup>4</sup> not with the steam of some cheap sacrificial smoke, but with your own spirit; not by spending the life of a beast, but with your very soul. To them you sacrifice your talent, for them you pour out the libation of your sweat, and for them you light the fire of your wisdom. You are more to them than a priest, since it is because of you that they have a priest; your own hard work<sup>5</sup> <note>original: *diligentia*; implying the careful industry of the craftsman</note> is their divinity. Do you deny that you worship what you make? They certainly do not deny it—those for whom you slaughter a victim that is more gilded and grander<sup>6</sup> than any other: your own salvation.

<margin>
CHAPTER VII.

How monstrous that Christian worshippers, nay, even Christian ministers, should be engaged in idol-making!
</margin>
All day long, the zeal of faith will cry out on this point, groaning that a Christian comes to the church<sup>1</sup> from the idols, that he comes from the workshop of the enemy into the house of God; that he raises 

---

<sup>4</sup> *You worship them*. Observe the sacrificial terms <note>Tertullian uses these technical pagan terms ironically to show the craftsman's "devotion" to his trade</note>: *smoke*, *life of a beast*, *sacrifice*, *libation*, *lighting a fire*, *fattened*, *gilded*, *greater*, *to slaughter a victim*.

<sup>5</sup> *your hard work*. Both Dodgson and Neander translate *diligentia* as if it were a naming noun. It is no doubt an "ablative of means." The sense is: "By your industry their divinity exists."

<sup>6</sup> *more gilded and greater*. In Roman ritual, the horns of sacrificial animals were often covered in gold leaf. A bull or cow was called a *greater victim*, as opposed to *lesser victims*, such as sheep or goats.

Ch. VII. <sup>1</sup> *church*. See *On the Spectacles*, ch. 25, note 3. The scholars Pamelius and La Cerda have collected thirty-three different names for buildings set apart for Christian divine service. Their goal was to prove such buildings existed very early. In these names, we see several categories: 1. Referring to the congregation, such as *church* <note>original: *ecclesia*</note> and *meeting-places*; 2. To the sacred character of the place, such as *house of God*, *the Lord's house*, 

<column-break/>

*shrine*; 3. To the purpose of the meeting, such as *oratory*, <term>house of prayer <note>original Greek: εὐκτήριον (euktērion)</note></term>, and *place of prayer*; 4. To sites used during persecution, such as *martyr-shrine*, *place of confession*, *cemetery*, and *cells*; 5. To buildings given to them later, such as *basilica* and *temple*. The earlier names imply nothing more than fixed meeting places, which might not have been permanent. Indeed, there could hardly have been more as long as Christianity was, at best, only tolerated. Another class of names refers us to the secret recesses of the catacombs, where Christians fled to celebrate their shared worship in safety. The terms *basilica* and *temple* remind us how the Emperor Constantine gave up *basilicas* (originally Roman judgment-halls) to the Christians, and how Christian worship displaced pagan worship, often occupying former heathen sanctuaries. Tertullian contrasts the Christian place of worship with pagan splendor in *Against the Valentinians*, ch. 3: "The home of our dove is simple, always in high and open places and facing the light. The figure loves..." <note>A reference to the Church as a dove seeking the light of Christ</note>.

# ON IDOLATRY. 69

<margin>CHAPTER VII.</margin>
...to God the Father, hands that are the mothers of idols! To worship with those hands, which outside the church are themselves worshipped <note>original: *adorantur*; refers to the idea that the craftsman’s skill is venerated through the finished idol</note> in opposition to God; to apply those hands to the body of the Lord—hands which fashion bodies for demons. Nor is this enough. It would be bad enough if they merely received from the hands of others that which they contaminate, but they even deliver to others that which they themselves have contaminated. Idol-makers are actually chosen for the ecclesiastical order <note>the clergy or leadership of the church</note>. Oh, what a crime! The Jews laid hands upon Christ only once; these men harass His body daily. O, hands that ought to be cut off! Let it now be seen whether it was said merely as a figure of speech: 
<margin>Matthew 5:30.</margin>
*If your hand causes you to stumble, cut it off.* What hands are more deserving of amputation than those by which the body of the Lord is offended?

<columns>2</columns>

<margin>CHAPTER VIII.</margin>
<margin>
To provide the furniture of idolatry is alike forbidden.
</margin>
There are also other varieties of many arts which, although they do not involve the actual shaping of idols, yet provide those things without which idols are powerless, and thus they share the same guilt. For it makes no difference whether you build or decorate, if you have furnished its temple, its altar, or its niche <note>original: *ædiculam*; a small shrine or housing for a statue</note>, if you have beaten out the gold leaf <note>original: *bracteam expresseris*</note>, or fashioned the ornaments or even the building itself. Work of this kind is even greater, for it confers not just an image, but authority.

<margin>
Every trade may find innocent employment in supplying the wants of man.
</margin>
If the necessity of making a living <note>original: *exhibitionis*</note> is stretched so far <note>as to justify making idols</note>, these arts also have other branches which provide a means of subsistence without straying from the path of discipline <note>Christian moral training</note>—that is, without the fabrication of an idol. A plasterer <term>albarius tector; literally a "whitening-coverer," a worker who used lime and plaster</term> knows how to repair roofs, apply plaster coatings, smooth a cistern <note>original: *liare*; derived from the Greek meaning "to make smooth"</note>, extend mouldings <note>original: *cymatia*; decorative architectural features resembling the ripple of waves</note>, and add many other relief flourishes <note>original: *incrispare*</note> to walls besides mere statues. The painter, the marble-worker, the bronze-smith, and every engraver also know that their own broader applications <note>original: *latitudines suas*</note> are certainly much easier to manage. For he who sketches a statue <note>original: *signum*</note>, how much more easily can he polish a sideboard? He who carves a Mars out of linden wood, how much faster can he assemble a wardrobe? There is no art that is not the mother or relative of another art. Nothing exists in isolation from another. There are as many veins of crafts as there are human desires—

---

Ch. VIII. ¹ *if you have beaten out gold-leaf*, "If you shall have beaten out gold-leaf for the purpose of gilding images." The context shows that the purpose must be idolatrous, in order to make the act idolatrous.

² *is stretched so far*, "is stretched so far," as to authorize idol-making. Rigaltius, following Ursinus, reads "is offered as an excuse" <note>original: *obtenditur*</note>. Below, in chapter 11: *Even more serious crimes, according to the magnitude of the sin, require a diligent extension of observation.*

³ *they have*, namely: *the arts have other varieties.*

<column-break/>

⁴ *plasterer*, <note>original: *albarius tector*</note>. Oehler quotes Pliny's *Natural History* 36.23: *On the other hand, in plaster work, let the soaked lime stick like glue.*

⁵ *to smooth*, <note>original: *liare*; from the Greek *leianein*</note> "to make smooth" by lining it with cement, or some such material. La Cerda quotes Apicius 5.1: *You mix and smooth them, so that it appears like juice.*

⁶ *mouldings*, <note>original: *cymatia*</note> "mouldings," projecting and breaking the surface of a building with lines like the ripple of waves. *to put on work in relief* <note>original: *incrispare*</note>. Oehler quotes Pliny’s *Natural History*.

<margin>CHAPTER VIII.</margin>
...elegance <note>original: *munditiæ*; referring to the refinement or decorative beauty of a home</note>. But there is a distinction regarding the wages and the price of labor. There is likewise a distinction regarding the effort involved. A smaller wage is compensated by more frequent work. How many walls require decorative carvings! How many temples and shrines are built for idols! And how many private houses and apartment blocks <term>insulæ; literally "islands," these were multi-story urban apartment buildings that stood detached from other blocks</term>! The slipper <term>soccus; a light, low-heeled shoe or a comic actor's slipper</term> and the sandal <term>baxa; a shoe made of vegetable fibers, often worn by philosophers or as luxury footwear</term> are gilded every day; Mercury and Serapis <note>Mercury was the Roman god of trade; Serapis was a Graeco-Egyptian deity whose cult was popular in Rome</note> are not gilded every day. Let this suffice for the profit of the trades: luxury and ambition <note>original: *luxuria et ambitio*</note> are more frequent than any superstition. Ambition will demand platters and cups more readily than superstition will. Luxury also spends more on wreaths than any religious festival does. Since, therefore, we encourage these types of craftsmanship—which do not touch upon idols or the things belonging to idols, yet provide things common to both men and idols—we must also take care that nothing is requested from our hands for an idolatrous purpose with our full knowledge. If we allow this and do not act with the precautions so usually adopted <note>original: *remediis tam usitatis*; referring to established Christian strategies for avoiding complicity in pagan rituals</note>, I do not believe we are free from the contagion of idolatry, as our hands—aware of what they do—are caught in the service or in the honor and use of demons.

# TERTULLIAN’S BOOK

<margin>CHAPTER IX.</margin>
...certain [crafts] liable to idolatry. Regarding astrologers <note>original: *astrologis*</note>, there is no need to even speak. But since a certain person in these days <note>original: *istis diebus*</note> has raised a challenge, defending for himself the right to persist in that profession, I will say a few words. I do not even bring up the fact that he honors idols, whose names he has inscribed in the heavens, and to whom he has assigned all of God's power. Because of this, men do not think God needs to be sought, assuming that we are driven by the unchangeable will <note>original: *immobili arbitrio*</note> of the stars.

<margin>Genesis 6:2</margin>
I propose one thing: that those angels were the deserters of God, the lovers of women <note>original: *amatores feminarum*</note>, and the betrayers of this forbidden knowledge <term>curiositatis; literally "curiosity," but here referring to the "curious arts" or occult sciences</term>, and for that reason were also condemned by God. O divine sentence, reaching even to the earth, to which even those who are ignorant bear witness! Mathematicians <term>mathematici; in the Roman world, this term was commonly used for astrologers who calculated horoscopes and star charts</term> are expelled, just like their angels. The City [Rome] and Italy are forbidden to mathematicians, just as heaven is to their angels. The same penalty of destruction applies to both disciples and masters.

<margin>Matthew 2:1</margin>
But the magi and astrologers came from the East. We know the alliance between magic and astrology. Therefore, the first interpreters of the stars [announced] the birth of Christ...

---

<columns>2</columns>

Ch. IX. ¹ *astrologers* <note>original: *astrologis*</note>. The Coptic and Greek constitutions exclude magicians, enchanters, astrologers, diviners, users of magic verses, etc., from admission into the Church. Bunsen’s *Hippolytus* Vol. III. p. 7; Bingham’s *Christian Antiquities* XI. 5, 8.

² *in these days* <note>original: *istis diebus*</note>. Apuleius, *Metamorphoses* Book I, chapter 4: *with this double gaze* <note>original: *isto gemino obtutu*</note>.

³ *by unchangeable will* <note>original: *immobili arbitrio*</note>. This well-known pagan belief was entertained also by the Pharisees. Bull’s *Harmonia Apostolica*, Second Dissertation XV. 18.

⁴ *lovers of women* <note>original: *amatores fœminarum*</note>. This interpretation of Genesis 6:2 was commonly, but not universally, received by early ecclesiastical writers. See in the Oxford Translation a note on the *Apology*,

<column-break/>

chapter 22. Compare *On Prayer* <note>original: *De Oratione*</note> chapter 22; *On the Veiling of Virgins* <note>original: *De Virginibus Velandis*</note> chapter 7; *On the Spectacles* <note>original: *De Spectaculis*</note> chapter 4, note 2.

⁵ *Mathematicians are expelled* <note>original: *Expelluntur mathematici*</note>. Tacitus tells us of decrees *concerning the expulsion of mathematicians and magicians from Italy* <note>original: *de mathematicis magisque Italia pellendis*</note> under Tiberius, 16 A.D. <margin>CHAPTER IX.</margin>
...announced [the birth of Christ], and were the first to present him with gifts. By this service, I suppose, they put Christ under an obligation to them. What then? Shall the religion of those Magi now provide a defense for "mathematicians" <term>mathematicis; here referring specifically to astrologers who calculated charts</term>? I suppose astrology <term>mathesis; the study of the stars for divination</term> today is concerned with Christ—it observes and preaches the star of Christ, is it? Not the stars of Saturn, or Mars, or any other from that same rank of the dead <gloss>7</gloss>. But the truth is, that science was permitted only until the Gospel was reached, so that once Christ was born, no one from that time forward should interpret any person’s birth from the heavens. For this reason, they offered that incense, myrrh, and gold to the Lord while he was an infant, as if it were the "closing" <gloss>8</gloss> of ancient sacrifice and worldly glory, which Christ was destined to take away. Therefore, a dream—undoubtedly by the will of God—suggested to those same Magi that they should return to their own lands, but by a different way than they had come. This means they were not to walk in their former "sect" <note>He means they were to abandon their practice of astrology/magic</note>, rather than being a warning to avoid Herod’s pursuit—for Herod did not actually pursue them; he was even igno...

*Metamorphoses* and *Apology* shows the extent to which such arts were practiced in his day. There is a detailed account of the system of Astrology, and the arts of Magic in the book of Hippolytus published as Origen's *Philosophumena* (Oxford, 1851), Book IV.

6 **the star** <note>original: *stellam*</note>. Codes Ag. and Gangn. read *of the stars*. Gel. and Pamel. read *the stars*, which is probably a guess. Rig. following Ursinus reads *the star*, which seems a satisfactory correction. Oehl. keeps *of the stars*, explaining it as "astrology is of the stars of Christ," and assuming the word "stars" is implied before "of Saturn," etc. Observe that Tertullian is speaking with heavy irony: 'I suppose astrology is concerned about Christ; I suppose it is the star of Christ, not of Saturn, and of Mars,

<column-break/>

and of the other deified dead men that it watches and proclaims.' The argument is: 'If the Magi of Scripture are to be an authority for astrology, astrologers ought to be occupied concerning Christ and his star, as those Magi were; whereas it is notorious that Saturn, Mars, and the like are the stars observed by astrologers.'

<margin>
CHAPTER X.
The occupation of a schoolmaster is idolatrous. A Christian master may not teach, though a Christian may learn in a heathen school.
</margin>
We must also inquire about **schoolmasters** and other professors of literature. Indeed, we cannot doubt that they are closely allied to many-sided idolatry. First, it is necessary for them to preach about the gods of the nations, to recite their names, genealogies, myths, and all their honorary distinctions. Then, they must observe the gods' solemnities and festivals, as it is by these that they calculate their own income. What schoolmaster is without a <term>table of the seven idols</term> <note>likely a calendar of the seven planetary gods for whom the days of the week were named</note>, yet will still attend the <term>Quinquatria</term>? <note>A five-day festival held in March in honor of Minerva, the goddess of wisdom; it was a primary time for paying school fees.</note>

---

*...then those who [describe] the world for nations, what times the reaper and the curved plowman should have?* Virgil, *Aeneid* vi. 850, *and they map out the motions of the heavens with a rod.* <note>The editor OEHL. cites Virgil to explain the "radius" or rod used by astronomers.</note>

Chapter X. ¹ *What schoolmaster...* The scholars Gelenius and Pamelius, instead of "without a table of the seven," read "if not the account-books," which has been commonly adopted but not satisfactorily explained. The reading in the text is that of the Agobardine and Gangnerian Codices. Rigaltius would prefer "will he not frequent?" but, as a smaller change, puts the question mark after "idols?" and reads the rest as a separate sentence: "What schoolmaster is without his pagan calendar? Or if he is, he will at all events keep the Quinquatria." The reading in the main text seems more intelligible: "What schoolmaster will keep the

<column-break/>

Quinquatria (which he must of necessity keep) without a pagan calendar to reckon by?" *Table of the seven idols* refers to "the calendar of the seven planets." Rigaltius quotes *To the Nations* book 1, chapter 13: *“You are certainly the ones who have even received [the gods] into the list of the seven days.”* The *Quinquatrus Games* were held on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of April. This was a general holiday-time for schoolboys. Horace, in his *Epistles* book 2, verse 197 says: *“Rather, like a boy in the festive Quinquatrus of old, you may snatch a brief and pleasant time.”* Ovid, on behalf of the goddess Minerva, would win over certain stern <term>pedagogues</term> <note>Teachers or tutors</note> (who, I presume, were paid by the lesson) for their loss of payment during this festival by the hopes of new pupils and of the <term>Minerval</term> <note>A fee paid to schoolmasters, named after the goddess Minerva</note>. *Fasti* book 3, verse 829:

<margin>CHAPTER X.</margin> He dedicates the very first payment <note>original: *stipem*; a small contribution or fee. The <term>wives of the priests</term> <note>original: *flaminicæ*</note> and the <term>public officials</term> <note>original: *ædiles*</note> offer sacrifices; the school is honored on these newly established holidays. The same happens on the birthday of an idol; every procession of the devil is attended <note>original: *frequentatur*; here meaning to celebrate or observe the rites rather than just physical presence.</note>. *“Nor do you, O fierce crowd of schoolmasters, despise being cheated of your income; that very income will attract new students.”* <note>A poetic quote suggesting that the financial rewards of the profession are tied to these pagan traditions.</note>

*Celebrate* does not imply actual attendance at the festival, but is equivalent to our word ‘celebrate.’

$^2$ *the first... payment*. This payment was called *Minerval*. The master did not actually dedicate it, but receiving it in the name and in honor of Minerva, recognized it as sacred to a heathen goddess.

$^3$ *avoided as an idolater*. One ancient manuscript reads: *so that although he be not said, as far as mere words go, to eat of what is offered to idols, having been bound over to the unholy service of any idol, he should be avoided as an idolater*... Another reading omits the words, meaning: *so that although not bound over to the unholy service of any idol, as

<column-break/>

$^4$ *from that which*. Various manuscripts differ on the exact wording here. The sentence is ironical: ‘What less pollution is there than that which is produced by a payment dedicated to an idol, both in name and honor.’

$^5$ *As much*. The Latin uses a comparison: ‘The Minervalia are as much sacred to Minerva, as the Saturnalia to Saturn.’

<meta>This page continues Tertullian's rigorous examination of the schoolmaster's profession. He moves from the financial links to paganism (the fees paid to Minerva) to a more complex problem: the necessity of classical education itself. He addresses the counter-argument that if a Christian cannot teach literature because of its pagan content, perhaps they cannot learn it either—a situation that would leave Christians uneducated and unable to study the Scriptures.</meta>

<page-num>77</page-num>
<header>### ON IDOLATRY.</header>

<columns>2</columns>

<margin>CHAPTER X.</margin>
<margin>a.</margin>
Who will think it fitting even for one who is not a schoolmaster? <note>original: *etiam non magistro*; Tertullian’s point is that if an ordinary Christian would find these pagan rituals inappropriate, it is even more problematic for a teacher who makes them a central part of his professional life.</note> We know it can be said: "If it is not permitted for the servants of God to teach literature, then it will not be permitted to learn it either." And: "How shall anyone be trained in human wisdom, or for any basic understanding or action, since literature is the instrument for all of life?" How can we reject secular studies, without which divine studies cannot be pursued? Let us therefore look at the necessity of literary education; let us consider that, on one hand, it cannot be fully admitted, yet on the other, it cannot be fully avoided. It is more possible <note>original: *capit*; in the sense of being "admissible" or "feasible." See note 10 below.</note> for the faithful to learn literature than to teach it; for the logic of learning is different from the logic of teaching. If a believer teaches literature, he undoubtedly recounts the praises of idols while [he teaches]...

---

<note>Note 6</note> *which* <note>original: *quæ*</note>. The Agobardus Codex and Gangneius read *whom even the lowliest servants*. Gelenius, Pamelius, and Rigaltius read *which even to lowliest servants*. Oehler retains *whom* <note>original: *quem*</note> on account of the phrase *during the time of the Saturnalia* in the same sentence. But the antecedent of *which* is not "the festival of the Saturnalia," but "the presents exchanged at the time of the Saturnalia." Lipsius (*Saturnalia* Book I, chapter 16) quotes this passage, illustrating it from Suetonius, *Life of Augustus*, chapter 75: *At the Saturnalia... he used to distribute gifts*; and from Spartianus, *Life of Hadrian*: *He frequently sent Saturnalia and Sigillaria <term>clay figurines given as gifts</term> to his friends when they least expected it, and gladly accepted the same from them.*

<note>Note 7</note> **New Year's gifts** <note>original: *strenæ*; gifts presented on any religious day</note>, especially New Year’s day, connected with the worship of Janus. Ovid, *Fasti* Book I, lines 183 and following. These gifts were received even by the emperor from the people, and applied by him to certain public works. Ursinus, in his commentary on Suetonius’ *Life of Augustus*, chapter 91, quotes inscriptions found in the **Sacred Way** <note>original: *Via Sacra*; the main street of ancient Rome</note> commemorating the erection of certain buildings, *from the contribution which the Roman People conferred at the passing of the New Year.*

<column-break/>

**The Seven Hills Festival** <note>original: *Septimontium*</note>, a gift presented to magistrates on the 11th of December <note>original: *III. Id. Decemb.*</note>, on which day the enclosure of the city was celebrated. Tertullian (*Against the Nations* Book II, chapter 15) speaks of a god named Septimontius. **Winter Solstice gifts** <note>original: *Brumæ*</note>, gifts of the winter solstice, like our Christmas presents.

<note>Note 8</note> **honorary gifts of the dear kinship** <note>original: *caræ cognationis honoraria*</note>, presents given at the **Caristia**, a festival celebrated on the 22nd of February <note>original: *XI. Kal. Mart.*</note>, consecrated to the memory of departed relatives. Ovid, *Fasti* Book II, line 617 and following.

<note>Note 9</note> *even for one who is not a schoolmaster*. "If a Christian who is not a schoolmaster may fitly join in these idolatrous rites, then, and then only, may a schoolmaster do so." A schoolmaster’s business makes these rites necessary for him. A Christian to whom they were not necessary would not think of practicing them. The necessity shows the business to be unlawful.

<note>Note 10</note> *it is possible* <note>original: *capit*</note>. In Greek: *it is admissible* <note>original: ἐνδέχεται</note>. Oehler, in *On Flight*, chapter 1, quotes *Apology*, chapter 17: *it is not possible to be estimated*. *On Modesty*: *it is possible also to be indulged*. *On Baptism*, chapter 1: *it is possible to be numbered*, and other passages.

...[The teacher] teaches them, commends them, and while he hands them down, he affirms them; while he commemorates them, he bears witness to them. He <term>seals<note>original: *obsignat*. A legal and religious term for formally validating or dedicating something.</note></term> the gods themselves with this name "god," even though the law forbids—as we have said—
<margin>Exodus 23:13.

the gods to be pronounced and this name to be "placed upon a vain thing." <note>original: *in vano collocari*. Tertullian is interpreting the commandment against taking God's name in vain as a prohibition against giving the title of "God" to empty idols.</note> From this, the first step of faith in the devil is built from the very beginnings of education. Ask yourself whether he commits idolatry who <term>catechizes<note>Tertullian uses the Greek-derived word for Christian instruction (*catechizat*) to ironically describe a teacher instructing children about pagan myths.</note></term> about idols. But when a believer learns these things, if he already understands who he is <note>note 13: regarding the believer's character and profession as a Christian.</note>, he neither receives nor admits them; and much more so if he does not yet understand. <note>note 14: if the student is too young to be spiritually compromised.</note> Or rather, when he begins to understand, he must first understand what he learned first: that is, concerning God and the faith. Therefore, he will reject those pagan tales and not receive them, and he will be as safe as a man who, knowing he is being offered poison by someone who does not know it is toxic, takes it but does not drink it. To such a student, "necessity" is assigned as an excuse, because he cannot learn anything else. However, it is as much easier *not to teach* literature than it is *not to learn* it, just as it is easier to avoid the other defilements of schools regarding public and private <note>note 15: local or municipal</note> festivities...

¹¹ **Seals the gods**, sets a seal to their divinity. Below, in chapter 12, *after the faith has been sealed*. *Obsignare* means to seal by way of dedication. In *To His Wife* (book 1, ch. 6): *immediately after the washing [baptism] they seal their flesh*. In *On the Apparel of Women* (book 2, ch. 9): *they seal themselves to eunuch-hood*, where some read *assign*.

¹² **placed upon a vain thing.** The law forbids ‘the name of God to be put upon a vain thing.’ Dodgson refers to *Against Praxeas* (ch. 7). Tertullian is there arguing against heretical views as to the Word: *Is the Word of God a void and empty thing, He who is called the Son, who Himself has been named God, and "the Word was with God, and the Word was God"? It is written: "Thou shalt not take the name of God in vain."*

¹³ **who.** Oehler suggests by conjecture the word *what*. "Who he is," i. e. what is his character and profession as a Christian.

<column-break/>

¹⁴ **if he does not yet understand.** Rigaltius suggests by conjecture *long ago*. *Nondum* ("not yet") is better: ‘if the person is yet so young as not to know what he is.’

¹⁵ **public and private.** The Agobardus Codex and early Editions read *public, private*. Ursinus by conjecture, and later editors Oehler and Rigaltius, read *public and private*. Compare *On the Crown* (ch. 13), *the particularity of municipal festivities*. Also *On the Spectacles* (ch. 6), *public prosperities and municipal feasts*.

Chapter XI. ¹ **Concerning generations if...** Thus in the Agobardus Codex and other early editions. Pamelius reads *We shall degenerate, if*. Rigaltius and Heraldus read *concerning negations*. Rigaltius omits *if*. The punctuation in the text follows La Cerda and Oehler. The conclusion of the sentence is the question: *is trade... fitting?* "If upon the subject of the producing [of idols]..."

Commerce is at best doubtful, considering its origin; but that commerce is surely forbidden (the commerce in incense and the like) which respects the very essence of idolatry. 1 Timothy 6:10. 1 Timothy 1:19. Colossians 3:5. Matthew 5:33, 34.
</margin>
If we consider the origins <note>original: *de generationibus*. Literally "of the lineages" or "beginnings" of these activities.</note> of other sins, first and foremost is greed, the root of all evils, in which some being ensnared have suffered shipwreck concerning the faith (although greed is also called idolatry by the same apostle), and then there is falsehood, the servant of greed—I say nothing of perjury, since it is not even permitted to swear—is commerce <term>negotiatio<note>This term refers to business, trade, or wholesale dealing, which Tertullian views as inherently driven by a desire for profit that often leads to sin.</note></term> fit for a servant of God? Furthermore, if greed is removed, what is the reason for acquiring? When the reason for acquiring ceases, there will be no necessity for trading. Let there now be some justice in profit, secure from the observation of greed and falsehood; yet I believe it falls into the crime of idolatry, which pertains to the very soul and spirit of idols, and which fattens every demon. Truly, is that not the primary form of idolatry? Let them see to it, whether those same goods—I mean incense—

¹ "If we review the other vices as causes [of commerce]; first, covetousness, the root of all evils, in which some having been ensnared, have made shipwreck of their faith (although covetousness has by the same apostle been also called idolatry): then falsehood, the handmaid of covetousness (not to speak of perjury, seeing we are forbidden even to swear)—[when we see, I say, that commerce has its origin in covetousness, and in falsehood, we are tempted to ask in general] Is commerce fitted for the servants of God?" <margin>CHAPTER XI.</margin> ...and the rest of these foreign goods <note>original: *peregrinitatis*. Certainly, when the processions, the priesthoods, and the sacrifices of idols are supplied through dangers, losses, inconveniences, anxieties, and the travels of trade, what else are you shown to be but a manager for the idols? Let no one argue that in this way a controversy could be raised against all types of business <term>negotiationibus<note>Refers to wholesale trade or commercial enterprise, which Tertullian views with suspicion because of its proximity to pagan life.</note></term>. The more serious crimes, in proportion to the greatness of the danger, require an increase of careful watching, so that we do not merely withdraw from the crimes themselves, but also from those acts through which they are made possible^10. For even if the act is performed by others, it makes no difference if it is done through my agency. I ought to be necessary to no one else when he does what is not lawful for me. From the fact that I am forbidden to do a thing, I ought to understand that I must take care that it is not done through me. In short^11, I observe this same principle in another case of no lighter guilt. For although I am forbidden from debauchery <note>original: *stupro*. <margin>CHAPTER XI.</margin> I show no service or complicity in the matter. **CHAPTER XI.** ...does the incense-seller <term>thurarius<note>A merchant of frankincense and other aromatics used in religious ceremonies.</note></term> serve demons? For idolatry can exist more easily without an idol than without the incense-seller’s goods. Let us question the very conscience of our faith. With what face shall a Christian incense-seller, if he passes by temples, with what face shall he spit upon and blow away^18 the smoking altars for which he himself provided? With what consistency will he exorcize his own "fosterlings"^19, for whom he provides his own house as a storehouse? If such a man should indeed cast out a demon, let him not take pride in his faith^20, for he has not cast out an enemy. He ought to have easily obtained his request from one whom he feeds daily. Therefore, no art, no profession, no trade which provides anything for either the equipping or the forming of idols can be free from the label of idolatry; unless we interpret idolatry as something entirely different from the service of worshipping idols.

**CHAPTER XII.** ...of faith. None of those whom the Lord has chosen has ever said, "I have nothing to live on." Faith, however, does not fear. Propose the rule^8 by which you wish to be treated. For why should you remain hidden, when <margin>1 Cor. 8:7.</margin> by the ignorance of another you contaminate your own conscience? If it is not ignored that you are a Christian, you are being tested; and by acting as if you were not a Christian, you act against the conscience of the other person. Indeed, you will even be overlooked <note>original: "dissimulaberis," meaning your status as a Christian will be intentionally ignored by the heathens so they can keep your company</note>. Having been tested, you are condemned^9. Certainly, in either this way or that, you are guilty of shame before God. "But whoever is ashamed <margin>Luke 9:26.</margin> of me before men," He says, "of him will I also be ashamed before my Father who is in heaven."

<margin>
CH. XIV.
We may not propitiate our enemies by joining in unlawful festivals, much less join in such festivals unsolicited.
</margin> But indeed, many have already convinced themselves that they must acknowledge [these customs] whenever they do what the heathens <note>original: "ethnici," referring to non-Christians or pagans</note> do, so that "the Name be not blasphemed." Furthermore, the blasphemy which we must altogether avoid is this, I think: if any of us leads a heathen to a just blasphemy by de—

---

<columns>2</columns>
^8 *Propose the rule...* The dilemma is this: In observing these days, you are either not known, or you are known to be a Christian. If you are not known, you defile your own conscience in disguising your profession by such compliances; if you are known to be a Christian, you wound the conscience of others (giving them a false idea of what Christianity is) by doing what a Christian ought not to do.

^9 *Indeed, you will even be overlooked. Having been tested, you are condemned.* Thus in the Agobardine Codex, and the editions of Gangneius and Gelenius. The passage has been variously amended. Pamelius: *Indeed, even if you have pretended.* Latinius and Junius: *But if truly you have also overlooked.* Rigaltius: *Indeed you shall also have overlooked.* Oehler: *But if truly and*

<column-break/>

*overlooked.* The agreement of the early manuscripts <note>original: "MSS."</note> of different families in a reading, whose meaning is at least not obvious, makes for, not against its genuineness. I have therefore retained the ancient reading, with a punctuation slightly different from that usually adopted. The first clause is connected with what precedes. "You act as if you were no Christian. For in truth, even though known to be one, it will be pretended that you are not a Christian." The heathen, though they know you to be a Christian, will wink at it, and will be glad to accept the act as a virtual abnegation of your faith. Tertullian then goes on to state the consequence which follows on either alternative: "You have [been tested and found wanting]."

<summary>Tertullian warns Christians against attending pagan festivals, arguing that trying to blend in to avoid "blasphemy" actually compromises one's conscience and misleads others. He emphasizes that being ashamed of Christ in social settings leads to being disowned by Christ in heaven.</summary>

On the contrary, as long as we exist <note>original: "dum sumus," meaning as long as we remain Christians.</note>, let it be blasphemed: in the keeping of our discipline, not in its straying; while we are being approved, not while we are being rejected. Oh, what a blasphemy akin to testimony <note>original: "martyrii," used here in its original sense of "bearing witness" rather than simply dying.</note>, which then witnesses that I am a Christian, when for its sake the world detests me! The cursing of a discipline that is strictly kept is a blessing of the Name. If I wanted to please men, he says, <margin>Gal. 1:10.</margin> I would not be a servant of Christ. But the same man elsewhere commands that we take care to please all: "just as I," he says, <margin>1 Cor. 10:33.</margin> "please everyone in all things." 'But whoever,' etc. *Tempted.* La Cerda says that the word *to be tempted* <note>original: "tentari"</note> is used by early Christian writers to signify, 'to be overcome by temptation.' We may live with heathens <note>original: "ethnicis," referring to non-Christians or pagans.</note>, but we may not die with them <note>A metaphor for sharing in their spiritual death through sin.</note>. Let us live with all; let us rejoice together because of our common nature, not because of common superstition. We are equals in soul, but not in discipline; joint-possessors of the world, but not of error. <margin>CHAPTER XV.</margin> than that of the Christians. What is your opinion on this form of honor as well? If it is an honor paid to an idol, without a doubt, honor for an idol is idolatry. If it is for the sake of a man, let us consider that all idolatry is ultimately for the sake of a man. Let us reflect that all idolatry is the worship of humans, since it is well established—even among their own people—that the gods of the nations were formerly human beings.$^2$ Therefore, it makes no difference whether this superstition is performed for men of a past age or of this present one. Idolatry is condemned not because of the specific persons who are presented for adoration$^3$, but because of those services which belong to demons. We must render <margin>Matthew 22:21; Luke 20:25.</margin> to Caesar the things that are Caesar’s. It is well that$^4$ He added, "And to God the things that are God’s." What, then, are the things of Caesar? Specifically, those things which were then the subject of the inquiry: whether the tribute <term>census: the poll-tax or registration of citizens and property for taxation</term> should be paid to Caesar or not. For this reason, the Lord also demanded that a coin be shown to Him, and He asked whose image was on it; and when He had heard it was Caesar’s, He said, "Render to Caesar what is Caesar’s, and to God what is God’s." That is: render the image of Caesar to Caesar, which is on the coin, and the image of God$^5$ to God, which is in man; so that you may indeed give money to Caesar, but give yourself to God. Otherwise, what will belong to God, if all things [belong to Caesar?]

...of Caesar? Therefore, you might ask, is it an honor to God to have <margin>CHAPTER XV.</margin> lamps before the doors and laurel on the doorposts? Certainly not because it is an honor meant for God, but because it is an honor to that being who is worshipped in the place of God with such services. So far as it is visible, while setting aside the hidden intent, this honor reaches the demons. For we must be certain—in case anyone is unaware due to a lack of knowledge of secular literature—that the Romans even have "gods of the doors." They called **Cardea** the goddess of hinges <note>Latin: *cardinibus*</note>, **Forculus** the god of doors <note>Latin: *foribus*</note>, **Limentinus** the god of the threshold <note>Latin: *limine*</note>, and even **Janus** <margin>/</margin> himself takes his name from the doorway <note>Latin: *janua*</note>. Otherwise, demons have no individual names, but they find a name wherever they find a physical pledge of worship. We also read among the Greeks of **Apollo of the Door** <note>Greek: *Thyraeon*</note> and the **Sun-Facing** <note>Greek: *Antelios*</note> demons who act as guardians of entrances. Therefore, the Holy Spirit, foreseeing from the beginning that even doors would become objects of superstition, foretold this through the most ancient prophet **Enoch**. # THE BOOK OF TERTULLIAN

**CHAPTER XV.** ...the wreaths of laurel will belong. Whatever you do for the door, you have done for an idol. In this matter, I also bear witness by the authority of God, because it is not safe to hide away whatever has been shown to one person, since it was surely meant for everyone. I know of a brother who was severely chastised in a vision that very night because his servants had wreathed his door with greenery upon the sudden announcement of public festivals. And yet, he had not wreathed it himself, nor had he ordered it; for he had gone out before the event, and upon returning, he had condemned the act. Thus, before God, we are judged in such matters even by the conduct of our household <note>Latin: *disciplina familiae*. In the Roman world, the head of a household was morally and legally responsible for the behavior of his slaves and family.</note>.

Therefore, regarding the honors due to kings or emperors, we have a sufficient rule: we ought to be in all obedience, according to the apostle’s precept <margin>Romans 13:1</margin>, subject to magistrates and princes and powers—but within the limits of our religious discipline, as far as we are kept separate from idolatry. For this reason, the example of the three brothers <note>Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego.</note> came before us <margin>Daniel 3:12 ff.</margin>; though otherwise obedient toward King Nebuchadnezzar, they most firmly rejected the honor of his image. They proved that it is idolatry whenever anything is raised up beyond the measure of human honor toward the likeness of divine sublimity. Likewise Daniel <margin>Daniel 6:5 ff.</margin>, while supporting Darius in other matters, remained in his post only so long as he was free from the danger of compromising his faith. To avoid such a thing, he feared the king's lions no more than those others feared the king's fires. Let them, therefore, kindle [their lamps] daily...

<margin>CHAPTER XV.</margin>
<margin>Matthew 5:14.</margin>

...lamps, in which there is no light; let them fix to their doorposts laurels that are soon to be burned, over which fires already hang: to such people belong both the evidence of darkness and the omens of coming punishments. If you have renounced pagan temples, do not make a temple of your own doorway. I have said too little: if you have renounced brothels, do not give your own house the appearance of a new brothel <note>In Roman society, decorating a door with lamps and greenery was common practice for houses of prostitution during festivals; Tertullian argues that a Christian home decorated for a pagan feast becomes indistinguishable from a place of sin.</note>.

<margin>CHAPTER XVI.</margin>
<margin>In festivals of marriage, and the like, which originate not in idolatry, it is lawful to take part, provided we join in no idolatrous act that may accompany the celebration.</margin>
<margin>Deuteronomy 22:5.</margin>
Regarding the duties of private and common festivities—such as the ceremony of the pure toga <term>Latin: *toga pura*; the plain white garment assumed by Roman boys reaching manhood, also called the *toga virilis*</term>, betrothals, weddings, or naming ceremonies <term>Latin: *nominalia*; a festival held on the "day of purification" when a child was named</term>—I do not think there is any danger of being tainted by the "breath" of idolatry that may happen to be present. One must consider the reasons why the duty is performed. I believe these occasions are clean in themselves, because neither the manly dress, nor the ring <note>The Roman betrothal ring (*anulus pronubus*).</note>, nor the marital union originates from the honor of any idol. Finally, I find no style of dress cursed by God, except for a woman’s dress on a man. For He says, "Cursed is everyone who is clothed in woman’s garments" <margin>Deuteronomy 22:5</margin>. But the toga is specifically a name for a man's garment. God no more forbids weddings to be celebrated than He forbids the giving of a name. 

Yet, sacrifices are often attached to these events. If I am invited, and the reason for the invitation is not defined by the sacrifice, then the performance of my service <note>original: *operae meae expunctio*</note> is as much as I please. If only we could avoid seeing the things which it is a sin to do! But since—

# TERTULLIAN’S BOOK

<margin>CHAPTER XVI.</margin>
...[si]nce the Evil One has so surrounded the world with idolatry, it will be permitted to be present in certain instances where we are performing a duty to a human being, not to an idol. Clearly, if called to a priesthood or a sacrifice, I will not go (for that is the specific duty of an idol), nor will I contribute advice, expense, or any other labor in such matters. If I am present because I have been called for the sake of the sacrifice, I will be a partner in idolatry; if some other cause joins me to the person sacrificing, I will be merely a spectator of the sacrifice.

<margin>CHAPTER XVII. Christian slaves may serve heathen [masters]</margin>
But what shall faithful slaves or freedmen do,

---

The variations from Gangne <note>Jean de Gangne, a 16th-century editor who produced the first printed edition of this text</note> look very much like emendations <note>Scholarly corrections or improvements to a text</note>, to make out the sense. Others have corrected it by conjecture: as Ursinus and La Cerda read, *If I be called* <note>Latin: "Si sim vocatus"</note>; Latinius and Junius read, *If not even in the calling* <note>Latin: "Si nec in vocatu"</note>. Rigalt, looking as usual to the Agobardine Codex <note>A famous 9th-century manuscript of Tertullian's works</note>, adopts its reading, only altering *at sacrifices* <note>Latin: "ad sacrificiis"</note> to *assisting in sacrifice* <note>Latin: "adsacrificii"</note>, which word he illustrates by the term *assisting in military service* <note>Latin: "admilitia"</note>, from the Pandects <note>The "Digest," a massive compendium of Roman law compiled under Justinian</note>. The explanation which Rigalt offers is this: Tertullian is contemplating the case of slaves called upon to assist in such ceremonies. "Suppose I am called upon to take part, and the performance of my duty and service does not bear the title of assisting in sacrifice; let the heathen master do as much as he pleases, would only it were as much as he pleased himself to do, and we might avoid seeing, etc." Oehler adopts Rigalt's reading, and expresses his general concurrence in Rigalt's explanation, illustrating the use of *assisting in sacrifice* by the term *related to ancestry* <note>Latin: "adtradux"</note>, found in *On Patience* <note>Tertullian's treatise "De Patientia"</note>, chapter 5, and other instances. So Dodgson translates it. I differ from them, because, 1. the case of slaves seems to be first introduced in chapter 17, and the subject here is the general question

<column-break/>

of attendance on such ceremonies; 2. the words *called* <note>Latin: "vocatus"</note> and *duty* <note>Latin: "officium"</note> rather imply invitation than command; 3. the omission <note>The "ellipse" or missing words in a sentence</note> supposed before the phrase *as much as he pleases* <note>Latin: "quantum sibi libet"</note> is very harsh. Oehler endeavors to lessen the harshness by placing a comma before *and of labor* <note>Latin: "et operæ"</note>, and interpreting the sentence, "Suppose that I have been summoned, etc., let even the performance of my service be at its pleasure" <note>Latin: "etiam opera mea sibi expungatur in quantum sibi libet"</note>. As to the reading of the text, I observe, 1. that *If uninvited* <note>Latin: "Si invocatus"</note> may very probably have been a mistake made by Gangne in reading his manuscripts, expecting to find *if*; 2. that in the Agobardine Codex *at sacrifices* <note>Latin: "ad sacrificiis"</note> is clearly erroneous, and that the manuscript is more likely to be faulty where it disagrees than where it agrees with others; 3. *which then* <note>Latin: "quæ tum"</note> in Gangne is plainly wrong, and *as much as* <note>Latin: "quantum"</note> is right; 4. that *as much as for itself* <note>Latin: "quantum sibi"</note> in the Agobardine Codex in the next sentence is very probably the repetition of a copyist from the former sentence. But if *as much as for itself* be retained, it may be explained, as will be shown. For the explanation:—All commentators have supposed the answer to *should I be called* <note>Latin: "sim vocatus"</note> to lie in *how much*...

<margin>CHAPTER XVII.</margin>
<margin>masters even when sacrificing, provided they themselves abstain from any idolatrous act.</margin>
Likewise, what about officials who wait upon their masters, patrons, or governors while they are sacrificing? But if someone hands the pure wine <note>original: "merum"</note> to the person sacrificing, or even assists with a single word necessary for the sacrifice, he will be regarded as an attendant of idolatry. Remembering this rule, we can perform our duty toward magistrates and authorities according to the example of the patriarchs and other elders, who attended upon <note>original: "apparuerunt," a technical term for serving a high-ranking official</note> idolatrous kings up to the point where idolatry began.

---

*as much as it pleases itself* <note>original: "tum sibi libet"</note>. I believe the hypothetical case to include from *if I should be* <note>original: "sim"</note> to *it pleases* <note>original: "libet"</note>; and the answer to be in *it will be lawful* <note>original: "licebit"</note>. But the direct answer is interrupted by the wish *I would indeed wish* <note>original: "Utinam quidem"</note>; the *indeed* marking, as it so often does, that the sentence is introduced by way of contrast, the main sentence being that which begins with *but* <note>original: "sed"</note>, as in the Greek "on the one hand... on the other" <note>original: "μὲν...δὲ"</note>. Tertullian has been saying that ceremonies of a particular kind may be attended. But an objection is started: "Sacrifices are often mixed with them." Tertullian puts a case: "Suppose that I have been invited, and suppose both that the name of my attendance is not connected with sacrifices, and that the performance of my part is at pleasure." *Itself* <note>original: "Sibi"</note> referring to *my works* <note>original: "opera mea"</note>: *as much as it pleases itself* is illustrated by Oehler from *Against Hermogenes* chapter 23: *Let the matter be as much as it is allowed for itself, or rather for Hermogenes* <note>original: "Fuerit licet materia quantum sibi licet vel potius Hermogeni"</note>, and answers very much to the phrase *at pleasure* <note>original: "ad libitum"</note>. Tertullian proceeds to answer the hypothetical case: "Although I could wish we were exempt even from seeing idolatrous sacrifices; yet, situated as we are, it will be lawful to be present, etc." He then proceeds without doubt to the case where a person is invited to a sacrifice: *Clearly to the priesthood, etc.* <note>original: "Plane ad sacerdotium, etc."</note> If

<column-break/>

we read with Rigaltius, *Would that as much as it indeed to itself, nor* <note>original: "Utinam quantum sibi quidem, nec"</note>, we must interpret, "Would that it were indeed at its own pleasure," that is, "Would that the performance of the Christian’s part were really so free, as that he were excused from seeing what he would not do." For the use of the subjunctive *I should be* <note>original: "sim"</note>, see *On the Spectacles* chapter 6, note 3. *Social duty* <note>original: "Officium"</note> is especially applied to complimentary attendance upon nuptial feasts. Suetonius's *Life of Caligula* chapter 25: *Livia... when she was marrying, since he himself had also come for the social duty, he ordered her to be taken away to himself.* The *Life of Claudius* chapter 26: *he completed the marriage, though no one could be found to follow the example, except for a certain freedman and another primary centurion, whose social attendance at the wedding he himself celebrated with Agrippina.*
<sup>5</sup> *the world has surrounded idolatry*. Compare *On the Spectacles* chapter 8. *The Evil One* <note>original: "Malus"</note>, that is, Satan. Below, chapter 21.
Chapter XVII. <sup>1</sup> *children* <note>original: "liberi"</note>. La Cerda, Rigaltius, and Oehler read *freedmen* <note>original: "liberti"</note>. La Cerda remarks that *slaves* corresponds to *masters*, *freedmen* to *patrons*, and *officials* to *governors*. But Dionysius of Halicarnassus (Book II, 22) tells us that priests were assisted by their children, if they had any, and if not, by children of other families called *assistants* <note>original: "camilli," referring to noble youths who assisted in religious rituals</note>. Probably *children* refers to these.
<sup>2</sup> *attended upon* <note>original: "apparuerunt"</note>. See *On the Spectacles* chapter 17, note 8.

**Chapter XVII.**
The question whether Christians may bear office in heathen countries must be answered in the negative, because the insignia <note>The ceremonial symbols of office, such as robes and rods</note> of magistrates have their origin in idolatry.
**Genesis 41:42.**
**Daniel 5:29.**

From this, a debate has recently arisen as to whether a servant of God may take up the administration of any rank or power, if he is able—either through some favor or even by cleverness—to keep himself untouched by every form of idolatry. This is argued according to the examples of Joseph and Daniel, who, while remaining clean from idolatry, administered both rank and power in the finery and purple <note>The color of high-ranking Roman and Eastern officials</note> of the high office of all Egypt and Babylon. Let us grant, then, that it might be possible for someone to succeed in attaining some honor, walking only in the name of that honor, and that he neither sacrifices nor lends his authority to sacrifices; that he does not contract for sacrificial victims <note>original: "hostias locet"</note>, nor delegate the care of temples, nor manage their revenues; that he does not host spectacles <note>Public games or gladiator matches</note> at his own or public expense, nor preside over them when they are hosted; that he pronounces or proclaims no solemnity, nor even swears an oath. Furthermore, regarding matters of power: let us suppose he does not sit in judgment over a person’s life or legal standing <note>original: "pudore," literally "modesty," but here referring to civil status or honor</note> (for you might allow him to judge matters of money), and that he neither condemns nor pre-condemns, binds no one, and neither imprisons nor tortures anyone—if it is indeed believable that such things

<margin>Chapter XVIII.</margin> ...in bearing, than in dignity, than in <gloss>11</gloss> power. For who would have made more use of these things than the Son of God? What kind and how many ceremonial rods <note>original: "fasces," the bundles of rods and axes carried before Roman magistrates as a symbol of their power to punish</note> would have preceded Him! What purple <note>original: "purpura," the costly dye used for the robes of emperors and high-ranking officials</note> would have bloomed from His shoulders! What gold would have radiated from His head, if He had not judged the glory of this world to be alien to both Himself and His followers! Therefore, what He did not want, He rejected; what He rejected, He condemned; what He condemned, He assigned to the procession of the devil <note>original: "pompa diaboli," a phrase used in baptismal vows to refer to the vanities, public spectacles, and honors of the pagan world</note>. For He would not have condemned them unless they were not His own; and they could belong to no other than the devil, those things which are not of God. If you have renounced the devil's procession, know that whatever you touch from it is idolatry. Or let this remind you—that all powers and dignities of this world are not only foreign to God, but even His enemies—because by them punishments are devised against God's servants, and through them, the penalties prepared for the ungodly are ignored <gloss>12</gloss>. But both your birth and your status <note>original: "substantia," here referring to one's social standing or property</note> are troublesome to you in the face of idolatry. Means of avoiding it <gloss>13</gloss> cannot be lacking, since even if they were to fail, there remains that one unique path <gloss>14</gloss>, by which you are made a happier magistrate, not on earth, but in the heavens.

In this chapter, it might seem that a decision has already been reached regarding military service, which stands somewhere between social dignity and political power. One soul cannot be owed to two masters, God and Caesar.

### CHAPTER XX. [Since faith] may be endangered not only by deeds but even by words (for as it is written, *Behold the man and his deeds*,² <margin>Matthew 12:37.</margin> and likewise, *By your own mouth shall you be justified*), we must remember that the assault of idolatry must also be guarded against in our speech, whether it arises from the fault of habit or from fear. <margin>Exodus 23:13.</margin> The Law forbids naming the gods of the nations—not, of course, that we are never to pronounce their names, which the needs of daily conversation extort from us. For one must often say, "You can find him in the Temple of Aesculapius," or, "I live in Isis Street," or, "He has been made a priest of Jupiter," and many other such things, since names of this kind <gloss>3</gloss> are even given to men. I do not honor Saturn if I call him by his own name; I honor him no more than I do Marcus if I call him Marcus. <margin>Exodus 23:13.</margin> But the Law says, *Do not mention the name of other gods, nor let it be heard from your mouth.* This gives the command that we should not call them *gods*. For in the first part of the Law, <margin>Exodus 20:7.</margin> it says, *You shall not take the name of the Lord your God in vain*, that is, for an idol <gloss>5</gloss>. Therefore, anyone who honors an idol with the name of God has fallen into idolatry. But if it becomes necessary to speak of "gods," <gloss>6</gloss> something must be added to make it clear that I am not the one calling them gods. For even Scripture names them "gods," but adds "their [gods]" or "the gods of the nations";

<margin>CHAPTER XXI.</margin>
<margin>We must not be led astray by the words of others, either acquiescing when they swear by false gods, or showing anger when they curse us by such names;</margin>
It is, however, a mark of cowardice when someone else binds you with an oath or some form of testimony by their own gods, and you, for fear of being recognized <gloss>as a Christian</gloss>, remain silent. For by keeping quiet, you are confirming their majesty just as much, since you will appear to be bound for their sake. What does it matter whether you confirm the gods of the nations by calling them "gods" yourself or by listening to them being called so? Whether you swear by idols, or acquiesce when someone else adjures you by them? Why do we not recognize the tricks of Satan? What he cannot achieve through our own mouths, he attempts to do through the mouths of his own followers, bringing idolatry to us through our ears. Certainly, whoever this person is, they bind you in either a friendly or a hostile meeting. <margin>Chapter XXI.</margin> ...the obligation of the one through whom the Evil One <note>original: "Malus," a common epithet for Satan.</note> sought to bind you to the honor of idols—that is, to idolatry? Any such "patience" is itself idolatry. You honor those to whom you have rendered service by your compliance. I know of a certain man (may the Lord forgive him) who, when it was said to him in a public dispute, "May Jupiter be angry with you," replied, "No, may he be angry with *you*!" $^3$ <note>original: "Immo tibi."</note> How would a pagan, who believes Jupiter is a god, have acted any differently? Even if he had not thrown back the same curse, nor one by any god similar to Jupiter, he still confirmed Jupiter was a god by showing that he took the curse to heart. For why would you be indignant at a name you know to be nothing? If you are driven to fury $^4$, you confirm his existence, and your very fear will be a profession of idolatry $^5$. How much more so when you curse back in the same name; do you not grant Jupiter the same honor $^6$ as the one who provoked you?

<margin>Matthew 5:44. 1 Peter 3:9.</margin> A believer, however, ought to laugh at such things, not be driven to fury.
