<margin>Chapter XXII.</margin>
...[A baptized] believer will not tolerate it without always rejecting an impure blessing, and by turning it toward God, he cleanses it. To be blessed by the gods of the nations <note>original: "deos nationum," referring to the various pagan deities of the Roman world.</note> is to be cursed by God. If I give alms or perform some kind of benefit, and that person prays for the favor of his gods or the Guardian Spirit <note>original: "Genium," the protective deity or spiritual double of a person or place</note> of the colony upon me, then my offering or deed will be an honor to the idols, in whose name he repays me with the favor of a blessing. But why should he not know that I did it for God’s sake, so that God may be glorified and demons may not be honored in that which I did because of God? If God sees that I did it for His sake, He also sees that I was unwilling to show that I did it for Him, and thus I have made His commandment into a sort of "sacrifice to an idol" <term>idolothytum: traditionally meat sacrificed to an idol, here used metaphorically for a good deed tainted by pagan association</term>. Many may say, "No one is required to expose themselves"; but I think neither should one deny their faith. For whoever conceals his faith while being treated as a pagan in any situation denies it; and certainly every denial is idolatry, just as every idolatry is a denial, whether in deeds or in words.

### Chapter XXIII.

...the word is doubly sharp and hostile on both sides¹, even if it flatters you as if it were void in both cases, because the act is not seen, since the word is not held to have been spoken². There are those who, when borrowing money from pagans, give security under pledges³ and, having taken an oath⁴, they provide a guarantee, yet they deny that they know [they are swearing]. They claim, of course, that the time of persecution, the location of the court, and the person of the <margin>Matt. v. 34.</margin> judge⁵ [dictate their actions]. But Christ prescribes that one must not swear an oath. "I wrote it," such a person says, "but I said nothing. It is the tongue, not the written letter, that kills." At this point, I call upon nature and conscience⁷: nature, because the hand can write nothing—even if the tongue remains motionless and quiet while dictating—which the soul has not dictated; although the soul has also dictated to the tongue itself either what it conceived on its own or what it received from another.

---

**CH. XXIII.** ...I did not swear¹³. For even if you had done no such thing <note>referring to speaking the oath aloud</note>, you would still be said to have sworn a solemn oath <note>original: "dejerare"</note> if you consented to the act being recorded. A Christian soldier has refused to wear a crown. Even so-called Christians have censured him. I will show the unlawfulness of compliance with this heathen usage.

¹ Codex Agobardinus: **THE BOOK ON THE CROWN BEGINS HAPPILY.** <note>original: "INCIPIT LIBER DE CORONA FELICITER"</note> Hence Rigalt adopts the title **ON THE CROWN** for that of **ON THE SOLDIER’S CROWN**, observing that the subject of this treatise is the use of crowns in general, not only of military crowns. I have retained the fuller title, as being equally appropriate, and having more authority on its side.

Ch. I. ² In the Codex Agobardinus (followed by Rigalt and Oehler) the first sentences stand thus: *It happened very recently: the generosity of the most excellent emperors was being paid out in the camp, the soldiers were approaching while wearing laurels. In 200 Geta was associated with his father and brother.

Here *the soldiers were being paid off*, meaning 'the soldiers were being paid,' the names of each being pricked off as they received the largess <note>a "largess" was a formal distribution of money from an emperor to his troops to ensure loyalty</note>. ### THE BOOK OF TERTULLIAN

<margin>CHAPTER I.</margin>
...I do not doubt that some are abandoning the Scriptures <gloss>17</gloss>, packing their bags, and preparing for flight from city to city. For they care for no other memory of the Gospel. I know their pastors, too: they are lions in peace, but deer in battle. But regarding the questions of confessions <gloss>18</gloss> of faith, we shall teach elsewhere. Yet now, insofar as they also raise the objection, "But where are we forbidden from being crowned?" I will approach this more specific matter <gloss>19</gloss> of the present case, so that those who ask out of a concern born of ignorance may be instructed, and those who argue in defense of their sin may be refuted—especially those "crowned Christians" themselves, for whom the question itself serves as a comfort <gloss>20</gloss>, as if a sin that allows for questioning could be considered either non-existent or at least uncertain. However, I shall show for now that it is neither non-existent nor uncertain.

# ON THE SOLDIER'S CROWN.

<margin>CHAPTER II.</margin>
...thus they observe it <note>the practice of not wearing crowns</note>, from the trainees <term>catechumens<note>Those receiving basic instruction in the Christian faith before baptism</note></term> all the way to those who stand firm in their faith <term>confessors<note>Those who suffered for their faith but were not killed</note></term> and the martyrs, or even those who deny the faith <gloss>renegades</gloss>. Let them see <note>original: "Viderint"</note> for themselves from where the authority of this custom comes, which is currently being so heavily questioned. Furthermore, when it is asked *why* something is observed, it is clear that, in the meantime, it *is* being observed. Therefore, a sin committed against a religious practice cannot be seen as non-existent or uncertain; such a practice is already justified by its own name and sufficiently authorized by the support of general agreement. Clearly, the reason behind it should be sought, but only while the practice remains intact—not to destroy it, but rather to build it up, so that you might observe it more faithfully once you are certain of the reason. <margin>2 Corinthians 13:10.</margin> But what kind of behavior is it to call a practice into question only when one has already failed to keep it? To ask where the practice came from only after one has abandoned it? Even if someone wants it to appear as if they are raising the question merely to show they haven't sinned by abandoning the practice, it is nonetheless clear that they have indeed sinned...

---

who are comforted by the circumstance of there being any inquiry at all, as if anything which admits of an inquiry must be deemed either no crime, or at all events a very uncertain one.'

Ch. II. <gloss>1</gloss> *to know upon the head* <note>original: "capite nosse"</note>. See below, [chapter 5. *at other times*... 'in other times than those of such a trial as the present.']

<gloss>2</gloss> *from the catechumens... or renegades* <note>original: "a catechumenis...vel negatores"</note>, 'from the time of their first being trainees to that of their becoming either confessors and martyrs, or else renegades.'

<gloss>3</gloss> *Let them see* <note>original: "Viderint"</note>. Rigaltius and the Agobardine Codex read *you see* <note>original: "videris"</note>. The rest read *let them see*. 'Let them look to the source whence the authority for this custom is derived.' i. e. 'No matter from what source...'

⁵ *immersed three times*. <note>original: "ter mergitamur"</note> Tertullian himself says in *Against Praxeas*, chapter 26: *For we are baptized not once, but three times, at the naming of each person [of the Trinity] into their individual persons.* Chrysostom indicates that this rite was also in use in his time, commenting on the words in Acts 10:16, where Peter’s vision is described: *and this happened three times* <note>original Greek: "τοῦτο δὲ ἐγένετο τρίς"</note>. Chrysostom says: "the fact that this happened three times signifies baptism." Ammonius, on John chapter 21, where Christ asks Peter three times: *Simon, son of John, do you love me?* says: "From this, it became the custom to require three confessions from those about to be baptized." From this comes that formula which Pope Stephen II calls "rustic" <note>simple or unrefined</note>. *Response 14: In the name of the Father I immerse, and of the Son I immerse, and of the Holy Spirit I immerse. Vol. II. French Councils.* — RIGALTIUS. See Bingham’s *Antiquities of the Christian Church*, XI. II, 6—8.

Augustine, in *On Faith and Works*, chapter 9, says: *That eunuch, they say, whom Philip baptized, said nothing more than: "I believe that Jesus Christ is the Son of God."* Does it therefore

<column-break/>

please you that men should answer only this and be immediately baptized? Nothing of the **Holy Spirit**, nothing of the **Holy Church**, nothing of the **Remission of Sins**, nothing of the **Resurrection of the dead**? See Bingham, *Antiquities*, XI. 7, 8.

⁷ *received*. <note>original: "suscepti"</note> *To receive* <note>original: "Suscipere"</note>, meaning "to adopt," applied to those who acted as sponsors, hence called *susceptores* <term>godparents<note>Literally "those who take up" the child from the baptismal font</note></term>. The Council of Mainz in the year 1313, canon 55, states: *No one shall receive his own son or daughter from the font of baptism.* Bingham (XI. 8, 10) tells us that this was the first decree which forbade fathers to be sponsors for their own children.

In *Against Marcion*, Book I, chapter 14: *But He [the Creator] even now has not rejected the water of the Creator, with which He washes His own; nor the oil, with which He anoints His own; nor the fellowship of honey and milk, with which He treats His own as infants; nor the bread, with which He represents His own very body; even in His own sacraments He is in need of the humble things of the Creator.*

<margin>CHAPTER III.</margin> we refrain. The sacrament of the **Eucharist**, which the Lord commanded both at the time of a meal and to all people, we receive even in **assemblies held before dawn**⁹, and from no hands other than those of the **presiding ministers**¹⁰. We make **offerings for the dead**¹¹, and for the **birthdays [of the martyrs]**¹², on their annual anniversaries. On the Lord's Day...

---

⁹ The original mode of celebration was kept up on the anniversary of the *Lord's Supper* <note>original: "Cœna Domini"</note>. *Third Council of Carthage, canon 29*: "that the sacraments of the altar should not be celebrated except by those who are fasting, with the exception of the one anniversary day on which the Lord’s Supper is celebrated." See Pole’s *Synopsis* on Matthew 26:21; Bingham, xv. 7, 6—8. The account of the celebration of the Eucharist in Justin Martyr's *First Apology*, page 97, shows that it was then separate from the love-feast <note>A communal meal shared by early Christians</note>. Compare Pliny’s *Letters*, book 10, letter 101, quoted in *On Spectacles*, chapter 26, note 6.

¹⁰ *presiding ministers* <note>original: "præsidentium"</note>. Compare *On Idolatry*, chapter 7. Justin Martyr (in the place cited above) says that the **president** <note>original Greek: "ὁ προεστώς", the leader or bishop</note> took the bread and wine and gave thanks <note>original Greek: "εὐχαριστίαν ἐπὶ πολὺ ποιεῖται", literally "makes thanksgiving at length"</note>, and that the deacons distributed the elements to each person present.

¹¹ *Offerings for the dead* <note>original: "Oblationes pro defunctis"</note>. The Eucharistic offering was made not for deliverance from a place of punishment <note>purgatory</note>, but for the increase of happiness and for the merciful judgment of those who rest in the Lord. See the note in the Oxford Translation of Tertullian’s *On Monogamy*, chapter 10: "For indeed she both prays for his soul, and requests refreshment <note>original: "refrigerium"</note> for him in the meantime, and companionship in the first resurrection, and offers [the sacrifice] on the anniversary days of his falling asleep." Heraldus, in his commentary on Arnobius, book IV, page 152, has a long extract from the *Ecclesiastical Hierarchy* by the Pseudo-Dionysius. This work, which is probably from the 6th century (see Cave’s *Life of Dionysius*), shows the character of the funeral services at

<column-break/>

that time. The writer enters into the question of prayers for the dead; expressly saying that the prayers are only for those who have led a holy life; that they are offered because it is known that God is willing to perform them; that they are not offered for sinners, and if they were, they would not be granted, according to the passage, "Ye ask and obtain not, because ye ask amiss." Originally the bread and wine were an offering of some pious Christians. Cyprian, in *On Works and Almsgiving*: "You are rich and wealthy, and you think you celebrate the Lord's service when you do not even look at the offering box <note>original: "corbanam"</note>; you who come to the Lord’s service without a sacrifice; who take a part of the sacrifice which the poor man has offered." Hence the term **offering** <note>original: "oblatio"</note> was used for: 1. this physical offering, 2. the prayer with which they were presented, 3. the whole celebration of the Lord's Supper. The Eucharist celebrated at a marriage was an "offering for the marriage" <note>original: "oblatio pro matrimonio"</note>. See Neander’s *Church History*, English Translation, vol. 1, page 457 onwards. Heraldus quotes Cyprian’s *Letter III*, 6: "Finally, note down the days on which they depart, so that we may celebrate their commemorations among the memories of the martyrs. Although Tertullian... indicates to me the days on which our blessed brothers in prison pass to the immortality of a glorious death, let the offerings and sacrifices for their commemorations be celebrated here by us." See Bingham, XXIII. 3, 12—17.

¹² *birthdays* <note>original: "natalitiis"</note>. The day of martyrdom was celebrated as the birth- [day of the soul into heaven].

# TERTULLIAN’S BOOK

### CHAPTER IV.

...I find [none], it follows that tradition gave this practice to custom, which would later possess the authority of an apostle through the interpretation of its underlying reason⁴. Therefore, through these examples it will be shown that even an unwritten tradition can be defended through its practice, having been confirmed by custom—a reliable witness that the tradition was approved at that time by the very persistence of its observation⁵. Furthermore, custom is accepted as law even in civil affairs when a written law is missing; it makes no difference whether it rests on Scripture or on reason, since reason is what justifies law itself. Indeed, if law is based on reason, then everything based on reason—no matter who introduced it—will function as law⁶. Do you not think that any faithful person has the right to conceive and establish a rule, provided it is fitting for God, helpful for discipline <note>In this context, "discipline" refers to the regulated way of life and moral conduct of the Christian community.</note>, and beneficial for salvation? For the <margin>Luke 12:57</margin> Lord says, *“And why even of yourselves judge ye not what is right?”* The <margin>Philippians 3:15</margin> Apostle speaks this way not only regarding legal judgment, but regarding every opinion in the examination of things: *“If in anything you are otherwise minded, God shall reveal this to you.”* He <margin>1 Corinthians 7:25; 2 Corinthians 8:8</margin> himself was also accustomed to offer counsel when he did not have a specific command from the Lord, and to speak from his own [authority]...

---

⁴ *“would later possess...”* Tradition first established this custom as a common usage; later, an apostle would provide its authority by explaining the logic behind it. Tertullian refers here to the argument of Saint Paul in 1 Corinthians 11:3–15.

⁵ *“confirmed by custom.”* An unwritten tradition can be defended by the fact that people actually do it. Long-standing usage serves as proof that the tradition was considered valid when it first became a custom. *Then* <note>original Latin: "tunc"</note> refers to the time it became a standard practice.

<column-break/>

⁶ *“if by reason...”* Even a formal law is only binding because it expresses a logical principle <note>original Latin: "ratio"</note>. Therefore, any rule based on such a principle has the power of law, regardless of who first proposed it.

⁷ *“but he himself.”* These words are left out by the editor Oehler because the physical gap <note>original: "lacuna"</note> in the Agobardine Codex <note>A 9th-century manuscript, the most important source for Tertullian’s texts.</note> isn’t big enough to fit the phrase “from himself, but he himself.” However, removing them does not change the essential meaning of the passage, and as the other [manuscripts...]

<summary>Tertullian argues that when written Scripture is silent, long-standing custom serves as law, provided it is rooted in "reason" and promotes godliness. He asserts that any believer, guided by the Holy Spirit and reason, can establish practices that eventually carry the weight of tradition.</summary>

...but he himself <note>Referring to the Apostle Paul.</note> also possessed the Spirit of God as the guide into all truth <note>original: "Spiritum Dei habens deductorem omnis veritatis"</note>. Therefore, his counsel has already attained the status of a divine precept, supported by the advocacy of divine reason. Demand this <note>original: "Hanc" refers to "rationem" (reason).</note> reason now, while still preserving respect for tradition—regardless of who the transmitter is deemed to be. Do not look to the author, but to the authority, and especially to the authority of custom itself. Custom must be respected for this very reason: so that it may serve as the interpreter of reason. Thus, if God grants you the ability to grasp the reason as well, you will learn not *whether* you must observe the custom, but *why*.

To wear crowns on the head is unnatural.

The logic behind Christian practices is strengthened when nature itself defends them, for nature is the primary discipline for us all. Therefore, nature is the first to prescribe that a crown is not suitable for the head. Now, I believe our God is the God of nature, who fashioned man and—so that man might desire, judge, and attain the fruits of the earth—arranged certain senses within him through what we might call the specific organs of the limbs. He dug the sense of hearing into the ears, kindled sight in the eyes, enclosed taste within the mouth, ventilated the sense of smell in the nostrils, and established the sense of touch in the hands. ...the organs <note>original: "ministeria"</note> serving the inner man bring the fruits of divine gifts down to the soul from the external senses. What, then, is the fruit derived from flowers? Use flowers, therefore, by means of sight and smell, since those are the senses meant to enjoy them; use them through the eyes and nostrils, which are the physical organs of those senses. <note>The following notes discuss technical variations between different ancient hand-written versions of the text.</note>

...criterion of touch in the hands. The Agobardine Codex <note>A famous 9th-century manuscript of Tertullian.</note> and two other manuscripts read *extimavit*. Rigaltius (followed by Oehler) adopts this reading, explaining *extimare* as "to place in the extremities," derived from *extimus* (meaning "outermost" or "at the end"). Rigaltius cites from Tertullian's work *On the Apparel of Women* (Book II, Chapter 9), "in the estimation of the times" <note>original: "in extimatione temporum"</note>, but in that instance the Agobardine Codex actually has *existimatione* (judgment). The two manuscripts that have *extimavit* here, have *extimationem* there, while the rest have *æstimationem* (valuation). Ducange <note>A famous scholar of Medieval Latin.</note> tells us that in church writers, *extimare* is used interchangeably with *existimare* (to judge) or *æstimare* (to value). This seems to me to be a final argument against Rigaltius’s new interpretation of "placing in the extremities," and in favor of the standard reading of the text, even though "he valued" <note>original: "æstimavit"</note> seems like a weak expression after stronger words like "he dug" or "he kindled."

Therefore, the ears, eyes, and hands—through which the soul hears, sees, and touches—are rightly said to "agree" <note>original: "adsentire"</note> with the sensing soul. This is, as Oehler remarks, an instance of Rigaltius’s excessive devotion to the Agobardine Codex. The reading in the main text is easier and more understandable. Through the help of the organs of sense, which serve the outer man and also serve the inner man, the enjoyment of God's gifts is passed from the physical sensations to the soul.

## ON THE SOLDIER’S CROWN

<margin>CHAPTER VI.</margin>...presuming Him to be good and invoking Him as judge. You ask whether we ought to be guided by nature in enjoying His creation <note>original: "conditioni," referring to the state of created things</note>, lest we be swept away by that influence through which the rival of God <note>The Devil</note> corrupted the entire creation—which had been handed over to man for specific uses—along with man himself. This is why the Apostle says that creation was subjected to vanity against its will <note>Romans 8:20</note>, overturned first by vain uses, <margin>Romans 8:20.</margin> and then by shameful, unjust, and ungodly ones. Thus, the state of things regarding the pleasures of the public shows has been brought into ill repute by those who perceive that, by nature, everything used to stage the shows belongs to God, but who lack the knowledge <note>original: "scientia," here meaning spiritual discernment</note> to understand that all these things have been changed by the devil. But I have already addressed this subject for the sake of our pleasure-seekers <note>original: "suaviludios," a term for those fond of the games or theater</note> in a work written in the Greek style <note>original: "Græco quoque stilo," referring to a lost Greek treatise by Tertullian on the same subject</note>.

<margin>CHAPTER VII.</margin> <margin>Not only the law of nature, but the law of Christianity, forbids crowns, because the origin of them is idolatrous.</margin> Therefore, let these "crown-wearers" <note>original: "coronarii," those who advocate for or wear crowns</note> meanwhile acknowledge the authority of nature under the name of common wisdom <note>original: "sapientiæ," though some manuscripts read "patience" or "parent"</note>, by which they are human beings, and by the pledges of their own religion <note>original: "propriæ religionis pignora," the sacred obligations of the Christian faith</note>, by which they serve God...

## CHAPTER VII.
...worshipping nature from close at hand <note>original: "de proximo"</note>, and thus, as if from an abundance of evidence, they may also discern the other reasons which specifically forbid our heads <note>that is, the heads of Christians</note> from wearing decorations—indeed, from all such things. For we are compelled to turn from the shared principles of natural discipline to the specific requirements of the Christian life, defending it now in its entirety regarding all other types of crowns. These other crowns seem intended for different uses and are constructed from different materials. Because they are not made of flowers (whose use nature has designated), such as this very military laurel wreath, some might believe they do not fall under the prohibition of our sect <note>our religious way of life</note> because they have escaped the specific rules of nature. I see, therefore, that I must deal with this more carefully and fully, from the very origins of the matter to its development and its excesses. Secular literature is necessary for this purpose, for worldly things must be proven by their own records. ### CHAPTER VII.

According to Hesiod, this first head <note>referring to Pandora, mentioned at the end of the previous page</note> was crowned by the Graces <note>original: *Charitibus*, the three goddesses of charm and beauty</note> when she received gifts from everyone—hence her name, Pandora <note>from the Greek words meaning "all-gifted"</note>. For us, however, Moses—a prophetic shepherd, not a poetic one <note>Both Moses and Hesiod were shepherds; Tertullian contrasts the divine truth of the former with the fiction of the latter</note>—describes Eve as the first woman, and he shows her as having her private parts wrapped in leaves rather than her brow encircled with flowers. Therefore, there was no Pandora. Even the origin of the crown is something to blush at, being born from a lie. Now, let us consider its "truths" <note>Tertullian uses "truths" sarcastically here to mean the historical claims of pagan culture</note>. For it is certainly clear that the others were the originators or promoters of the practice. Pherecydes records that Saturn was the first of all to be crowned; Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian</note> says that Jupiter was honored with this gift by the others after the Titans were defeated. The same author also assigns ribbons to Priapus, and to Ariadne a garland of gold and Indian gems—the work of Vulcan <note>the god of fire/blacksmithing</note> and a gift from Bacchus <note>original: *Liberi*</note>—which later became a constellation. Callimachus introduced a vine-wreath for Juno. Thus, her statue at Argos is shown crowned with a vine branch, with a lion’s skin spread under her feet, displaying her mocking her stepmother-like nature by using the spoils of both... <note>The vine is a symbol of Bacchus and the lion a symbol of Hercules, both illegitimate sons of Jupiter whom Juno persecuted</note>

Aesculapius <note>The Greek god of medicine and healing.</note> may have been the first to explore medicines; but Isaiah also remembers having ordered something medicinal for the ailing Hezekiah <note>Referring to the poultice of figs used to heal the king.</note>.

<summary>Tertullian argues that Christians can use everyday items like ships, medicine, and linen—even if pagans credit their invention to gods—because biblical figures like Paul, Isaiah, and Christ used them. He distinguishes between the "rational" use of these tools for life's needs and the "promiscuous" or "vague" use that fails to distinguish between sacred and profane.</summary>

...that one ought not to be crowned. The truth <note>The "truth" refers to the reality of Christian life, which should match the "image" or precedent set by Christ.</note> must correspond to its image. But perhaps you will object that Christ Himself was crowned. To this, for now, hear this brief reply: If you are crowned in that same way <note>That is, with thorns as a mockery.</note>, then it is permitted. However, even that crown of insulting impiety was not of the [Jewish] people's making. It was an invention of the Roman soldiers, following a secular custom—a custom which the people of God never admitted, whether for public joy or for their own natural luxury. Indeed, they returned from the Babylonian captivity more readily with drums, flutes, and harps than with crowns; and after eating and drinking, they rose up to play <note>A reference to the Israelites at Mount Sinai and the Golden Calf.</note> without crowns. For neither a description of joy nor a record of luxury would have remained silent about the honor or dishonor of a crown. So much so that since Isaiah says, "With drums and flutes and harps they drink wine," he would have also said, "With crowns," if this custom had ever existed in the things of God.

...the reality of use ceases. With the nature of sensation failing—by which one might choose to act⁹—who could misuse a thing when he has no means even to use it? For us, however, the Apostle <margin>1 Corinthians 7:31.</margin> tells us that misusing¹⁰ is not permitted; he teaches that it is better¹¹ not to use at all, except that those who feel nothing cannot even be said to misuse. But the whole matter is empty, and the act itself is dead insofar as it concerns idols, but clearly alive insofar as it concerns the demons¹² to whom such superstition belongs.

---

...those who lack sensation, and similarly for "those who lack sensation and therefore." The Agobardine Codex <note>A 9th-century manuscript, one of the primary sources for this text.</note> reads: *they would wish to misuse it.* Rigaltius and Oehler read: *they would wish to misuse them* [the flowers], while the rest read: *they would wish to misuse.* For the phrase *of which they lack sensation and*, the Agobardine Codex reads: *of whose sensation they lack and.* Rhenanus reads: *of whose sensation they are lacking and.* Gagneius, Gelenius, and Pamelius <note>Various 16th and 17th-century editors of Tertullian.</note> read: *of whose sensation they would equally lack, if they wished to misuse it, even if they were not without sensation.* Tertullian is referring to the misuse of flowers by wearing them upon the head, as discussed above in Chapter 5. But since idols and the dead cannot smell them, Tertullian will not call such a custom an "misuse," because there is no reality of "use"; rather, it is what *would* be a misuse if they were capable of feeling. Observe the opposition between *it will be their lot to use* and *for us, however, to misuse.* "Therefore, to those who are without sensation, it will belong to them to use that of which they have no sensation, just as if they would misuse it if they were not without sensation."

# ON THE SOLDIER’S CROWN

<margin>CHAPTER X.</margin>
This is something sacrificed to an idol <note>original: "idolothytum." This Greek term refers specifically to food or objects offered to pagan gods.</note>; do not touch it. It is even more forbidden when it is contaminated by the dress, rite, and preparation of those things sacrificed to idols. Thus, even a crown is made into an idol-offering. For it is sacrificed with this rite, dress, and preparation to the idols of its own inventors—to whom its use is so uniquely belonging <gloss>17</gloss> that it cannot be admitted into common use, because it is not found among the things of God. Therefore the apostle cries out: "Flee from idolatry." <margin>1 Corinthians 10:14.</margin> He means every kind and in its entirety. Think back on the forest and how many thorns lie hidden there. Nothing should be given to an idol, and so nothing should be taken from an idol. <margin>1 Corinthians 8:10.</margin> If reclining in an idol's temple is foreign to the faith, what about being seen in the dress of an idol? "What fellowship has Christ with Belial?" <margin>2 Corinthians 6:15.</margin> <note>Belial is a term used here to represent Satan or the personification of lawlessness and paganism.</note> And therefore flee. For he commands a long divorce from idolatry; we should not even come near it in any matter. Even the terrestrial dragon <gloss>20</gloss> sucks in men from a distance with its breath.

made an idol-offering. For this offering is made by ceremony and dress and decoration to idols who were its inventors. On the use of *sacrificing* <note>original: "immolare"</note>, see *On the Spectacles*, chapter 10, note 11.

<sup>18</sup> *because* <note>original: "quod"</note>. There is no comma before "because" in the editions of Rigaltius or Oehler, and Dodgson interprets it as: ‘that nothing maybe allowed for common use which is not found in the things of God.’ But this would require a different Latin verb form. La Cerda tells us that "because" is a conjunction answering to "to whom its use is peculiar, so that it cannot be admitted to common use, even especially on this account, because it is not found in the divine economy."

<sup>19</sup> *idol's temple* <note>original: "idolio"</note>. In Greek: <term>in an idol's temple reclining</term> <note>original: "en eidōleiō katakeimenon"</note>. The Vulgate reads: *For if anyone sees him who has knowledge reclining in an idol's temple*, etc. Prudentius in his *Apotheosis* (line 186) writes: *reclining in an idol's temple among*

<column-break/>

*a thousand sacred things*. Du Cange’s Glossary states: ‘An *idolium* is the place where sacrifices are made to idols; an *idolothytum* is the sacrifice itself; an *idol* is the thing to which the sacrifice is made.’

<sup>20</sup> *Terrestrial dragon* <note>original: "Draco terrenus"</note>. Junius and Rigaltius interpret this as Satan, or as the Beast from the Book of Revelation (chapter 13). However, Rhenanus and others correctly refer this passage to the fable of the basilisk. <note>The basilisk was a mythical serpent-king believed to kill with a single glance or a breath of poison.</note> Isidore in his *Etymologies* (Book 12, chapter 4, section 6) says: *Basilisk in Greek is interpreted as 'little king' in Latin, because it is the king of serpents, so much so that when they see it they flee, because it kills them with its smell. For it even kills a person if it just looks at them. Indeed, no flying bird passes by its sight unharmed, but, even if it is far off, it is devoured, consumed by its mouth.* Horus Apollo (Book 2, section 57) writes: ‘For that creature (the basilisk) kills those who approach it by its own breath.’ <term>OEHLER</term>.

<summary>Tertullian argues that Christians must completely shun crowns because their pagan origins and ritualistic use make them "idol-offerings," warning that idolatry can "infect" a believer even from a distance, like the breath of a legendary basilisk.</summary>

# TERTULLIAN'S BOOK

<margin>1 John 5:21.</margin>
**CHAPTER X.** John speaks more deeply when he says, "Little children, keep yourselves from idols!" <note>original: "custodite vos ab idolis!"</note> He does not mean merely from idolatry as an act of worship, but from idols themselves—that is, from their very image. For it is unworthy that the image of the living God should become the image of an idol and a dead thing. Up to this point, we claim the specific nature of this dress <note>referring to the wearing of the crown</note> for idols, based on the account of its origin <gloss>21</gloss> and the practice of superstition. Furthermore, because it is not counted among the things of God, it is assigned more and more to those in whose antiquities, festivals, and duties it is frequently found. Finally, the very doors, the victims, the altars, and even their ministers and priests are crowned. You may find the crowns used by all the priestly colleges described in the writings of Claudius <note>Likely Claudius Saturninus, a writer on Roman religious law.</note>. But we have also inserted that distinction between rational and irrational things <note>Tertullian argues that humans, as rational beings made in God's image, should not follow the "irrational" customs of pagans</note> to counter those who defend participating in all customs by citing certain examples of common usage.

<margin>Look then to the occasions of crown-wearing. Is the chief cause, military service, allowable? It may not be entered into, but may perhaps, under certain conditions, be continued in,</margin>

# ON THE SOLDIER’S CROWN.

<margin>CHAPTER X.</margin>
...let us prove that this argument is supported by the defense of reason, so that this kind of custom <note>referring to the wearing of the crown</note> might also be claimed for common usage, just as certain examples are thrown in our faces <gloss>24</gloss>.

<margin>CHAPTER XI. Exodus 20:12. Matthew 10:37. Matthew 26:52. Luke 10:6. 1 Corinthians 6:7. Romans 12:19. 1 Peter 3:9.</margin>
**To approach the very matter of the military crown, I think we must first inquire whether military service is suitable for Christians at all.** Otherwise, what is the point of reconsidering the secondary details <note>the "accidents" or consequences of service, like the crown</note> when the prior actions themselves are a fault? Do we believe it is permissible for a human oath <note>original: "sacramentum" — this term referred both to the military oath of allegiance and the Christian sacrament of baptism</note> <gloss>2</gloss> to be superimposed upon a divine one <gloss>3</gloss>, and to answer to another master <gloss>4</gloss> after Christ? Is it lawful to swear away <note>original: "ejerare" — to renounce by oath</note> one's father and mother <gloss>5</gloss> and every neighbor, whom the Law commanded to be honored and loved after God, and whom the Gospel also honored in this way <gloss>6</gloss>, though making no one more important than Christ alone? Will it be permitted to live by the sword, when the Lord declares that he who uses the sword shall perish by the sword? And shall the "son of peace" <note>original: "filius pacis" — a person dedicated to peace</note> <gloss>7</gloss> work in battle, for whom it is not even fitting to go to law? And shall he administer chains and prison and tortures and punishments <gloss>8</gloss>, he who is not even the avenger of his own injuries? Furthermore, will he perform watches <note>original: "stationes" — guard duties</note> <gloss>9</gloss> for another more than...

---

<columns>2</columns>

...and I will hold my own [family] dearer than Gaius and his sisters. Arrian, *Discourses of Epictetus* i. 14: <note>original: "τῷ θεῷ ἔδει καὶ ἡμᾶς ὀμνύειν ὅρκον οἷον στρατιῶται τῷ Καίσαρι· ἀλλ’ ἐκεῖνοι μὲν μισθοφορίαν λαμβάνοντες ὀμνύουσι πάντων προτιμήσειν τὴν τοῦ Καίσαρος σωτηρίαν."</note> "We too ought to swear an oath to God such as the soldiers do to Caesar; but they, receiving pay, swear they will prefer the safety of Caesar above all."

<gloss>6</gloss> **in this way too**. "That is, the Gospel commanded that parents and every neighbor be honored no less than was prescribed by the Mosaic Law. For the Law commanded to honor them immediately after God, the Gospel immediately after Christ." — RIGALTIUS.

<gloss>7</gloss> **son of peace**. Luke 10:6: <note>original: "ὁ υἱὸς εἰρήνης"</note> "the son of peace." See also *On Spectacles*, chapter 16, note 7.

<gloss>8</gloss> **And chains... will he administer.** Compare *On Idolatry*, chapter 17, near the end.

<column-break/>

<gloss>9</gloss> **watches**. "Moreover will he keep vigils either for another than Christ, or on the Lord’s day too, when he does not keep them even for Christ?" *Statio*, originally meaning a "military watch." Hence the vigils of the Church were called *stationes*. *On Prayer*, chapter 14 (Oehler 19): "If the watch <note>original: "statio"</note> received its name from a military example (for we are also the army of God)," etc. *Stationes* were the regular vigils held on the fourth and sixth days of the week <note>Wednesday and Friday</note>, as opposed to the extraordinary fasts (proclaimed fasts). The fast was not broken until the ninth hour <note>3:00 PM</note>. Tertullian defends the Montanist fasts in *On Fasting*, chapter 10: "For our watches, as [indigent]..."

<summary>Tertullian begins a famous argument against Christian military service, claiming that the military oath (sacramentum) conflicts with the baptismal oath to Christ and that the violence of the soldier is incompatible with the "son of peace." He plays on the double meaning of "stationes" as both military guard duty and Christian prayer vigils.</summary>

<gloss>16</gloss> [The commentator notes:] "that the military service must be immediately abandoned, which is not allowed by the laws of the service; or one must take care in all ways that nothing is committed against God, which is scarcely possible under the laws of the Roman military; or the greatest extremes must be endured for God, which every Christian has agreed to by the oath of faith given to Christ." Oehler reads *extra militiam* <note>outside the military</note>, meaning: "since even outside the military, that is in private affairs, it is not permitted to abandon the faith once accepted, or to dodge and elude it." Both refer the phrase "which are permitted" back to "abandoning" and "dodging." Tertullian means to say that if the converted soldier remains in the army, he must either manage to avoid transgressing God's laws, or he must die for the cause of Christ. The root of "which" is found in the phrase "lest anything be committed," meaning: "provided nevertheless that when faith has been embraced and sealed, we must either quit the ser-

<column-break/>

vice, as many have done, or must demur in all ways to doing anything against God's will (which doings are not allowed on the ground of military service more than on any other ground); or in the last place, we must endure for God's sake, what the faith of citizen, no less than soldier, has agreed to suffer."

<gloss>17</gloss> *pagana* <note>civilian</note>. *Paganus* is opposed to *miles* <note>soldier</note> just as we oppose "citizen" to "soldier." Juvenal, *Satires* xvi. 33: "You could more quickly produce a false witness against a civilian <note>original: "paganum"</note> than one speaking the truth against the life and status of an armed man." *Paganus* was not used to mean "heathen" before the Roman Empire became Christian, after which the name was applied to the remote and unrefined country-dwellers, as opposed to the more enlightened inhabitants of towns. Heraldus, *Notes on Arnobius*, at the beginning. Prudentius, *Against Symmachus* I. 449: "Let these be the ancestral deities in barbarian villages <note>original: "pagis"</note>."

<summary>This page discusses the difficult position of soldiers who convert to Christianity, arguing they must prioritize God's law over military commands, even if it leads to martyrdom. <meta>This page continues Chapter XI of Tertullian's treatise, following the argument that a Christian's primary loyalty is to God, regardless of their professional status as a soldier or civilian.</meta>

-># TERTULLIAN’S BOOK<-

<columns>2</columns>

<margin>CHAPTER XI.</margin> ...[destroyed] for the sake of His name. In His sight, the believing civilian is just as much a soldier, as the believing soldier is a civilian <gloss>18</gloss>. The state of faith does not admit an excuse of "necessity." There is no necessity for sinning for those who have but one necessity: that of not sinning. For one may even be pressed by the necessity of tortures or punishments to offer sacrifice <note>to Roman gods</note> or to deny Christ outright <gloss>19</gloss>; yet Christian discipline does not blink at even that necessity, because the necessity of fearing denial and undergoing martyrdom is more powerful than that of escaping suffering and fulfilling an official duty. Otherwise, an excuse of this kind subverts the entire essence of the sacrament <term>sacramentum: the sacred oath of loyalty taken by a Roman soldier, which Tertullian compares to the baptismal vow of a Christian</term>, to the point that it might even loosen the fastener <gloss>20</gloss> for voluntary sins. For even the will could be called a "necessity,"

---

<gloss>18</gloss> *believing soldier*. [Editors] Gangnaeus, Gelenius, Pamelius, and Rigaltius read "unbelieving soldier." Dodgson, following Rigaltius, translates: "In his sight the believer who is no soldier is as much a soldier as the unbeliever who is a soldier is no soldier." But the Agobardine Codex, the other manuscripts, Rhenanus, and Oehler read as in the text. "In his sight the believing citizen is as much a soldier, as the believing soldier is a citizen," meaning that in God's sight, there is no difference between the duties of a soldier and a citizen.

<gloss>19</gloss> *For even to sacrifice*. The argument of necessity might just as easily be applied to performing pagan sacrifices or to direct apostasy. In those cases, there is a compelling necessity caused by tortures and punishment. Yet this is outweighed by the counter-necessity of enduring martyrdom for the sake of duty. But the whole essence of the baptismal vow is destroyed by an excuse of this kind, which would loosen the restraint even upon wilful sins.

<gloss>20</gloss> *loosen the fastener*. Oehler quotes *On Modesty* chapter 16: "Who does not know that he reluctantly loosened the fastener <note>original: "fibulam," a buckle or brooch</note> of this good thing, so that he might meet fornication halfway?" 

<column-break/>

Seneca, quoted in Lactantius, Book I, chapter 16: "What then is the reason why, among the poets, the most lustful Jupiter ceased to have children? Has he become a sixty-year-old, and has the Papian law <term>lex Papia: a Roman law that encouraged marriage but restricted the rights of those who remained childless or were past a certain age</term> put a fastener on him?"

<gloss>21</gloss> *For even the will...* "For even the will may be maintained to be necessity, since it admits of being constrained."

<gloss>22</gloss> *Or this itself.* The Agobardine Codex, Rigaltius, and Oehler read "this itself," referring to "necessity." Tertullian has reluctantly allowed the possibility of a converted soldier remaining in the army, provided he is ready to suffer martyrdom rather than perform an unlawful act, such as wearing a laurel crown. He insists on this condition, rejecting the plea of necessity. If such a necessity exists, it would only show that the profession in which it occurs is fundamentally unlawful. "I might," Tertullian says, "even myself have advanced these arguments of necessity as a barrier not only to military service, but to all other occupations which provide an occasion for the official use of crowns."

<summary>Tertullian argues that "necessity" is no excuse for a Christian soldier to sin or avoid martyrdom, asserting that the baptismal oath (sacramentum) overrides military duty. He emphasizes that both soldiers and civilians are held to the same standard of faith and must be prepared to die rather than compromise their beliefs.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the argument in Chapter XI regarding the "necessity" of military service and begins Chapter XII, where Tertullian shifts focus from the lawfulness of the service itself to the specific idolatry of the military crown. -># ON THE MILITARY CROWN<-

<columns>2</columns>

...striven, since he clearly has grounds for being compelled <gloss>21</gloss>. <margin>CHAPTER XI.</margin> Or perhaps I myself have laid these foundations for other cases of official crowns, for which that most familiar guidance <term>ducatio: the state of being led or directed; Tertullian uses this to describe being "led" by necessity</term> <gloss>23</gloss> of necessity is used; since, for that reason, either offices must be avoided lest we fall into sins, or martyrdoms must be endured so that we may break the ties of office. Regarding the first kind of question—that of military service itself being unlawful—more words do not achieve <gloss>24</gloss> this: that the second question might be granted; lest, if I have driven out military service with all my might, I should then have challenged the matter of the military crown in vain.

<margin>CHAPTER XII. <br/> But suppose the service lawful, crowns are unlawful</margin> Suppose, finally, that military service is lawful right up to the point of the crown <gloss>25</gloss>. But I will also speak of the crown first. That laurel crown is sacred to Apollo or Bacchus <note>original: "Libero"</note>; to the former as the god of weapons, to the latter as the god of triumphs. Thus teaches...

---

which cases are perfectly familiar with the sway of necessity, whereas on account of that very necessity the consequence follows that we should either shun office, lest we fall into sin, or else undergo martyrdom to break the ties of office.'

<gloss>23</gloss> *that guidance* <note>Latin: "ista ducatio"</note>. Rigaltius and Latinus [conjecture] from "that advocacy" <note>Latin: "ista advocatio"</note>. But Oehler remarks that *ducatio* is for *ducatus* <note>leadership or sway</note> as *ambitio* is for *ambitus*. See *On Idolatry* chapter 1, note 3. *Ducatus* occurs in *On Modesty* chapter 5: 'I behold a certain procession and platform of adultery, here the leadership <note>ducatum</note> of preceding idolatry, there the retinue of following homicide.' DUCATOR, a leader. Tertullian, *Against the Jews* chapter 13. Saint Augustine, book 3 *Against Maximus*, in the *Life of Saint Frontonus the Abbot* chapter 7. Ancient Glosses: *Ducator*, a leader, one who goes before <note>Greek: ἀγὸς, προηγούμενος</note>. DUCATRIX <note>female leader</note>. Apuleius, book 1, *On the Teachings of Plato*: 'Those truly are the leaders of vices: anger and lust.' DU CANGE LEXICON.

<gloss>24</gloss> *achieve* <note>Latin: "faciunt"</note>. So all the manuscripts and early editions. Ursinus conjectured "I shall achieve" <note>Latin: "faciam"</note>, which has been adopted by Rigaltius

<column-break/>

and Oehler. Codex Agobardine and Rigaltius read "lest if" <note>Latin: "ne si"</note>. Vienna and Leyden manuscripts read "nor if" <note>Latin: "nec si"</note>. Florence, Rhenanus, Gangnaeus, Gelenius, and Pamelius read "Unless" <note>Latin: "Nisi"</note>. Oehler by conjecture reads "Truly if" <note>Latin: "Næ si"</note>. The first question was as to the lawfulness of military service. The second as to the lawfulness of crowns. *Even of the unlawful service itself*, "that is, because the service is even in itself unlawful." OEHLER. 'More words on the first head of inquiry (that of military service being even in itself unlawful) do not bring it about, that the second question be answered, lest after I have with my whole force driven military service from the field, I shall in vain have put forth my challenge on the subject of the military crown.' Tertullian will not let the unfaithfulness of the crown depend on the unlawfulness of the service, but will proceed to prove that point independently.

<gloss>25</gloss> *Suppose, finally...* 'Suppose, in short, that military service is allowable up to the point of its being the cause of the military crown.' In order to come to the point now at hand.

<sig>7—3</sig>

<summary>Tertullian concludes that military necessity is no excuse for sin, arguing that Christians must either avoid office or accept martyrdom. He then transitions to proving that military crowns are inherently idolatrous, regardless of whether the service itself is considered lawful.</summary>

Both in themselves and their occasions; whether these occasions be military,

### CHAPTER XII. Claudius also says that even soldiers are usually crowned with myrtle <gloss>1</gloss>. For the myrtle belongs to Venus, the mother of the descendants of Aeneas, and also the mistress of Mars; it is considered Roman through Ilia and the Romuluses <gloss>2</gloss>. But I do not believe that Venus, in this context, is "Roman" alongside Mars—for here we find the resentment of a mistress <gloss>3</gloss>. When the military is also crowned with olive, the idolatry is directed toward Minerva, who is equally a goddess of weapons, but who was also crowned with this tree for the peace established with Neptune <gloss>4</gloss>. In these matters, the superstition of the military garland will be seen as polluted everywhere and polluting everything. Let them now be polluted <gloss>5</gloss> by their occasions as well. Look at the annual public pronouncement of vows <term>votorum nuncupatio: a formal ceremony held at the beginning of the year where the army and officials swore oaths for the safety of the Emperor</term> <gloss>6</gloss>—what does it seem like? The first takes place in the headquarters, the second on the Capitoline Hill. Consider the locations and then the words: "To you, O Jupiter, we vow that this bull with horns decorated in gold will be offered" <gloss>7</gloss>. Regarding which sentiment—

---

issue, Tertullian supposes (for the sake of argument), that the preliminary question has been determined in favour of the lawfulness of military service.

Ch. XII. ¹ Pliny, *Natural History* xv. 38: "Postumius Tubertus, triumphing over the Sabines during his consulship (he was the first of all to enter the City in an ovation), because he had performed the feat easily and without bloodshed, entered crowned with the myrtle of Venus the Victorious, and made this tree desirable even to enemies. This later became the crown for those celebrating an ovation." <note>An 'ovation' was a lesser form of a Roman triumph.</note>

² *Roman*, "by his connection with Ilia and the Romuluses (Romulus and Remus) a Roman."

³ *But I do not suppose that Venus...* "But I do not suppose that Venus as well as Mars was a Roman by virtue of this connection, wherein is the resentment occasioned by an intruder." <note>Tertullian is likely mocking the mythological adultery between Venus and Mars.</note>

⁴ *the peace established with Neptune*. Oehl. refers to Pliny, *Natural History* xvi. 44, and others.

<column-break/>

⁵ *be polluted*. So all the manuscripts except the Agersbach Codex, which has *will be polluted*. Oehl. follows La Cerda, who conjectured *let it be polluted*. Tertullian is now proceeding to the discussion of the occasion of crowns, having first shown them to be in themselves superstitious. "On these foundations will rest the superstition of the military garland on every side polluted, and polluting all. Let all moreover be polluted (that is, be thought to be polluted) through the occasions also on which it is worn." Tertullian proceeds to point out the superstition connected with the occasions of wearing the garland.

⁶ *public pronouncement of vows*. This was in the beginning of the year, for the safety of the emperor. Oehl. refers to Suetonius, *Life of Nero* chapter 46: "At the public pronouncement of vows, with a great crowd of the ranks present, the keys of the Capitol could scarcely be found." Compare *Apology*, chapter 28, and following.

⁷ *we vow that it will be offered*. Ursinus.

<summary>Tertullian argues that military crowns made of myrtle or olive are inseparable from the worship of pagan deities like Venus, Mars, Minerva, and Jupiter. He emphasizes that the rituals surrounding these crowns, such as the annual vows for the Emperor's safety, are inherently idolatrous and "pollute" the wearer.</summary>

# ON THE SOLDIER’S CROWN

<columns>2</columns>

Is it a voice? Certainly one of denial. Even if the Christian remains silent with his mouth in that place, he has given his answer with the crown on his head. That same laurel is announced during the distribution of the imperial bonus <term>donativum: a financial gift given by Roman Emperors to the soldiers, often to celebrate an accession or anniversary</term> <gloss>8</gloss>. Clearly, this is not "free" idolatry; it sells Christ for a few gold pieces, just as Judas sold Him for silver ones. Will it be this: *You cannot serve both God and Mammon* <margin>Matthew 6:24</margin>, to give your hand to Mammon and depart from God? Will it be this: *Render the things that are Caesar’s to Caesar, and the things that are God’s to God* <margin>Matthew 22:21</margin>, neither to return the man to God nor to take the coin from Caesar? <gloss>9</gloss> Is the triumphal laurel <gloss>10</gloss> built of leaves, or of corpses? <gloss>11</gloss> Is it decorated with ribbons <gloss>12</gloss>, or with funeral pyres? Is it drenched in ointments <gloss>13</gloss>, or in the tears of wives and mothers? Perhaps even the tears of some Christians; for Christ is also among the barbarians <gloss>14</gloss>. Whoever wears this on their head—

---

quotes an inscription: <note>original: "QUOD . SI . FACSIS . TUNC . TIBI . IN . EADEM . VERBA . NOMINE . FRATRUM . ARVALIUM . BOVE . AURATO . VOVIMUS . ESSE . FUTURUM ."</note> "If you do this, then we vow that it shall be for you in the same words, in the name of the Arval Brothers <term>Arval Brothers: an ancient college of twelve Roman priests who performed sacrifices for fertility and the state</term>, with a gilded ox."
<gloss>8</gloss> *donative*. See above, chapter 1.
<gloss>9</gloss> *Will it be this...* "Will *You cannot serve God and Mammon* mean this—to surrender to Mammon and desert God? Will *Render to Caesar the things that are Caesar's, and to God the things that are God's* mean both not giving up man (who is God's image) to God, and taking the coin (which is Caesar's image) from Caesar? (i.e., in the imperial bonus.)" Compare his work *On Idolatry*, chapter 15: <note>original: "Reddite, ait, quæ sunt Cæsaris Cæsari, et quæ sunt Dei Deo, id est imaginem Cæsaris Cæsari, quæ in nummo est, et imaginem Dei Deo, quæ in homine est."</note> "He says, 'Render the things that are Caesar’s to Caesar, and the things that are God’s to God,' that is, Caesar’s image to Caesar, which is on the coin, and God’s image to God, which is in man."
<gloss>10</gloss> *triumphal laurel*. La Cerda quotes the poet Tibullus, Elegies II. 5, 117: <note>original: "Ipse gerens lauros, lauro devinctus agresti,"</note> "Wearing the laurels himself, bound with rustic laurel,"

<column-break/>

"The soldier, crying 'Hail, Triumph!' with a loud voice, shall sing."
<gloss>11</gloss> *or of corpses?* In other manuscripts, "built with these adverbs" was found, which led to many guesses. However, the Agobardine Codex <term>Codex Agobardinus: a 9th-century manuscript that is a primary source for Tertullian's works</term> restores the text to read "or of corpses."
<gloss>12</gloss> *ribbons*, "fillets binding and hanging from a crown." La Cerda quotes Festus: <note>original: "Lemnisci sunt fasciolæ purpureæ dependentes ex coronis. Solebant enim veteres coronas fasciis laniis ex purpura alligatas donare."</note> "Ribbons are small purple strips hanging from crowns. For the ancients used to give crowns tied with woolen bands of purple." Hesychius <note>original Greek: "λημνίσκους, τὰς στενὰς ταινίας"</note> defines them as "ribbons, the narrow bands." It appears these ribbons were later made of gold. See below, chapter 13, note 2.
<gloss>13</gloss> *ointments*. La Cerda quotes Plutarch’s *Table Talk*, Book 7, where a Persian king sends to Antalcidas "a crown of mixed roses and saffron, having dipped it in ointment." Regarding the use of ointments, see Athenaeus, Book 15.
<gloss>14</gloss> *among the barbarians*. See the *Apology*, chapter 1.

<summary>Tertullian argues that wearing a laurel crown during the imperial bonus ceremony is an act of idolatry that prioritizes worldly wealth (Mammon) over God. He highlights the bloody origins of the triumphal laurel, associating it with corpses and the grief of war rather than honor.</summary>

CHAPTER XII. ...the cause <gloss>15</gloss>, did he not also himself <gloss>16</gloss> fight? There is also another military service within the royal households <gloss>17</gloss>. For they are also called "camp-officers" <gloss>18</gloss>, and they are themselves officials <note>original: munificæ</note> of the imperial solemnities <gloss>19</gloss>. But you <gloss>20</gloss> are just as much a soldier as you are a servant of another <note>meaning: a servant of God</note>; and if you serve two masters—God and Caesar—you certainly do not belong to Caesar at the moment when you owe yourself to God, even in common matters where, I believe, the higher power takes precedence.

<margin>
**CHAPTER XIII.**
Concerning crowns that are:
magisterial,
triumphal,
provincial,
festal, nuptial, gymnastic, or other.
</margin>

Public occasions <gloss>1</gloss> also crown the public orders with laurel; but magistrates, moreover, are crowned with gold ones <gloss>2</gloss>, as in Athens and in Rome. Even the Etruscan <gloss>3</gloss> crowns are carried above them.

---

*Christians in the fields, in the forts, in the islands.*

<gloss>15</gloss> *causam.* <note>original: "causam"</note> Tertullian calls the triumphal crown the "cause" of the horrors of war, because men fought specifically to attain this honor.

<gloss>16</gloss> *et ipse.* <note>original: "et ipse"</note> He who has worn on his head the "cause" of all this may be considered to have personally taken part in the unholy warfare. Oehler suggests by conjecture the reading "even they themselves" <note>original: "et ipsi"</note>, meaning "has fought even with Christ himself."

<gloss>17</gloss> *regiarum familiarum.* <note>original: "regiarum familiarum"</note> "There is also another military service in the royal households." This refers to the various military officers in the emperor's court who were known generally as court officials <term>aulici: members of the imperial court or household</term>. These officers included the Palatines, Tent-keepers, Caesarians, Praetorians, Camp-officers, Attendants, Scouts, Bodyguards, Protectors, Cohort-officers, Ministers, Display-guards, Tent-mates, and Domestics.

<gloss>18</gloss> *castrenses.* <note>original: "castrenses"</note> In the early days of Rome, the "camp crown" <note>original: "castrensis corona"</note> was the crown worn by the first person to enter an enemy's camp. But under the empire, it belonged to the court officers called "Camp-officers." La Cerda quotes Vopiscus’s *Life of Tacitus*: "He obeyed the in-

<column-break/>

-structions and the will of the most noble order of the Camp-officers."

<gloss>19</gloss> *munificæ et ipsæ...* <note>original: "munificæ et ipsæ..."</note> "being themselves also officials in the imperial solemnities." Tertullian views the crowns (which were necessary in all such ceremonies) as a kind of office-bearer in the court. "Officials" <note>original: "Munifici"</note> is the proper term for soldiers who hold certain duties <term>munia: official duties or administrative tasks</term>. Oehler quotes from the Theodosian Code (xii. 1, 192): "Voluntary record-keepers who are officials"; and Isidore’s *Etymologies* (x. 166): "One is called 'munificus' either because he gives many gifts <note>original: munera</note> to someone, or because he fulfills his gift, that is, the duty <note>original: officium</note> he owes." Note that "Imperial" <note>original: Cæsareanorum</note> is the adjective describing the "solemnities," and it has nothing to do with the "Caesarian" court officials.

<gloss>20</gloss> *Sed et tu.* <note>original: "Sed et tu"</note> Oehler suggests the reading "then" <note>original: tum</note>. He interprets it: "For he says: but even if you serve in this military service of the sacred house, rather than in that other which prepares its rewards with corpses and tears—thereby offending God—nonetheless in this one too you are constantly forced to wound your holy duty toward God." But "another" <note>original: alterius</note> refers to "of another," i.e., of God. On the use of "the other" <note>original: alter</note> for "another" <note>original: alius</note>, see *On the Spectacles* chapter 14, note 4. "Just as much" <note>original: proinde</note>; Dodgson translates this as "henceforth," but it is more properly used for "just as" <note>original: perinde</note>. See *On the Spectacles*.

Chapter 2, note 10: "But if they of Caesar’s household are soldiers, you too are as much a soldier as a servant of another <note>meaning: a servant of God</note>, and if you are a soldier and servant of two persons, of God and Caesar (as soldiers must necessarily in a certain sense be), at any rate you are not a servant of Caesar on those occasions on which your service is due to God, a master to be preferred, I suppose, even in things indifferent."

# ON THE SOLDIER’S CROWN.

<page-num>153</page-num>

<header>ON THE SOLDIER’S CROWN.</header>

<margin>CH. XIII.</margin>
How shall a world that is alien to God set you free? Even if it seems like freedom, it will also be seen as slavery. Everything in this world is imaginary and nothing is true. For even then you were a free man belonging to man, but you were redeemed by Christ; and now you are a servant of Christ, though you have been set free <term>manumissus</term> <note>original: "manumissus." Manumission was the formal Roman legal process of freeing a slave, often accompanied by the wearing of a cap or a wreath to signify their new status.</note> by a human. <margin>1 Cor. 7:22.</margin> If you think the world's freedom is so true that you seal it with a crown, you have returned to human slavery (which you mistake for freedom) and you have lost the freedom of Christ (which you mistake for slavery). Shall we also debate the causes of athletic competitions <note>original: "agonisticæ causæ." Tertullian refers to the Greek-style games—such as the Olympics—which involved both athletic and religious elements.</note>, which their very titles condemn at once—namely, the "sacred" and "funeral" games? For this is what remains: that Olympian Jupiter and Nemean Hercules and poor little Archemorus and the unhappy Antinous <note>Archemorus was a child whose death inspired the Nemean Games; Antinous was the deified favorite of Emperor Hadrian. Tertullian finds it scandalous that a Christian would wear a crown associated with these figures.</note> should be crowned in the person of a Christian, so that the Christian himself becomes a spectacle that he ought not to watch.

<margin>All these occasions are unlawful, and alien from Christ, being founded on idolatry.</margin>
We have, I believe, enumerated all the reasons for wearing crowns, and none is compatible with us: all are alien, profane, illicit, and already renounced once in the testimony of our oath <note>original: "sacramenti." Here referring to the baptismal vow, which was compared to a soldier's oath of loyalty.</note>. For these were the "pomps" of the devil and his angels—the offices of the world, honors, solemnities, popularities, false vows, human services, vain praises, shameful glories <margin>Phil. 3:19.</margin>, and in all of these, idolatry is found in the foundation...

---

*On Spectacles, ch. 11: What wonder is it, if the equipment of the games is defiled by idolatry regarding profane crowns? Ibid: From there, the sacred or funeral games themselves are established either for the gods of the nations or for the dead. Accordingly, the titles are: the Olympics for Jupiter... likewise the Nemean for Hercules, the Isthmian for Neptune, and other games for the dead.*

^14 *Archemorus. The son of Lycurgus, in whose honor annual games were held. Antinous. La Cerda quotes Hegesippus in Jerome's "On Illustrious Men": They built*

<column-break/>

*tombs and temples for the dead, as we see to this day, among whom is also Antinous, the slave of Hadrian Caesar, for whom even a gymnastic game is celebrated at the city of Antinoopolis, which he founded in his name and where he appointed prophets in the temple. They who were crowned in such games are considered by Tertullian to represent the person in whose honor the games were celebrated.*

^15 *spectare non debeat. The Agreius and Rigaltius manuscripts read: "ought to watch." Oehler, from*

<sig>7—5</sig>

<summary>Tertullian argues that Roman manumission and athletic games are steeped in idolatry, making their associated crowns unfit for Christians. He emphasizes that a Christian's true freedom comes from Christ, not from the worldly honors of the Roman state or its pagan festivals.</summary>

<margin>Ch. XIII.</margin> ...and by the very status of crowns <term>censu coronarum</term> <note>original: "censu coronarum." This refers to the "reckoning" or "inventory" of how wreaths are utilized in various contexts.</note>, with which all those things are adorned. Claudius <note>Likely Claudius Saturninus, a Roman legal writer who wrote a treatise on crowns.</note> even prefaces his work by saying that in Homer’s poems the heaven is crowned with stars—certainly by God, and certainly for man: therefore, man himself must be crowned by God. But in this world, crowns are also placed on brothels, latrines, bakeries, the prison, the gladiatorial school, the amphitheatres themselves, the stripping-rooms where the dead are laid <term>spoliaria</term>, and even the very biers of the dead. How "sacred" and "holy," how "honorable" and "clean" this custom is—do not judge it by that one poetic sky, but by the common practices of the whole world. Indeed, a Christian will not even disgrace his own door with laurel wreaths if he knows how many gods the devil has attached to doorways: Janus from the "door" <term>janua</term>, Limentinus from the "threshold" <term>limen</term>, Forculus and Carna from the "doors" <term>fores</term> and "hinges" <term>cardines</term>—and even among the Greeks, "Apollo of the Door" <note>original: "Thyræum Apollinem." A title for Apollo as a protector of entrances.</note> and the "Demons of the Dawn." <note>original: "Antelios dæmonas." Deities whose statues stood before the house facing the sun.</note>

conjectured reading: *it is wearying to watch.* Flor., Rhen., Gangn., Gel. and Pam. as in text. Vien., Leyd. *it was necessary.* The Christian by wearing a crown becomes a part of the show, of which he ought not even to be a spectator.

<sup>16</sup> *on account of the crowns alone.* On "status" <term>census</term>, see *On Idolatry* ch. 4, note 4.

<sup>17</sup> *crowned*. Iliad 18.485: *all the constellations, with which the heaven is crowned.* <note>original Greek: "ἐν δὲ τὰ τείρεα πάντα, τά τ᾽ οὐρανὸς ἐστεφάνωται."</note> La Cerda quotes Pliny’s *Natural History* 16.4: *In ancient times, indeed, no crown was given except to a God.* For this reason Homer attributed them only to the heaven and to the entire battle. The argument of Claudius is this: The heaven is crowned with stars. It was certainly so crowned by God for man’s benefit. Therefore man himself ought to be crowned by God.

<sup>18</sup> *brothels*. See *On Idolatry* ch. 15, note 1.

<column-break/>

<sup>19</sup> *the gladiatorial school*. Schools in general were so bedecked. *On Idolatry* ch. 10: *the school must be crowned with flowers.*

<sup>20</sup> *stripping-rooms* <term>spoliaria</term>, "the place where the corpses of gladiators were stripped." Lipsius (on the Amphitheatre, ch. 21) quotes Lampridius in his life of *Commodus*: *Let the gladiator’s corpse be dragged by a hook; let the gladiator’s corpse be placed in the stripping-room.*

<sup>21</sup> *biers of the dead*. See above, ch. 10, note 3. La Cerda quotes Sidonius Apollinaris 2.8: *When everyone, even strangers, weeping, were grasping the bier itself, lingering over it, kissing it, etc.* The gate of the stripping-room was called the "Gate of Death" <note>original: "Porta Libitinensis." Named after Libitina, the goddess of funerals.</note>.

<sup>22</sup> *the door*. Compare *On Idolatry* ch. 15.

<sup>23</sup> *Carna*. The Agrellian and Rhenanus manuscripts read *Carna.* Gangneius, Gelenius, and Pamelius read *Carda.* In *On Idolatry* ch. 15, we have Cardea. But Ovid's *Fasti*...

<summary>Tertullian argues that Christians should avoid wearing crowns because they are used to decorate profane and sordid places like brothels and prisons, and are associated with a multitude of minor Roman "doorway" deities.</summary>

<margin>Chapter XIV.</margin>
So far is it from the truth that a Christian should offer his head to the service of an idol; indeed, I would say it is an insult to Christ himself, since Christ is the head of the man. 
<margin>To crown the head is to dishonour Christ, who is the true head of man. Christ was crowned with thorns. That crown alone befits his members.</margin>
The man’s head is as free as Christ is, not even subject to a veil, much less a binding <note>Tertullian distinguishes between a "velamento" (veil) and an "obligamento" (a crown or headband). A crown was seen as a binding ritual object.</note>. Furthermore, that which is already subject to a veil—the head of the woman—is already occupied and has no room for a crown. She bears the burden of her own humility <term>humilitatis suæ sarcinam</term> <note>original: "humilitatis suæ sarcinam." This refers to the veil as a symbolic "weight" or "pack" representing the woman's social and spiritual status.</note>. 
<margin>1 Cor. xi. 3—10.</margin>
If a woman ought not to be seen with her head uncovered because of the angels, she would perhaps offend those crowned ones <note>Referring to the twenty-four elders in Revelation 4:4 who wear crowns of gold in heaven.</note> even more if she were seen with a crowned head. 
<margin>Rev. iv.</margin>
For what is a crown on the head of a woman but a procuress of her beauty, a mark of total wantonness, an utter denial of modesty, and a fabrication of allure? 
<margin>1 Tim. ii. 9. 1 Pet. iii. 3.</margin>
For this reason, the woman shall not be too elaborately adorned, according to the Apostle’s view, so that she is not even "crowned" by the artifice of her own braided hair. He who is both the head of the man and the face of the woman, the Husband of the Church, Christ Jesus—what kind of crown, I ask you, [did He wear]...
<margin>2 Cor. xi. 2. Eph. v. 23, sqq.</margin>

<note>original Latin verse: "Prima dies tibi, Carna, datur. Dea cardinis hæc est, Numine clausa aperit, claudit aperta suo."</note> Ovid, Fasti VI. 101: *The first day is given to you, Carna. She is the goddess of the hinge; by her power she opens what is closed, and closes what is open.*

Ch. XIV. ¹ *So far is it from* <note>original: "Tanto abest."</note>, used instead of *tantum abest*. See *On the Testimony of the Soul*, ch. 1: "So far is it from men agreeing with our writings." *On Flight in Persecution*, ch. 2: "so far is it from his possessing it by right." Oehler supposes a missing word "more" <note>original: "magis"</note>. However, the case used seems to mark the distance—"it is distant by so much"—rather than implying a comparison. 'So far,' not 'so much farther.' On the missing "more," see *On the Spectacles*, ch. 16, note 8.

² *the burden of her humility.* 1 Corinthians 11:8–10 is discussed in *On Prayer*, ch. 22, and *On the Veiling of Virgins*, ch. 7. In the latter, the Greek word for "authority" <note>original: "ἐξουσίαν"</note> is rendered into Latin as "power" <note>original: "potestatem"</note> without further comment. La Cerda remarks that "burden" <note>original: "sarcina"</note> implies the same as "authority" or "power"—

<column-break/>

*namely, 'that which is placed upon the head, and which has, as it were, the power of compelling the woman to preserve her modesty, to cast down her head, and to lower her eyes.'* **On the Veiling of Virgins, ch. 17:** *Others are covered only moderately with linen cloths—I suppose so as not to weigh down the head—which do not even come down to the ears, covering only the brain.* The veil is called by Tertullian the *yoke of subjection*, by Chrysostom the *badge of subjection*, and by the Council of Gangra the *memorial of subjection. Those crowned ones*, referring to Revelation 4:4, means "much more if her head is crowned will she give offense to those who are perhaps at that very moment crowned in a different manner."

³ *For what... but* <note>original: "Quid enim... quam"</note>, that is, *what else than*. *On Idolatry, ch. 20:* "what will an oath be but..." *On the Veiling of Virgins, ch. 11:* "they felt nothing first but a reason to blush." Apuleius, Metamorphoses IV. 6: "nothing nearby but..."

<columns>2</columns>
⁴ *hundred-petaled* <note>original: "centenariis"</note>. The ancient reading was *centaureis* (centaury-flowers). Beatus Rhenanus, by conjecture, suggests *centenariis*, followed by Gagnaeus, Gelenius, and Pamelius. La Cerda conjectures *spontaneis* (wild-growing), which he defends by the Greek word *automata* (self-growing) in Herodotus, and remarks upon the passages brought forward in support of *centenariis*. *Centenariis* is, however, found in the Codex Agobardinus. Herodotus, Book 8.138: "Those who arrived in another land of Macedonia lived near the gardens said to belong to Midas, son of Gordias, in which roses grow spontaneously, each one having sixty petals, and surpassing others in fragrance." Theophrastus, *On Plants*, 6.6: "hundred-petaled roses." Pliny, *Natural History*, 21.10: "Caepio, in the reign of Tiberius Caesar, denied that the hundred-petaled rose <note>original: "centifolia"</note> should be added to crowns, except at the very ends of the bindings."

Athenaeus, 15.27: "Theophrastus says that lilies are also purple-flowered. Philinus says the lily is called *leirion* by some, and *ion* (violet) by others."
⁶ *all types of violets*, namely: purple, yellow, and white. Pliny, *Natural History*, 21.14.
⁷ *honeycombs after gall*. Proverbial.
Chapter XV. ¹ *meadow. They sit.* <note>original: "prato. Sedent."</note> So the Codex Agobardinus, Rigaltius, and Oehler. Others read *Protosedent* or *proto sedent*. Ursinus by conjecture reads *Porro sedent* (furthermore they sit). Rigaltius explains "celestial meadow" as a synonym for the rainbow, "on account of its appearance, which is green like an emerald." Greek: "and a rainbow."
