<margin>Chapter XIV.</margin>
...repay Him as best you can with such a head as He offered for yours; or at least do not crown yourself with flowers, if you cannot crown yourself with thorns—for you cannot wear flowers [while He wore thorns].

<margin>
CHAPTER XV.
Christ will hereafter crown his saints, as he crowns his angels. Look for no other crown but that which is eternal in the heavens.
Revelation 2:7, 10.
2 Timothy 4:7, 8.
Revelation 6:2.
Revelation 10:1.
Revelation 4:4.
Revelation 14:14.
</margin>
Keep for God His own property <note>Tertullian views the human body, specifically the head, as God's property which should not be defiled by pagan customs.</note> undefiled. He will crown it if He wills; indeed, He even desires it and invites us to it. "To him who overcomes," He says, "I will give the crown of life." Be faithful even unto death, and you too must fight the good fight, for which the Apostle [Paul] rightly trusted that a crown was laid up for him. Even the angel of victory receives a crown, riding forth on a white horse to conquer; and another is adorned with a rainbow, like a heavenly meadow¹. The elders also sit crowned, and the Son of Man Himself shines above a cloud with the same gold. If such images are seen in the vision, what must the truths be in their actual representation! Gaze upon those, and breathe in their scent. Why do you condemn your head—which is destined for a royal diadem—to a headband² or a snake-shaped ornament³? For Christ Jesus has made us kings to God and His Father. <margin>Revelation 5:10.</margin> What have you to do with a flower that is destined to die? You have the flower⁴ from the rod [of Jesse] <margin>Isaiah 11:1.</margin>

---

¹ <note>original Greek: "round about the throne like an emerald to look upon." (Revelation 4:3).</note>

² *headband.* Pliny, *Natural History* XXI. 2: "The ancients used thinner ones, calling them *stropi*, from which the word *strophiola* [little headbands] was born."

³ *snake-shaped ornament.* <term>Dracontaria</term> were circlets of gold in the form of serpents worn on the neck and arms and sometimes (as Tertullian implies) on the head. Heraldus was the first to point this out, quoting Lucian’s *Affairs of the Heart*, chapter 41: <note>original Greek: "Those snakes around the wrists and arms—how I wish they were real snakes instead of gold!"</note> La Cerda quotes from Clement of Alexandria’s *The Instructor*, Book II, last chapter: <note>original Greek: "They are not even ashamed to wear the most obvious symbols of the Evil One [the Serpent]. For just as the serpent deceived Eve,"</note>

<column-break/>

<note>original Greek: "so too has this golden jewelry driven other women to madness and arrogance, using the shape of the serpent as a lure. The comic poet Nicostratus lists them: chains, necklaces, rings, bracelets, snakes, anklets, and hellebore [a medicinal plant]."</note> and Jerome’s letter to Marcella: "When she first took up this holy purpose, she sold the gold from her neck—which the common people call a *Muraenula* <note>A "little moray eel," a type of flexible, wavy gold chain.</note>—because it is a chain of metal woven into a winding, flexible pattern, and she did this without her parents' involvement."

⁴ *flower.* Isaiah 11:1, according to the Greek Septuagint: <note>original Greek: "And there shall come forth a rod out of the root of Jesse, and a flower shall rise up out of that root."</note>

<summary>Tertullian concludes his treatise by contrasting the temporary, dying flowers of earthly crowns with the eternal, golden crowns of the Apocalypse. He specifically warns against snake-shaped jewelry (dracontaria), viewing it as a symbol of the devil who deceived Eve.</summary>

<meta>Continuing from page 157, Tertullian is concluding his argument by contrasting the fading floral crowns of Roman culture with the eternal "flower" of Christ. He uses the mystery cult of Mithras—popular among the Roman military—as a stinging example of discipline that Christian soldiers ought to emulate or exceed.</meta>

## CHAPTER XV.
...of Jesse <note>The text continues from the previous page, identifying Christ as the "flower" springing from the root of Jesse, a common Messianic reference from Isaiah 11:1.</note>, upon whom the full grace of the Divine Spirit rested—that incorruptible, unfading, eternal flower. By choosing this flower, the good soldier has been promoted in heavenly honor and rank⁵. Blush, you Roman fellow-soldiers of His! You are destined to be judged not by Christ Himself, but by some soldier of Mithras⁶. For when such a soldier is initiated in a cave—which is truly a camp of darkness—a crown is offered to him on the point of a sword as a kind of mockery of martyrdom. Then, as it is placed upon his head, he is instructed to push it away with his hand and perhaps shift it to his shoulder, declaring that Mithras is his crown. From that moment on, he never wears a crown, and he keeps this as a mark to prove his character if he is ever tested regarding his oath <term>sacramentum: the sacred oath of allegiance sworn by Roman soldiers</term>. He is immediately believed to be a soldier of Mithras if he throws down a crown and says that his crown resides in his god. Let us recognize the cleverness of the devil, who mimics certain aspects of divine things for the purpose of shaming us and judging us by the faithfulness of his own followers.

---

⁵ *has been promoted in heavenly honor and rank.* This lack of connecting words is common in Tertullian's writing. The Agobard Codex (followed by Oehler) omits the word *dignatione* (honor). Rigaltius reads "has been promoted to honor in the ranks of heaven," which was translated by Dodgson as: "hath been promoted to honour in the ranks of heaven."

⁶ *Mithras*. The Persians worshipped the sun under the name of Mithras. See Bähr’s notes on Herodotus i. 131, and Barthius’s notes on Statius's *Thebaid* i. 719: <note>original: "seu Persei sub rupibus antri Indignata sequi torquentem cornua Mithram"</note> "or Mithras, beneath the rocks of a Persian cave, who indignant at following, twists the horns [of the bull]." Herodotus mentions "Mitra"

<column-break/>

as a synonym for Venus; and some suppose that the Persians worshipped the sun as Mithras, and the moon as Mithra. The word Mithras constantly forms part of Persian proper names, such as *Mithridates, Mitrobates, Ithamitres, Siromitres*, and the like. Compare *On Prescription Against Heretics*, chapter 40: <note>original: "Et si adhuc memini, Mithra signat illic in frontibus milites suos ; celebrat panis oblationem, et imaginem resurrectionis inducit, et sub gladio redimit coronam."</note> "And if I remember correctly, Mithras marks his soldiers there on their foreheads; he celebrates an offering of bread, introduces a representation of the resurrection, and earns back a crown at the point of a sword." Also *Against Marcion* book i, chapter 13: <note>original: "sicut aridæ et ardentis naturæ sacramenta leones Mithræ philosophantur."</note> "just as the 'lions' of Mithras practice the mysteries of a dry and burning nature." <note>The "Lions" were a specific grade of initiation within the Mithraic mysteries.</note>

<summary>Tertullian concludes his treatise by shaming Christian soldiers who wear crowns, pointing out that even followers of the pagan god Mithras refuse crowns to show total devotion to their deity.</summary>
<keywords>Mithras, Jesse, Christ as Flower, Roman Army, Mystery Cults, Martyrdom, Sacramentum, Initiation Rites</keywords>
